Practical View: These "Non-Core" Elements Are Often the Pain Points

Although these items fall outside the main scope of this guide, they often cause problems in real engineering design:

  • Fire protection: sprinkler systems inside cleanrooms are a source of contamination and need special design (for example, pre-action systems).
  • Egress routes: emergency exits must not defeat the cleanroom pressure differential system, yet they must still meet building codes.
  • Noise: HVAC systems, especially high-grade HEPA fans, may exceed 85 dB.

Analogy: The "Hidden Costs" of Buying a House

Just as you cannot look only at the price of a house and must also consider management fees, parking and neighborhood security, the same applies to sterile facility design: if needs such as fire protection, egress and noise control are discovered only late in design, the cost of rework will be very high.

S

Section Summary

Key takeaways from Sections 2.6–2.10

Key Takeaways

  1. Harmonized Classification: Three parallel systems exist globally (EU Grade A-D, ISO 5/7/8, old US Class 100/10K/100K). Facilities serving multiple markets must design to the most conservative requirement across all applicable regulations.
  2. At Rest vs In Operation: EU Annex 1 defines limits for both conditions; US FDA is primarily "in operation." This distinction affects classification strategy, especially for Grade D areas.
  3. CNC Designation: "Controlled Not Classified" areas are increasingly common for support functions where formal classification is not required but access control and basic cleanliness are maintained.
  4. Operator Protection: Engineered controls (containment, isolators, automation) are preferred over PPE. The distinction between hazard and risk is fundamental to designing appropriate protection.
  5. Open vs Closed Processing: Open processes require ISO 5/Grade A at the point of exposure; closed processes can operate with Grade D background. The choice has significant cost and design implications.
  6. Isolator Advantage: Isolators allow background environment reduction from ISO 7/Grade B to ISO 8/Grade C while maintaining ISO 5/Grade A at the critical zone.
  7. Integrated Design: Personnel flow, material flow, zoning, and segregation must be designed holistically. The facility is a system, not a collection of isolated rooms.
  8. Lifecycle Cost: Higher initial investment in quality materials and design may yield lower total cost over the facility lifecycle through reduced maintenance, downtime, and energy consumption.

Key Takeaways

  1. Harmonized classification: three systems run in parallel (EU Grade A-D, ISO 5/7/8, legacy US Class). For multinational markets, the strictest standard must be adopted.
  2. At rest vs in operation: the EU defines both conditions, while the US focuses on in operation. The difference in Grade D between the EU and the US is a design trap.
  3. CNC areas: controlled but not classified, suitable for support areas such as testing and terminal sterilization.
  4. Personnel protection: engineering controls > administrative controls > PPE, the golden rule of the protection hierarchy.
  5. Open vs closed: closed processing can greatly reduce background environment requirements, but system integrity must be demonstrated.
  6. Isolator advantage: the background drops from ISO 7 to ISO 8 while the critical zone stays at ISO 5.
  7. Integrated design: personnel flow, material flow, zoning and isolation must be considered as a whole; a facility is a system, not a set of isolated rooms.
  8. Life-cycle cost: a high-quality initial investment may bring a lower total cost of ownership.

Self-Check List

  • Can I state which ISO class each of Grade A/B/C/D corresponds to?
  • Do I understand the difference between "at rest" and "in operation" and its impact on design?
  • Can I explain why an isolator allows the background environment to be downgraded?
  • Can I distinguish open from closed processing and state the environmental requirements of each?
  • Do I understand the importance of separating personnel and material flows in integrated design?
2a

Chapter 2a: 3a. Process Equipment (3.1–3.2.3)

p37-p49

ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 3 (3rd Ed.) | p37 – p49

Learning Objectives

  1. Understand the principles for selecting and integrating process equipment in sterile manufacturing, and master the seven considerations: performance, functionality, construction, instrumentation, air quality, layout and services
  2. Master the typical sterile product process flow (from compounding to inspection), distinguish aseptic processing from terminal sterilization, and understand the key risk factors for bioburden control
  3. Understand centralized versus decentralized design strategies for compounding/weighing operations, as well as cross-contamination control measures and the choice of weighing method
  4. Understand the requirements for maintaining sterility of components after sterilization, including transfer methods, wrapping strategies and the principles for maintaining an ISO 5/Grade A environment

Section Navigation

3.1 Introduction 3.2 Process Description 3.2.1 Dispensing & Weighing 3.2.2 Post-Sterilization Aseptic Control 3.2.3 Compounding Section Summary
3.1

Introduction

Process Equipment Considerations Overview | p37–p38

Original Text

3.1 Introduction

This chapter focuses on process equipment aspects. The use of integrated component washing, depyrogenation, siliconizing, and transport technology should be considered where applicable and feasible.

Process descriptions are provided to assist in understanding the process equipment considerations. Detailed User Requirements Specification (URS) documents should be the defining source for process equipment requirements and operating parameters. For catalog equipment, use of a data sheet in lieu of a URS may be acceptable.

The information contained within this chapter is intended to:

  • Recommend baseline practices intended to apply to sterile processes
  • Inform the facility design team of typical sterile product manufacturing schemes
  • Provide points for consideration in selecting sterile processing equipment
  • Provide points for consideration when integrating sterile processing equipment into the facility design

Section 3.2 provides a general description of each process stage and some aspects of process equipment selection for typical aseptic processing and processing with terminal sterilization. Illustrative process flows for both schemes, aseptic processing and terminally sterilized, are provided in Figure 3.1 and Figure 3.2, respectively.

Section 3.2 also includes information on equipment selection for isolators, and reference is made to RABS selection and to BFS operations. The use of separation and customization to supplement processes that allow direct personnel interventions should be utilized to the extent possible to minimize intervention impact.

General Points for Equipment Selection and Integration

  • Performance: This may include more detailed capacity attributes, but also covers specification of machine performance criteria, which controls product and container quality and cleanliness. Consideration should also be given to the extent of aseptic preparation activities that are routinely required for production use, due to the potential adverse impact of these manipulations on product sterility.
  • Functionality: This includes key functional attributes, such as the ability to maintain equipment from outside critical areas. Sampling and access points for qualification and validation testing should be incorporated in the equipment design.
  • Construction: This includes the durability, cleanability, and sterilizability of the materials of construction of the equipment that may contact product. Release of particulate from surfaces inside the cleanroom during operating and cleaning can be detrimental to the process; materials should be selected to minimize release.
  • Instrumentation: This includes a consideration of process parameter criticality and, therefore, the need for instrumented monitoring/detection. Instrumentation also may support a Process Analytical Technology (PAT) approach.
  • Air Quality: Equipment location within the facility is controlled by process and material flows, the criticality of operations performed, and by the consequent requirements for local and room air quality control. When designing an HVAC system, the heat loads and the particle generation from both operators and equipment should be considered along with humidity requirements.
  • Layout: Where possible, facility layouts should be designed to support functionality of the process equipment. Personnel and material flows needed for a particular process significantly affect the equipment layout and, therefore, the overall facility layout.
  • Services: Definition of both the instantaneous and daily demands of the equipment and on connecting services should be considered to support the sizing of the supporting services infrastructure. Consideration should be given to designs that allow maintenance access without impacting critical process areas.
Commentary and Practical Analysis

Key Points of This Section

This chapter is the core process equipment chapter of ISPE Vol.3 and sets out the overall framework for equipment selection. Rather than listing specific brands or models, it offers a systematic way of thinking that gives the design team clear dimensions for evaluating equipment.

Core Concept: The URS Is the Foundation of Equipment Specification

The User Requirements Specification (URS) is the starting point for equipment procurement and design. The URS defines "what we need the equipment to do", not "what the equipment can do".

For catalog equipment, a data sheet may replace a full URS, but you still need to confirm that the specification meets the process requirements.

Analogy: The Seven-Axis Radar Chart for Equipment Selection

Think of equipment selection as a fitness assessment for an athlete: you cannot look at a single metric. The seven considerations proposed by ISPE (performance, functionality, construction, instrumentation, air quality, layout, services) are like the seven axes of a radar chart, and each one must meet a minimum standard to ensure overall suitability.

Key Point: Summary of the Seven Equipment Selection Considerations

  • Performance: Look beyond throughput to the machine's ability to control product quality and the complexity of the aseptic preparation operations
  • Functionality: Can maintenance be performed from outside the clean area? Are sampling points and validation ports designed in?
  • Construction: Product contact surface materials must be durable, cleanable, sterilizable and low in particle shedding
  • Instrumentation: Critical process parameters must be monitorable, and PAT can monitor quality in real time
  • Air Quality: HVAC design must account for the heat load and particle generation of equipment and personnel
  • Layout: People and material flows determine equipment layout, and equipment layout determines facility layout
  • Services: Instantaneous and daily utility demands must be matched, and maintenance access should not affect critical process areas

CDMO Perspective

For a CDMO, the "functionality" consideration is especially important in equipment selection:

  • Multi-product flexibility: Equipment must be able to switch quickly between container formats (vials, prefilled syringes, cartridges) and between products
  • Changeover efficiency: Changeover time directly affects capacity utilization, and CIP/SIP capability is key
  • Validation burden: Each new client product requires additional equipment validation, so consider the scalability of validation when selecting equipment
3.2

Process Description

Sterile Dosage Form Process Stages | p38–p42

Original Text

3.2 Process Description

The model process flow adopted as the basis of this chapter is that of a typical vial formulation, either aseptically processed or terminally sterilized. Designers may use this as the basis for design conditions for other processes and presentations—for example, APIs in bags or drums, glass or plastic ampoules, or syringes.

The general list of process stages for a sterile dosage form (not including equipment contact parts cleaning and preparation) is:

  • Dispensing
  • Post-sterilization aseptic control of components/change parts
  • Compounding (including aseptic compounding or buffer preparation, when applicable)
  • Sterile filtration
  • Sterile product bulk holding
  • Container preparation
  • Closure preparation
  • Transfer of components and equipment into aseptic area or across the isolator boundary
  • Filling and sealing
  • Transfer of uncrimped vials within aseptic area (for lyophilized product, transfer of partially stoppered vials from the filling line to lyophilizer, with subsequent transfer/unloading of fully stoppered, uncrimped vials)
  • BFS
  • Lyophilization, if applicable (this step is not assumed for terminally sterilized products)
  • Capping and crimping
  • Coding and code checking
  • Terminal sterilization
  • Inspection (may include cosmetic, particulate, container integrity, head space analysis, etc.)
  • Secondary packaging
  • Cleaning, sterilization and sanitization

Note: Application of continuous processing, automation and advanced processing techniques can eliminate or combine many of the above steps, to provide superior sterility assurance. For example:

  • For BFS, container/closure preparation and filling/stoppering are performed within the BFS filling machine.
  • For sterile APIs, it is usual for process steps—that is, from sterilize-in-place (SIP) of the process train through sterile bulk holding—to be truly closed, relying on the integrity of the closed system and of the associated cleaning and SIP techniques to ensure sterility.
  • Use of pre-sterilized, ready-to-use components can eliminate cleaning, sterilization, and aseptic staging steps for containers and closures.

Terminally Sterilized Products

Terminally sterilized products do not require the same level of environmental control as aseptically processed products. Despite these reduced requirements, steps should be taken to reduce the risk of introducing bioburden and/or endotoxin to the product. These steps commonly include sterilization and depyrogenation of components, sterilizing grade or bioburden reduction filtration of solution, and provision of LP/GAAS for filling operations. Bioburden control is particularly important when the terminal sterilization process has been validated for a specific bioburden, rather than using a standard overkill approach.

The background environment for filling should be ISO 8/Grade C, at a minimum.

Regulated companies may fill terminally sterilized products on the same production line as aseptically filled products, because of available production capacity. Aseptic environmental controls are then applied to maintain the more rigorous conditions required for aseptic filling of lyophilized product. However, this practice should not be construed as meaning that these controls are necessary for terminally sterilized products.

A documented risk assessment is recommended, to fully understand potential risks to a product.

Conditions that Elevate Bioburden Risk

  • Slow filling operations, including manual filling, where product and container/closure components are exposed to the environment for sustained durations
  • Open filling lines where operators are in close proximity to critical surfaces, product, and container/closure components
  • Use of semi-manual fill lines which require routine operator intervention
  • Long fill durations with products that are susceptible to bioburden; bulk bioburden reduction filtration may reduce bioburden levels and/or extend the allowable filling interval
  • Extended hold times prior to any pre-filtration or filling step

These risk factors can generally be mitigated through application of commonly available technology, such as automated filling systems with appropriate barrier technology.

Commentary and Practical Analysis

The Whole Process: From Weighing to Packaging

This section describes the complete flow of a typical vial process. Although the vial is used as the model, designers can extend it to other container formats such as prefilled syringes, ampoules and flexible bags.

Weighing/Dispensing → Compounding/Formulation → Sterile Filtration → Bulk Solution Hold → Filling/Stoppering → Lyophilization (if applicable) → Capping/Crimping → Inspection → Packaging

Key Point: Five Situations That Raise Bioburden Risk

  1. Slow filling/manual filling: Long product exposure time multiplies the contamination risk
  2. Open filling lines: Operators work close to critical surfaces, and personnel are the biggest source of contamination
  3. Semi-automated filling lines: Routine operator interventions are required
  4. Long filling duration: For microbiologically sensitive products, risk accumulates over long batches
  5. Long holds before filtration/filling: Microorganisms may proliferate during the hold

Mitigation: An automated filling system combined with appropriate barrier technology (RABS/isolator) is the most effective risk control measure.

Analogy: How Advanced Technology Simplifies the Process

Think of a traditional process as cooking in an open-air kitchen, where every step is exposed to the environment. BFS (blow-fill-seal) technology is like forming, filling and sealing the container in one continuous run inside a sealed vending machine, greatly reducing contamination risk. Likewise, using presterilized ready-to-use (RTU) components is like using disinfected disposable tableware directly, which saves you the washing and disinfecting steps.

Discussion Questions

  • A company manufactures both terminally sterilized products and aseptically filled products. Why can they share the same filling line, and which standard should be the design basis when sharing?
  • If your product is a nano-medicine, why does ISPE suggest that repeated bioburden reduction filtration may be needed?
  • In the lyophilized product process flow shown in Figure 3.3, which steps are specific to lyophilized products and not needed for liquid products?

CDMO Perspective

A CDMO equipment strategy needs to pay particular attention to the challenges of "shared lines":

  • Product scheduling logic: Terminally sterilized products are usually scheduled after aseptically filled products because the cleaning validation requirements differ
  • Environmental control switching: A shared line means always maintaining the highest standard (ISO 5), which raises operating cost but simplifies management
  • Documented risk assessments: Each client's product needs its own documented risk assessment, and document management is a major challenge
3.2.1

Dispensing and Weighing

Raw Material Handling Strategies | p42–p44

Original Text

3.2.1 Dispensing and Weighing

Components that undergo a subsequent sterilization step (e.g., filtration or terminal sterilization) are normally dispensed in an ISO 8/Grade C environment, at a minimum, with local protection (such as High Efficiency Particulate Air (HEPA) filtered unidirectional air) and the use of aseptic technique. The air cleanliness classification within the dispensary depends upon the process and product.

Consideration should be given to operator protection and mitigation of cross-contamination risk. In cases where additional separation/containment technologies (e.g., gloveboxes or isolators) are used for handling sensitive or high potency materials, lower background grade classifications may be appropriate.

Aseptically processed products that cannot be sterile filtered (e.g., sterile powders or suspensions) should be dispensed in an ISO 5/Grade A environment. In such cases, operator segregation via use of separation technology is generally considered to be necessary.

Two major concepts are generally applied in the industry for dispensing:

  • Centralized dispensing
  • Decentralized dispensing

Centralized dispensing is usually confined to solid actives and excipients. Decentralized dispensing is usually used for liquids (water, solvents, pH adjustment solutions), which are dispensed within the production areas (compounding room).

Advantages of Centralized Dispensing

  • It identifies dispensing as a separate process step that needs to be controlled.
  • It is easier to maintain a good working environment for operators.
  • Specialists with specific training and experience can be dedicated to one dispensing area, thereby reducing risk of mix-ups.

Advantages of Decentralized Dispensing

  • If compounding is for a single product, the risk of mix-ups and cross-contamination should be reduced, as only the specified raw materials are handled.
  • High hazard materials, that need to be contained (e.g., handled in gloveboxes) to protect operators, may be easier to control in a decentralized dispensing approach.

Liquid Measurement Methods

  • Gravimetric measurement may be performed using load cell(s), a balance, or a floor scale. The effect that attached components (cables, hoses, filter housing, valves) can have on the linearity and accuracy of the weighing range should be considered.
  • Volumetric measurement may be performed with flow meters or guided wave radar systems. If these types of instruments are used, calibration and desired accuracy should be reviewed.

Risk Reduction Methods for Cross-Contamination

  • Use of dedicated HVAC systems to handle airborne powders
  • Physical separation of dispensing areas
  • Cleaning (and inactivation, where appropriate) regime between products
  • System to separate dirty dispensing utilities from clean ones
  • System to compensate for room pressure changes due to loading of HVAC powder capture filters
  • Use of single-use disposable containers and weighing utensils
  • Use of appropriate local exhaust ventilation at point of generation sources

Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) software may be used to control and track raw materials; these systems can be particularly advantageous for high volume operations that use many different types of raw materials.

Commentary and Practical Analysis

Weighing/Dispensing: The Starting Point of the Process

Weighing looks simple, but it is the first step in the process that can introduce cross-contamination. The environmental requirements depend on whether a later sterilization step can "make up for" it.

Key Point: Pitfalls in Choosing a Weighing Method

Gravimetric considerations:

  • Piping, valves and filter housings connected to the vessel affect the linearity and accuracy of the weight measurement
  • The fill state of the cooling/heating medium in a jacketed vessel also affects the weight reading

Volumetric considerations:

  • The accuracy of guided wave radar is affected by vessel design and batch size
  • Flow meters need regular calibration, and fluid properties affect the measurement result

Analogy: Centralized Weighing Is Like a Central Kitchen

Centralized weighing is like a restaurant central kitchen, where professional chefs prepare ingredients in one place and reduce errors. Decentralized weighing is like a self-serve table where each diner picks up food: it suits a single dish (a single product) but becomes confusing with many dishes. For highly hazardous ingredients (high-potency drugs), decentralized is actually better because strict control can be applied in a dedicated area.

Key Point: Seven Lines of Defense for Cross-Contamination Control

  1. Dedicated HVAC system to handle dust
  2. Physical segregation of the weighing area
  3. Between-product cleaning (including deactivation) procedures
  4. Clean/dirty utensil segregation system
  5. Pressure differential compensation for dust collection filter loading
  6. Single-use containers and weighing tools
  7. Local exhaust at the point of generation

An ERP system can provide real-time inventory status, an electronic traceability matrix and barcode tracking, greatly reducing the risk of weighing errors.

CDMO Perspective

  • Biggest challenge in multi-product facilities: APIs and excipients from different clients are handled alternately in the same weighing area, and cross-contamination risk is an audit focus
  • Trend toward high-potency drugs: More and more clients are outsourcing high-potency products such as ADCs (antibody-drug conjugates), which require glove boxes or isolators, and the investment decision must be planned early
  • Single-use system (SUS) strategy: Disposable weighing containers and tools simplify cleaning validation but increase consumable costs, so a CDMO must weigh this in each client contract

Core Concept: The Logic for Deciding the Weighing Environment Grade

Key principle: where no later "kill step" can catch a problem, the front end must be made as strict as possible.

3.2.2

Post-Sterilization Aseptic Control of Components/Change Parts

Maintaining Sterility After Sterilization | p44–p45

Original Text

3.2.2 Post-Sterilization Aseptic Control of Components/Change Parts

For equipment that cannot be SIP, equipment and materials should be sterilized through pass-through style heat sterilizers, which open directly into an ISO 5/Grade A zone. Where sterilizers are not directly adjacent to the location where aseptic operations are performed, ISO 5/Grade A continuity should be maintained for the transfer of materials from the sterilizer to the place of storage or use.

Barrier protected carts which have active or passive airflow protection may be used; such carts should be qualified and routinely monitored. Where autoclave and oven carts are withdrawn from the sterilizer chamber into an ISO 7/Grade B room, there should be localized unidirectional ISO 5/Grade A airflow protection at the chamber outlet, so items may remain under these controlled conditions until the load has cooled. See Section 9.5.1 for equipment and component transfer on barrier and isolator style lines.

Autoclaved materials and components should be suitably wrapped to maintain sterile integrity of the contents from the point of removal from the autoclave to the point of use, including any intermediate staging steps. Multiple layer wrappings are recommended, as these provide redundant protection and permit removal of outer layers during transfer of materials into successively cleaner zones. The wrappings should permit air removal, steam ingress, and condensate removal as required for effective sterilization. Examples of suitable covering types include Tyvek, nonwoven Spunbond/Melt-blown/Spunbond (SMS) fabric sterilization wraps, sterilization bags, etc.

Items that are pre-sterilized by other methods, such as gamma irradiation or ethylene oxide, should be protected with appropriate wrappings to maintain their sterile integrity from the completion of the sterilization process until transfer into the ISO 5/Grade A environment. These items should be passed into the aseptic area via dedicated interlocked transfer hatches designed to prevent bio-contamination of the ISO 5/Grade A environment.

The packaging should be subjected to thorough surface disinfection—for example, using liquid chemical, VHP, or electron beam (e-beam)—which is validated for the control of bio-contamination of the ISO 5/Grade A environment. The transfer of the wrapped items into the ISO 5/Grade A zone should be performed in such a way as to ensure that the outer wrap can be taken off without introducing bio-contamination into the ISO 5/Grade A zone where product, product contact surfaces, containers or closures are exposed.

Commentary and Practical Analysis

Maintaining Sterility After Sterilization: The Most Easily Overlooked Risk

Successful component sterilization is only the starting point. The transfer between removal from the autoclave and actual use is the real test of sterility assurance.

Core Concept: Three Principles for Material Transfer After Sterilization

  1. Continuous ISO 5 protection: From the sterilizer to the point of use, materials remain under ISO 5/Grade A airflow protection at all times
  2. Multi-layer wrapping strategy: Multiple layers of packaging provide redundant protection, and one outer layer is removed on entry to each cleaner area
  3. Interlocked transfer design: Presterilized items enter the aseptic area through an interlocked pass-through, preventing cross-contamination from the environment

Analogy: Dressing in Layers Like an Onion

The multi-layer wrapping strategy is like layered clothing for hiking, where each layer has a specific function. The outermost layer is the soil barrier (worn in the non-clean area), the middle layer is the protective layer, and the innermost layer is the sterile layer (opened last, in the ISO 5 area). Each time you move into a cleaner area, it is like going from outdoors to indoors and taking off a jacket.

Core Concept: The Dual Requirements of Wrapping Materials

Sterilization wrapping materials must meet two seemingly contradictory requirements at the same time:

  • Sterilant penetration: They must allow air removal, steam penetration and condensate removal (otherwise sterilization is incomplete)
  • Microbial barrier: After sterilization they must block the ingress of microorganisms (otherwise sterility is compromised)

Common materials: Tyvek (DuPont), SMS nonwoven sterilization wraps, sterilization pouches, etc. The microporous structure of these materials lets steam through but blocks microorganisms.

Discussion Questions

  • Why must local ISO 5/Grade A airflow protection be provided at the exit when an autoclave cart is removed from the sterilizer into an ISO 7/Grade B room?
  • If you use presterilized ready-to-use (RTU) syringe components, what is the key challenge in validating surface disinfection?
  • How does a "barrier protected cart" achieve both material protection and operational convenience?

CDMO Perspective

  • Strategic value of RTU components: For a CDMO, using presterilized ready-to-use containers and stoppers greatly reduces the investment in washing/sterilization equipment and the validation burden, while also shortening product changeover time
  • Post-sterilization hold management: With multi-client product scheduling, managing the hold time of sterilized materials is a challenge, requiring clear maximum hold time limits and a tracking system
  • Pass-through sterilizer layout: In CDMO facility design, the location of pass-through autoclaves/ovens directly affects operating efficiency across multiple filling lines
3.2.3

Compounding

Formulation and Mixing Operations | p45–p49

Original Text

3.2.3 Compounding

The purpose of compounding is to formulate together API, excipients, and solvent components, to be subsequently filled. This may involve simple liquid mixing or dissolution of a solid active. It also may include more complex operations such as emulsification or liposome formation. Water for Injection (WFI) should be used as the solvent for most aqueous-based sterile products. Low endotoxin purified water is sometimes used for sterile ophthalmic and nasal products.

Product contacting surfaces of equipment and components (such as vessels, housings, and process piping) should be cleaned prior to use. See Section 3.2.15 for additional details on cleaning and sterilization.

If the subsequent compounding is an aseptic process, process equipment should be sterilized using a validated sterilizing cycle. The integrity of the sterile boundary should be ensured from the completion of sterilization through the end of processing.

Air cleanliness and cross-contamination prevention should be considered. Use of localized HEPA (ISO 5/Grade A air supply) protection is recommended to protect non-sterile product contact surfaces areas (e.g., vessel openings), where possible. For example, in many cases HEPA filters required to meet area cleanliness classifications can be located over tank manways, to reduce risk of contamination of product contact surfaces.

When handling dry powders, the design should minimize release of any fine particles into the air. Use of containment devices may be appropriate.

If, for product reasons, an aseptically processed product cannot be sterile filtered or sterilized by some other means (e.g., bulk heat) after compounding, then the charging of raw materials should be performed in an ISO 5/Grade A environment, preferably using a RABS or closed isolator. Special consideration should be given to the airflow inside the barrier when handling fine powders, as air speeds lower than 0.45 meters/second might be beneficial to better control the process.

Compounding Sequence

Compounding is normally performed in the following sequence:

  • Solvent, usually water, is metered into the compounding tank, to a pre-determined level that is less than the final batch size.
  • Excipients and API in powder or liquid form are charged into the compounding tank in a specified sequence.
  • The solution is mixed to make a homogenous solution.
  • Additional solvent is added, if necessary, to achieve the desired concentration and final batch size.

Additional steps such as temperature adjustment, pH adjustment, or oxygen displacement may be required during formulation. Sample collection should be performed only as required for in-process measurements or testing, to minimize risk of contamination of the bulk solution. Equipment for sampling should be easily cleaned.

Compounding Area Design Considerations

  • Powder handling may create airborne particulates. Airflows should be carefully managed to reduce the risk of cross-contamination and harmful exposure to operators. Use of Computational Fluid Dynamic (CFD) simulation(s) may be of benefit for optimizing airflow patterns.
  • Biologically active substances should not be vented to the atmosphere.
  • The compounding area should be easy to clean.
  • If tanks are to be sterilized, vents on tanks should be fitted with gas/vent filters of sterilizing grade that are arranged to facilitate integrity testing.

Use of flammable solvents in the formulation process requires specialized design activities to ensure personnel and facility safety.

Commentary and Practical Analysis

Compounding: Turning Raw Materials into a Fillable Solution

Compounding is the step of mixing the API, excipients and solvent according to the formulation. It covers everything from simple dissolution to complex emulsification or liposome preparation.

Core Concept: Choosing the Water for Compounding

  • Water for Injection (WFI): The standard solvent for most aqueous sterile products, with the strictest endotoxin limit
  • Purified water with low endotoxin: Used only for certain ophthalmic and nasal products; this is an exception, not the norm

Basis for selection: The route of administration of the final product determines the water grade. Injectables = WFI; ophthalmic/nasal use = low-endotoxin purified water may be considered.

Core Concept: The "Clean Then Sterilize" Principle for Product Contact Surfaces

All product contact surfaces, including containers, housings and process piping, must be cleaned before use. If an aseptic process follows, they must also be treated with a validated sterilization cycle, and the integrity of the sterile boundary must be maintained from the end of sterilization until the end of the process.

This is the core application of CIP (clean-in-place) and SIP (sterilize-in-place).

Key Point: Special Compounding Requirements for Non-Filterable Products

When a product cannot be sterile filtered because of its physical properties (such as suspensions or liposomes), charging of raw materials must be performed in an ISO 5/Grade A environment, preferably using a RABS or a closed isolator.

The airflow velocity trap in powder handling: When handling fine powders, the airflow velocity inside the isolator may need to be below 0.45 m/s. This runs against the usual intuition that "faster airflow is cleaner", because excessive airflow blows the powder around, which increases contamination risk and affects dosing accuracy.

Analogy: Compounding Is Like a Precise Baking Procedure

The standard compounding sequence is like making a cake: first add water (solvent) to a set quantity, then add the powders in order (excipients and API), mix until uniform, and finally make up with water to the target total. You cannot just dump everything in at once, because the order of addition affects dissolution efficiency and product quality.

Core Concept: Four Design Considerations for the Compounding Area

  1. Dust management: Powder handling generates airborne particles, and CFD (computational fluid dynamics) simulation is needed to optimize airflow patterns
  2. Release of biologically active substances: They must not be released to the atmosphere, so a closed system or suitable exhaust treatment is needed
  3. Cleanability: The compounding area must be easy to clean; this must be built into the design and cannot be fixed afterward
  4. Vessel vent filters: Vents on vessels that require sterilization must be fitted with sterilizing-grade gas filters that are easy to integrity test

Key Point: Balancing the Risk of Sampling

Sampling is a necessary in-process control (IPC) operation, but every sampling event is a contamination risk. ISPE recommends:

  • Sample only when necessary (in-process measurement or testing)
  • Sampling equipment must be easy to clean
  • Sampling points should be designed to minimize the risk of contaminating the solution

Key Parameters: Items That May Need Adjustment During Compounding

  • Temperature adjustment: Some APIs need a specific temperature to dissolve
  • pH adjustment: Acid/base solutions are used to adjust to the target pH range
  • Oxygen displacement: For oxygen-sensitive products, nitrogen is used to displace the headspace and the dissolved oxygen in the solution
  • Concentration adjustment: Solvent is finally added to bring the solution to the target batch size and concentration

Discussion Questions

  • Why is it best to install the HEPA filter in the compounding area directly above the vessel manway? How does this differ from ordinary room unidirectional airflow supply?
  • When compounding with flammable solvents, besides explosion-proof design, what other safety aspects must be considered?
  • If you are compounding a lipid nanoparticle (LNP) product, why can sterile filtration not be used? How should the compounding environment be adjusted?

CDMO Perspective

  • Flexible compounding vessel design: A CDMO needs compounding vessels of different sizes for different batch sizes (from tens of liters to thousands of liters), and mobile vessels or modular designs increase flexibility
  • Scale effects of CIP/SIP validation: Each new client product may require CIP cycle validation for its specific formulation, and residue limits vary by product
  • Opportunity for single-use compounding systems: For small batches or clinical-stage products, single-use mixer bags eliminate the need for CIP/SIP validation and speed up the time from order to production
  • Building capability for complex formulations: As demand grows for complex products such as mRNA vaccines and LNPs, a CDMO needs to invest in specialized compounding equipment such as emulsification and microfluidic mixing
S

Section Summary

Key Takeaways from Sections 3.1–3.2.3

Key Takeaways

Equipment Selection Framework

ISPE Vol.3 Chapter 3 establishes a seven-dimension framework for process equipment selection: Performance, Functionality, Construction, Instrumentation, Air Quality, Layout, and Services. Each dimension must be evaluated against the URS.

Process Flow Understanding

The typical sterile dosage form process involves 18+ discrete stages from dispensing through secondary packaging. Advanced technologies (BFS, RTU components, closed systems) can combine or eliminate steps to improve sterility assurance.

Environmental Requirements

Aseptic processing requires ISO 5/Grade A at the point of fill; terminal sterilization requires ISO 8/Grade C minimum. Bioburden control is critical for both approaches, with five key risk-elevating conditions identified.

Dispensing Strategies

Centralized vs. decentralized dispensing each have advantages depending on product type and facility design. Cross-contamination prevention requires a multi-layered approach including dedicated HVAC, physical separation, and procedural controls.

Post-Sterilization Control

The chain of sterile custody from sterilizer to point of use is maintained through pass-through sterilizers, barrier-protected carts, multi-layer wrapping strategies, and validated surface disinfection procedures.

Compounding Design

Equipment surfaces must be cleaned and sterilized (CIP/SIP). Products that cannot be sterile filtered require ISO 5/Grade A compounding with barrier technology. Airflow speed may need reduction for powder handling.

Key Takeaways

Equipment Selection Framework

Chapter 3 of ISPE Vol.3 establishes a seven-dimension evaluation framework for process equipment selection: performance, functionality, construction, instrumentation, air quality, layout and services. The URS is the starting point for everything.

Overall Process Flow

A typical sterile dosage form process comprises more than 18 discrete steps. Advanced technologies such as BFS, RTU components and closed systems can combine or eliminate steps and raise the level of sterility assurance.

Environmental Grade Logic

The filling point in an aseptic process needs ISO 5/Grade A; terminal sterilization needs at least ISO 8/Grade C. Bioburden control is critical for both approaches.

Choosing the Weighing Strategy

Centralized weighing suits solid raw materials in multi-product facilities; decentralized weighing suits liquids and highly toxic materials. Cross-contamination control requires a systematic approach with multiple lines of defense.

Maintaining the Sterile Chain After Sterilization

Pass-through sterilizers, barrier protected carts, multi-layer wrapping and validated surface disinfection: these four mechanisms ensure the sterility integrity of materials from sterilization to use.

Compounding Area Design

CIP/SIP is the foundation of product contact surface preparation. Non-filterable products must be compounded under ISO 5 with a RABS/isolator. Airflow velocity during powder handling needs special evaluation.

Preview of the Next Section

Starting with Section 3.2.4, the discussion turns to equipment considerations for the core aseptic operations: sterile filtration, filling, stoppering and lyophilization. These are the "critical zone" of sterile manufacturing, and equipment design directly determines the level of product sterility assurance.
