3.2.7 Terminal Sterilization

Original Text — ISPE Baseline Guide

3.2.7 Terminal Sterilization

Terminal sterilization refers to a process within which the product, filled and sealed in its final primary package, is sterilized via moist heat, irradiation, or other suitable method. It is a well-accepted principle that sterile drugs should be manufactured using aseptic processing only when terminal sterilization is not feasible due to instability in the drug formulation.

Design and qualification of terminal sterilization processes is a complex topic. For additional information, refer to USP <1229.2>.

Terminal sterilization can be undertaken as a full overkill process (F0 ≥ 15), or as an adjunct process (F0 ≥ 8) for products that cannot tolerate full overkill exposure. The endpoint objective of both processes is the same — to produce product having a Probability of a Non-Sterile Unit (PNSU) of ≥ 1 in 106. Pre-sterilization bioburden is reduced using validated methods and routinely monitored, in order to achieve this level of sterility assurance for the adjunct process.

Design Factors for Terminal Sterilization

Several factors should be considered when designing a terminal sterilization process:

  • D-value of target organisms: Many products exhibit a protective effect on challenge organisms, increasing the required target F0. This is particularly important for adjunct processes, due to their sub-overkill lethality.
  • Range of F0 for the process: Container type and nominal size, fill volume, autoclave size, autoclave type, and product load pattern all have significant influence on the range of F0 delivered throughout the load. F0 is accumulated during heat up, cool down, and the soak interval at and above 121°C.
  • Maximum allowable pre-sterilization hold time: The time between completion of filling and start of sterilization should be defined, in order to ensure control of pre-sterilization bioburden. The allowable hold times directly impact staging area size requirements and material flow.

For products that are not heat-labile, stability samples may be subjected to single and double terminal sterilization cycles (worst case). Data is generated during stability testing to support additional processing as may be required.

Commentary

Terminal Sterilization Overview

Terminal sterilization is the process of sterilizing a product in its final container after filling and sealing. Common methods include moist heat (steam autoclave), irradiation, and other suitable methods.

Core Principle: Terminal Sterilization First

International regulatory consensus: aseptic processing should be used only when the drug formulation cannot withstand terminal sterilization conditions (for example, heat-labile protein drugs). This reflects the basic logic that if a product can be terminally sterilized, it should not be aseptically processed.

F0 Value and Sterilization Strategy

The F0 value represents the equivalent sterilization time at 121°C:

  • Overkill: F0 ≥ 15 — no knowledge of the product bioburden is required; sterility is assured by a high F0 alone
  • Adjunct process: F0 ≥ 8 — suitable for heat-sensitive products, but requires strict pre-sterilization bioburden monitoring

Both approaches share the same goal: PNSU ≥ 10-6 (no more than one non-sterile unit per million units).

Analogy: Well-Done vs. Medium-Rare Steak

Overkill is like a well-done steak: whatever the quality of the meat, long high-temperature cooking will cook it through. Adjunct is like a medium-rare steak: you must be sure the meat source is of excellent quality (low bioburden) before a shorter cooking time can be considered safe.

Key Design Point: D-Value and F0 Distribution

The product solution may "protect" microorganisms (for example, high viscosity or high protein content), requiring a higher F0. In addition, F0 differs between locations in the autoclave: F0 accumulates during both the heating and cooling phases, but at rates that vary by location. The process design must ensure that the "cold spot" also achieves the required F0.

Facility Impact of Terminal Sterilization

Terminal sterilization also has a significant impact on facility layout/space requirements, process sequence, material flow and equipment flow. Factors for consideration include:

  • Products are often loaded into specialized trays and racks to promote good temperature uniformity, drainage during the cycle, and post-sterilization drying. After completion, they should be transferred into alternate trays or totes for inspection and secondary processing.
  • Terminal sterilization of syringes requires inversion during processing to avoid condensate accumulation in the syringe barrel, and may require de-nesting/re-nesting equipment.
  • Material flow and facility arrangement should be designed to segregate non-sterile and sterile material, such as via pass-through type autoclaves and segregated staging/drying areas.
  • Automated loading and unloading systems can be employed, especially for large volume containers or IV bags. Space requirements can be considerable.
  • Following sterilization, space should be provided for material draining and drying. HVAC equipment should be configured to control latent and sensible heat loads.
  • Container inspection for particulate matter, cosmetic defects, and container integrity should be performed after terminal sterilization, since the process may impact these attributes.
  • Utility requirements for large scale terminal sterilization operations are significant and should be carefully considered during facility design.

Impact on Facility Design

Terminal sterilization has a far-reaching impact on facility layout; it is much more than just placing an autoclave.

Key Facility Considerations

  • Non-sterile/sterile material segregation: Use pass-through autoclaves, with material entering from the non-sterile side and exiting on the sterile side, to maintain clean separation
  • Dedicated trays and return flow: Sterilization trays must be returned to the processing area for reuse, creating a reverse equipment flow
  • Special handling of syringes: Syringes must be inverted during sterilization to prevent condensate from accumulating inside the barrel
  • Drying and holding space: Product needs a draining and drying area after sterilization, and the HVAC system must handle the sensible and latent heat loads from steam
  • Utility loads: Large-scale sterilization operations demand substantial steam, cooling water, and compressed air

CDMO Practical Perspective

For a contract manufacturer, the facility requirements for terminally sterilized products are far greater than for a purely aseptic filling line. Additional holding areas, a dedicated tray inventory, drying rooms, and high-capacity utilities are needed. In capacity planning, autoclave turnaround time (loading, sterilization, cooling, unloading) is often the line bottleneck.

Air Over-Pressure and Container Integrity

During the sterilization of liquid-filled containers, differential pressures between the interior of the containers and the sterilization chamber may potentially impact container integrity. Air over-pressure (air ballasting) is used to minimize the pressure differential between the container and the sterilizer to protect the integrity of the container, especially pre-filled syringes and plastic containers.

The amount of internal overpressure in the container is proportional to the internal temperature and does not remain constant throughout the process. The overpressure component should therefore be adjusted during the course of the cycle.

Autoclave Types

Among the sterilization methods available, moist heat autoclaving is the most widely used. There are several autoclave designs:

  • Air steam mix autoclaves: Clean steam is injected directly into the chamber along with sterile filtered air for overpressure control. Suitable means (fans or air ejector nozzles) are employed for good temperature uniformity. Steam must be of compendial quality. Usually used for small volume materials; load is drier upon unloading.
  • Superheated water shower type units: Water is heated/cooled indirectly using external heat exchangers. A recirculating pumping system sprays water over the product load via nozzle arrays for uniform heating and cooling. Water used as heating medium should be of known quality (e.g., distilled or USP purified water). Usually used for larger volume materials, achieving faster heating/cooling rates and better temperature uniformity.

Air Ballasting and Container Integrity

During high-temperature sterilization, the internal pressure of liquid-filled containers rises with temperature. If the autoclave chamber pressure is lower than the container internal pressure, containers may bulge, burst, or lose seal integrity. Air ballasting is therefore used to balance the pressure difference.

Analogy: Steamer vs. Water Bath

An air-steam mix unit is like a steamer: steam surrounds the product directly, which suits small items but heats large items unevenly. A superheated water shower unit is like a water bath: water transfers heat efficiently and suits large-volume products, but the load is wetter after unloading.

3.2.8 Inspection

Original Text — ISPE Baseline Guide

3.2.8 Inspection

Products intended for parenteral administration in humans are subjected to various regulatory and compendial requirements for visual inspection. USP <790> establishes the expectation that each finished unit is inspected to ensure absence of particulate matter, as well as absence of any container or seal defect that could compromise sterility.

Requirements for final post-manufacture inspection vary depending on the product itself (e.g., lyophilized, liquid, suspension) as well as the primary package type.

The inspection process typically includes:

  • Foreign matter in solution
  • Fill volume
  • Ampoule and BFS container integrity
  • Vial cap/crimp and stopper (presence, color, visible defects)
  • Black spots at the seal of the ampoule
  • Cake appearance (for lyophilized products)

Inspection Process Design

The design of an inspection process should include which inspections to perform and how/when to perform them. A documented product risk profile/assessment should be developed.

In general, inspection operations can be implemented as:

  • In-process test (statistical sampling at defined intervals) during production
  • 100% in-line inspection (semi-automated or automated)
  • Finished product inspection only, 100%
  • Finished product inspection only, AQL basis
Commentary

Inspection Overview

All products intended for human injection must pass visual inspection to ensure they are free of particulate matter and that container closure is intact. USP <790> is the core regulatory basis for visual inspection.

Common Inspection Attributes

  • Foreign matter/particulates: extraneous substances in the solution
  • Fill volume: confirming conformance to the labeled volume
  • Container integrity: ampoule seal, BFS container integrity
  • Cap/crimp: presence and color of the stopper, crimp quality
  • Black spots at the ampoule seal: an indicator of a poor fusion seal
  • Lyophilized cake appearance: whether there is collapse (meltback)

Choosing an Inspection Strategy

Inspection can be implemented at different stages and in different ways:

  • In-process sampling: statistical sampling (low cost but limited coverage)
  • 100% in-line inspection: real-time full inspection, but it reduces line efficiency
  • 100% inspection of finished product: off-line full inspection, requiring additional space and personnel
  • AQL sampling of finished product: sampling according to the acceptable quality limit

CDMO Practical Perspective: Inspection Is a Capacity Bottleneck

At a contract manufacturer, inspection is often the biggest bottleneck on the entire line. A filling machine may output 300-600 vials per minute, while manual inspection can handle only a few dozen vials per minute. The return on investment for automated inspection equipment is very significant for high-volume products, but for a CDMO with many products in small batches, equipment changeover time is also a key consideration.

Factors for Inspection Process Design

Several factors should be considered:

  • Capital cost of inspection equipment
  • Space requirements for inspection equipment (in-line versus decoupled)
  • Impact of product investigations on in-process material flows and reinspection requirements
  • Staffing requirements for automated/high tech equipment, especially for off-shift operations
  • Decreased overall line efficiency for in-line inspections
  • Increased material handling requirements for decoupled inspections
  • Use of PAT to reduce/eliminate inspection for certain attributes (e.g., fill weight)

The specific product and package type dictates which inspections are required. For example, some liquid products are susceptible to bubble formation during filling and require an off-line "relaxation time" or use of a pre-spin system prior to particulate inspection.

For high value products, additional inspection steps and PAT may be justified based on decreased product reject rates. For low value products, finished product inspection(s) may be more cost effective.

Emerging Inspection Technologies

  • X-ray analysis of lyophilized cakes for particulate matter
  • Near Infrared (NIR) analysis of lyophilized cakes for moisture content
  • Headspace Analysis (HSA) for products sealed under vacuum or inert gas

Design Factors and Cost-Effectiveness

Trade-offs Between In-line and Off-line Inspection

  • In-line: reduces material handling, but lowers overall line efficiency (OEE)
  • Off-line (decoupled): does not affect line speed, but requires holding space (WIP) and additional handling personnel

The choice depends on product value, batch size, and facility space constraints.

PAT (process analytical technology) can monitor certain attributes in real time (such as fill weight), reducing or eliminating the need for off-line inspection of those attributes.

Emerging Inspection Technologies

  • X-ray analysis: detects invisible particles in lyophilized cakes
  • Near-infrared (NIR): non-destructive measurement of moisture content in lyophilized cakes
  • Headspace analysis (HSA): confirms container closure integrity (CCI) of containers sealed under vacuum or inert gas

These technologies should be evaluated case by case for inclusion in the inspection process.

Analogy: Bubbles vs. Particles

Some liquid products generate bubbles after filling, and automated inspection can misread these bubbles as particles. It is like a freshly poured soda: you need to wait for the bubbles to dissipate (relaxation time) or spin the container first (pre-spin) so the bubbles rise out, before real foreign matter can be detected accurately.

3.2.8.1 Visual Inspection

3.2.8.1 Visual Inspection

Many inspection criteria for products are visual; for example, "essentially free of visible particulate matter" or criteria based on product appearance/color or lyophilized cake appearance. Therefore, establishing a manual inspection baseline and challenge sets is important for training/qualification of human inspectors and for adjustment/qualification of automated equipment.

Manual inspection capability is also required when investigating production anomalies or high reject rates from automated equipment. A manual inspection capability should be developed and maintained.

Defect Library

Establishing and maintaining a defect library is required for construction and maintenance of challenge sets. Considerations include:

  • The library should consist of actual defects as well as defect photos or videos. Clear, written descriptions of defect types should be provided.
  • The library should include examples of each type of defect, with a focus on critical defects. Where possible, examples should be obtained from actual production rejects.
  • The quality of defects degrades over time due to repeated handling, so the library should be continuously refreshed with new reject material. This is particularly important for lyophilized products.

Factors Influencing Inspection

  • Human capabilities
  • Process and environmental conditions
  • Defect type and characteristics (particle size, color, shape, movement)
  • Product characteristics and package type

The Knapp methodology classifies containers based on their Probability of Rejection (PR):

  • Reject: 0.7071 < PR < 1.0
  • Gray Zone: 0.30 < PR < 0.7071
  • Accept: 0 < PR < 0.30

The security of rejecting "must-reject" containers is the Reject Zone Efficiency (RZE). Manual and automatic inspection processes should be qualified to ensure adequate removal of reject containers (high RZE) and acceptably low false reject rates.

Visual Inspection Methods

Many inspection criteria are inherently visual, such as "essentially free of visible particulates" or lyophilized cake appearance. It is therefore extremely important to establish a manual inspection baseline and challenge sets.

Defect Library

The defect library is the foundation of the inspection system:

  • Contains actual defect samples, photographs/videos, and written descriptions
  • Focuses on collecting examples of critical defects
  • Samples deteriorate through repeated handling and must be continually refreshed; defect samples of lyophilized products in particular degrade more easily

Key Point: Balancing RZE and False Reject Rate

The inspection system must meet two objectives at once: (1) a sufficiently high RZE to ensure that truly defective units are rejected; and (2) a sufficiently low false reject rate to avoid wasting acceptable product. The false reject rate can be reduced through a reinspection strategy (reinspection of 1x rejects), provided the combined RZE still meets the target.

Knapp Methodology: Container Classification

Reject zone efficiency (RZE) measures the proportion of defective containers that must be rejected that are actually rejected successfully.

3.2.8.2 Operator Qualification

3.2.8.2 Operator Qualification

Operator qualification and training programs are required for manual and semi-automated inspection processes. Considerations include:

  • Inspectors should be qualified using a manual test set having a known proportion of defect containers. RZE (or POD) and false reject rates are calculated against acceptance criteria.
  • For new inspectors, multiple successful inspections are required for qualification.
  • Operators should be requalified annually, at a minimum.
  • Qualified shift times should be established.

Operators should be tested initially and at regular intervals for near vision acuity and color perception.

Operator fatigue is an important factor. Environmental conditions (ambient light, background noise, activity) and ergonomics should be optimized. Operators performing inspection should take routine breaks (e.g., once per hour) to reduce risk of eye fatigue.

Inspector Qualification and Training

Inspector Qualification Requirements

  • Initial qualification: multiple successful inspections using a test set with a known proportion of defects
  • Annual requalification: revalidation at least once a year
  • Vision testing: near-vision acuity plus color discrimination (initially and periodically)
  • Qualified shift time: establish the maximum time each person may perform inspection per day

Fatigue Management

Visual inspection depends heavily on eyesight, and operator fatigue is a major source of quality risk. ISPE recommends:

  • Mandatory break every hour
  • Optimize lighting, background noise, and ergonomics
  • Establish a rotation scheme to avoid long continuous inspection periods

Analogy: Air Traffic Controller Shift Schedules

Fatigue management for visual inspectors is similar to that for air traffic controllers: highly concentrated work cannot continue for too long. Controllers must rest after every 1.5-2 hours of work, and the same applies to visual inspectors. Neglecting fatigue management means accepting the risk that inspection quality declines over time.

3.2.8.3 Visual Inspection Methods and Equipment

Manual Visual Inspection (MVI)

Sealed, filled containers are inspected by qualified inspectors under controlled conditions. Critical Process Parameters (CPPs) for MVI include:

  • Light wavelength and intensity
  • Background and contrast
  • Inspection rate (pace)
  • Container handling and movement

Magnification can be employed; however, it can increase eye strain and may not improve overall detection rates. It is therefore not recommended for routine inspection.

Throughputs for MVI are low compared to semi-automated or automated equipment. For this reason, MVI is generally performed off-line.

Visual Inspection with Semi-Automatic Machines

A semi-automatic inspection machine transports and rotates the product while being inspected by an operator. Adjustable factors include: light, angle of product, angle of mirrors, background, and container rotation speed.

During inspection, the operator marks containers to be rejected; these are discarded automatically by the machine.

Throughput rates are higher than for manual inspection, but are often overestimated in the process design stage. Semi-automated systems can be designed for sequential or parallel inspection to increase throughput.

Manual Visual Inspection (MVI)

MVI is the most basic inspection method: operators examine containers one by one under controlled conditions. Critical process parameters (CPPs) include light source wavelength/intensity, background contrast, inspection rate, and container handling method.

MVI Limitations

  • Lowest throughput, usually performed off-line
  • Magnifiers can be used but are not recommended for routine use; they increase eye fatigue and do not necessarily improve detection
  • Remains a necessary capability for investigating anomalies and when automated equipment has a high reject rate

Semi-Automated Inspection Machines

The machine conveys and spins the product, and the operator makes the judgment. The light source, product angle, mirror angle, background, and spin speed can be adjusted to enhance defect visibility.

Analogy: Sushi Conveyor Belt + QC Inspector

A semi-automated inspection machine is like a sushi conveyor belt: product is spun and delivered in front of the inspector, who only needs to focus on looking (no picking up and putting back), greatly improving efficiency. However, the actual throughput is often overestimated at the design stage, so capacity analysis should use the "worst-case throughput."

Fully Automatic Inspection Machines

A fully automatic inspection machine consists of an automated material handling/transport system, outfitted with one or more camera stations and/or other instruments designed to inspect product for various defects.

Automated inspection systems may not be suitable for some container types, such as flexible containers. In these cases, a mix of automated, semi-automated, and manual operations may be employed.

Automated equipment is capable of high output rates and is suitable for in-line or off-line (decoupled) installations. In-line installations reduce material handling but impact line efficiencies. For off-line systems, material handling and WIP storage should be considered.

Examples of inspection capabilities include:

  • Particulates in solution
  • Fill level
  • Flip seal presence and color
  • Ampoule banding color
  • Crimp quality (absence of dents/wrinkles)
  • Cracks in tip, neck, shoulder, sidewall, or heel
  • Plunger placement (syringes and cartridges)
  • Needle shield presence
  • Lyophilized cake appearance

Improvements in image capture, processing rates, vision tools, and lighting systems allow capture and analysis of multiple images of each container in real time. Machines can capture and store large numbers of images; these video libraries are helpful during investigations and machine setup. Using video libraries, virtual inspection of container sets is possible, optimizing machine parameters while avoiding degradation of sample sets.

Inspection systems may have unique requirements impacting facility design, such as control of ambient lighting conditions or shielding for X-ray systems.

Fully Automated Inspection Machines

Fully automated systems use automated material transport together with one or more camera stations and other detection instruments (such as X-ray or laser headspace analysis).

Overview of Automated Inspection Capabilities

  • Particulates in solution
  • Fill level
  • Flip-off cap presence and color
  • Ampoule color ring
  • Crimp quality (no dents/wrinkles)
  • Glass cracks (vial tip, neck, shoulder, wall, bottom)
  • Plunger position (syringes/cartridges)
  • Needle shield presence
  • Lyophilized cake appearance

Value of the Image Library

Modern automated inspection machines can capture and store large numbers of images, forming an "image library." Uses include:

  • Retrospective analysis when investigating abnormal reject rates
  • Using images for "virtual inspection" during machine tuning, avoiding the deterioration of physical samples through repeated handling
  • Optimizing machine parameters without consuming challenge set samples

Discussion Question: Choosing an Inspection Strategy

A CDMO produces both a high-value biologic (10 batches per year, 5,000 vials per batch) and a low-value small-molecule injectable (50 batches per year, 50,000 vials per batch).

  • What inspection strategy should be adopted for the high-value product, and why?
  • What about the low-value, high-volume product?
  • How can the inspection needs of the two be balanced in a shared facility?

Facility Design Reminder

Automated inspection equipment may have special facility requirements: X-ray systems require shielding, and optical systems require ambient light control. These requirements should be considered at the facility design stage to avoid the high cost of later retrofitting.

3.2.9 Secondary Packaging

Original Text — ISPE Baseline Guide

3.2.9 Secondary Packaging

The same general principles used for packaging of non-sterile products apply to sterile products. For further information, refer to the ISPE Good Practice Guide: Packaging, Labeling and Warehousing Facilities.

Note: Many regulatory markets are in the process of, or are considering, implementing product serialization requirements as an anti-counterfeiting measure. This involves application of a unique identifier code to the product (unit of use) during packaging that can be checked and verified throughout the distribution channel. Appropriate expertise should be sought during line design to accommodate future equipment and technology requirements in this area.

Commentary

Secondary Packaging

The principles of secondary packaging for sterile products are the same as for general products, including labeling, cartoning, and case packing. ISPE also has dedicated guidance on packaging, labeling, and warehousing facilities that can be consulted.

Serialization Trends

Many regulatory markets worldwide are promoting or have already implemented product serialization requirements:

  • Purpose: anti-counterfeiting; every product unit carries a unique identifier
  • Technology: a unique code (such as a 2D barcode) is applied during packaging and can be verified throughout the distribution chain
  • Facility impact: space and interfaces must be reserved on the packaging line for serialization equipment (coders, camera verification systems, data management systems)

Design Foresight

Even if the market does not currently mandate serialization, when building or modifying a packaging line, space and utility interfaces should be reserved so that serialization equipment can be added in the future. The cost of retrofitting is far higher than the cost of reserving space.

CDMO Practice: Serialization Challenges

For a CDMO, serialization adds complexity: different customers may require different serialization formats and standards (EU FMD, US DSCSA, China traceability codes, and so on). Packaging lines need flexible software configuration and fast changeover capability. This is a key evaluation item when selecting packaging equipment suppliers.

Section Summary

  • Terminal Sterilization (3.2.7): Products sealed in final packaging are sterilized via moist heat or irradiation. Overkill (F0 ≥ 15) and adjunct (F0 ≥ 8) processes both target PNSU ≥ 10-6. Facility design must address non-sterile/sterile segregation, specialized trays, drying areas, and significant utility loads.
  • Autoclave Types: Air steam mix units (small volumes, drier load) vs. superheated water shower units (large volumes, faster heating/cooling, better uniformity). Air ballasting protects container integrity during sterilization.
  • Inspection (3.2.8): USP <790> requires visual inspection of all parenteral units. The Knapp methodology (RZE, PR zones) provides a scientific framework for qualifying both manual and automated inspection. Operator qualification, fatigue management, and defect libraries are essential.
  • Inspection Methods (3.2.8.3): MVI (lowest throughput, off-line), semi-automatic (operator + machine, higher throughput), and fully automatic (camera-based, highest throughput, real-time image analysis). Emerging technologies include X-ray, NIR, and HSA.
  • Secondary Packaging (3.2.9): Same principles as non-sterile products. Product serialization for anti-counterfeiting is an emerging requirement; line design should accommodate future serialization equipment.

Chapter 2d: 3d. Process Equipment (3.2.10–end)

p73-p78

ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 3 (3rd Ed.) | p73 – p78

Learning Objectives

  1. Understand the requirements for cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization of facilities and equipment in sterile manufacturing.
  2. Distinguish between cleaning of critical parts (product-contact) and facility surfaces (non-product-contact).
  3. Evaluate the advantages, limitations, and implementation considerations of single-use systems.
  4. Design effective equipment flow and cleaning equipment strategies (CIP, parts washers, ultrasonic).
  5. Apply steam sterilization (autoclave and SIP) design principles, including air removal, condensate drainage, and qualification.
  6. Understand considerations for other sterilization methods (VHP, gamma irradiation, EtO) and their facility impact.

3.2.10 Cleaning, Disinfection and Sterilization

Cleaning and Disinfection of Facility and Stationary Equipment

Cleaning, disinfection and sterilization are critical processes in a sterile facility as they have the potential to adversely impact critical quality attributes of finished product.

Note: The terms disinfection and sanitization are often used interchangeably, which can lead to confusion about the efficacy of the process. Regulated companies should ensure that their in-house terminology is well defined.

Facility space and stationary equipment surfaces (non-product contact) should be cleaned and disinfected on a routine basis to maintain a state of environmental control as demonstrated by environmental monitoring data.

Written procedures for cleaning and disinfection should contain information on:

  • Frequency
  • Approved cleaning/disinfecting solutions
  • Equipment/utensils/consumables
  • Methodology
  • Operator protection requirements

Solutions used for cleaning and disinfecting should be qualified as effective against a broad range of microorganisms on prevalent surface materials in use in the facility. Multiple agents should be rotated, where appropriate. Surface material compatibility with cleaning/disinfecting solutions should be evaluated during the selection process.

To prevent introduction of contamination, disinfectants should be:

  • Sterile
  • Handled appropriately in suitable (e.g., sterile) containers
  • Labeled and expiry dated
  • Used for no longer than the predefined period specified by written procedures

Critical areas (ISO 5/Grade A) likely require cleaning on a more frequent basis than less critical areas (ISO 8/Grade C), due to higher environmental standards.

Interpretation and Application

The Core Role of Cleaning and Disinfection

Cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization are the three core lines of defense in a sterile manufacturing facility. ISPE Vol.3 discusses these processes together with the process equipment chapter to stress that equipment design must consider, from the very beginning, how the equipment will be cleaned and how it will be sterilized.

Terminology Warning: Disinfection vs. Sanitization

Disinfection and sanitization are often used interchangeably in industry. FDA uses "disinfection" as the standard term. Companies should define and use one term consistently in their internal documents to avoid questions during audits.

Analogy: Cleaning Levels in a Restaurant Kitchen

Imagine a high-end restaurant: the kitchen floor is scrubbed every day (facility surface cleaning), cutting boards and knives are thoroughly disinfected after every use (critical part cleaning), and the whole kitchen gets a periodic deep clean (deep sterilization). This maps directly onto the three-tier cleaning strategy in sterile manufacturing.

Four Elements of Disinfectant Management

  • Sterile: the disinfectant itself must not be a source of contamination
  • Appropriate containers: avoid introducing microorganisms during transfer
  • Labeling and expiry: the basis of traceability and effectiveness
  • In-use time limit: an opened disinfectant does not stay effective forever

CDMO in Practice: Standardizing the Disinfection Strategy Across Product Lines

In a CDMO operating multiple lines, it is advisable to establish a "disinfectant matrix": a single approved list of disinfectants and a rotation plan applicable to all production suites, which reduces the duplicated cost of each line validating its own.

Cleaning of Critical Parts

Critical parts, which are defined as parts either in direct contact with product or have the possibility to contaminate the product, should be subjected to a qualified cleaning process a short period after use to remove product residue.

Critical parts should be identified via a documented risk assessment. Clean hold times for parts should be established; when these clean hold times expire, the parts should be cleaned again prior to next use.

Chemical cleaning agents may be necessary to remove residual product from product contacting surfaces. Selection of an appropriate agent should be based on the type of soil and cleaning process (e.g., ultrasonic, high impingement) and may be undertaken in conjunction with the cleaning agent vendors.

When cleaning agents are used, the cleaning process should include qualified rinse steps to demonstrate removal of these agents to a safe level.

Note: Endotoxins are not appreciably retained by most sterilizing grade filters, nor are they appreciably reduced by moist heat sterilization. Control of endotoxins, therefore, requires a comprehensive approach including bioburden control, cleaning, dry heat depyrogenation, and filtration processes.

Interpretation and Application

Time Pressure on Critical Part Cleaning

Critical parts must be cleaned "within a short time" after use, because product residues dry and harden over time, greatly increasing the difficulty of cleaning. Establishing the Dirty Hold Time and Clean Hold Time is the foundation of cleaning validation.

Endotoxin Control: An Integrated Strategy

Endotoxin cannot be retained by filters and cannot be eliminated by steam sterilization. The only reliable removal method is dry-heat depyrogenation (typically above 250°C). This is why glass vials and ampoules usually pass through a depyrogenation tunnel.

Exercise: Risk Assessment in Practice

Suppose your CDMO production line has three stations: a compounding tank, a filtration line, and a filling platform:

  • Which parts are "critical parts"?
  • What Dirty Hold Time should be set for each station?
  • How would you use a risk assessment to prioritize the cleaning processes?

Single-Use Systems

Single-Use Systems

Implementation of single-use disposable technology and single-use systems is an increasing practice. Single-use disposable systems are available for a variety of fill/finish unit operations, including formulation, material addition, buffer prep, filtration, product transfer, and product filling.

Single-use systems offer several advantages such as:

  • Elimination of cleaning steps
  • Reduced operator exposure to high potent or toxic materials during cleaning
  • Elimination of cleaning validation
  • Reduced risk of cross-contamination
  • Flexible scalability
  • Reduction of capital costs

Single-use systems are not suitable for all product types. For example, temperature limits on the film may exclude products requiring heating for formulation/filtration/filling.

Implementation of single-use systems requires a cross-functional corporate effort in areas such as:

  • Primary and secondary film/vendor selection (includes quality audits and supplier agreements)
  • Single-use system design (includes film selection, component selection, tubing selection, packaging, sterilization, etc.)
  • Testing for extractables, leachables and particulates (primary and backup systems)
  • Integrity testing of single-use assemblies, including filters (pre and/or post-use)
  • Batch record modifications

Single-use systems entail higher operating costs (consumables) than traditional systems. A careful financial analysis is required to evaluate costs versus potential savings. The timeframe associated with completion of these activities is quite lengthy, and is in fact much longer than the typical timeframe for facility conceptual and detailed design.

Interpretation and Application

Key Advantages of Single-Use Systems

The greatest value of single-use systems is that they "eliminate cleaning validation" and "reduce the risk of cross-contamination". For a CDMO, this means faster product changeover and a lower validation burden per batch.

Analogy: Disposable Tableware vs. Porcelain Tableware

A single-use system is like throwing a party with disposable tableware: no dishes to wash, you throw everything away after use, and it is simple to handle; but you have to buy new ones every time, and the cost adds up. A traditional stainless steel system is like fine porcelain: it costs more up front, but you wash and reuse it, so the long-term cost is lower.

Implementation Timeline Warning

ISPE specifically warns that the implementation timeline for single-use systems is "much longer than the facility design itself". This includes film selection, supplier audits, E&L testing, and integrity test validation. A CDMO should start these activities during the facility design phase rather than waiting until the facility is built.

CDMO in Practice: A Hybrid Strategy

Most CDMOs adopt a hybrid strategy: single-use systems for high-value, small-batch products (such as cell therapy), and fixed stainless steel equipment for large-scale products. The key is to reserve enough flexible space during facility planning.

Equipment Flow

Careful consideration of equipment flow during cleaning, preparation and staging operations is required to effectively mitigate risk of cross-contamination. This cross-contamination can be either batch to batch for Product A, or from Product A to Product B.

Use of pass-through type washers and autoclaves and unidirectional equipment flows are recommended to ensure that clean parts do not come in close proximity to dirty parts.

Segregated staging areas of sufficient size should be provided for soiled, cleaned, and sterilized equipment. Segregation of pre and post-use filter integrity testing should also be considered.

Interpretation and Application

The Unidirectional Flow Principle

Equipment flow is as important as personnel flow and material flow. The core principle is that dirty equipment and clean equipment must never meet in the same area. Pass-through washers and autoclaves ensure that equipment enters from the "dirty side" and is removed from the "clean side".

Analogy: Freight Elevator vs. Passenger Elevator in a Building

This is like the circulation design of a high-end hotel: garbage uses the freight elevator and guests use the passenger elevator, and the two never cross. In a sterile manufacturing facility, dirty equipment and clean equipment must likewise follow separate paths.

Additional Challenges in Multi-Product Facilities

In a CDMO multi-product facility, the cross-contamination risk is not only batch-to-batch but also from Product A to Product B. This calls for stricter segregated storage of equipment and tighter flow management.

Cleaning Equipment

Semi-Automated and Automated Cleaning Systems

Semi-automated and automated cleaning systems can provide an enhanced level of process control and reliability. Use of such systems is recommended over manual cleaning processes.

Examples of semi-automated cleaning systems include ultrasonic baths and parts (cabinet) washers. These systems are useful for components and equipment that require disassembly for effective cleaning. Load mapping of items in automated and semi-automated cleaners is required to ensure reproducibility.

Some equipment, such as formulation vessels and filling line process pathways, lend themselves to fully automated CIP systems. The advantage of automated CIP is its potential to configure both the CIP system and the component for cleaning, execute the cycle, and return the component to service or subsequent sterilization without disassembly/assembly.

CIP systems should be designed from the beginning for cleanability and proper CIP to avoid potential issues with product contamination. Considerations include:

  • Elimination of dead legs
  • Adequate flow rates (to ensure turbulent flow in piping systems)
  • Complete drainability
  • Cleaning of piping high and low points
  • System drying
  • Material surface finishes

Modern cleaning devices and CIP equipment include electronic controls that allow for programming, monitoring/alarming, and recording of critical parameters such as cycle time, water temperature, water pressure, flow rate/totalized flow, and detergent addition (volume/weight).

Design considerations for CIP systems include:

  • Single versus multi-tank
  • High impingement dynamic spray devices versus static spray balls/nozzles (or combination)
  • Recirculating or once through

Interpretation and Application

Three Levels of Automated Cleaning

  • Semi-automated (ultrasonic baths, parts washers): suited to parts that must be disassembled, such as filling pumps
  • Fully automated CIP: suited to fixed equipment such as compounding tanks and piping, with no disassembly required
  • Manual cleaning: should be avoided wherever possible because of poor repeatability, although some special parts remain unavoidable

Six Key Elements of CIP Design

  • Elimination of dead legs: places in the piping that the cleaning solution cannot reach
  • Adequate flow velocity: ensure turbulent flow to remove residues thoroughly
  • Complete drainability: no pooling points in the piping
  • High and low point cleaning: both the highest and lowest points of the piping must be cleanable
  • System drying: residual moisture promotes microbial growth
  • Surface roughness (Ra value): the smoother the surface, the easier it is to clean

Mechanical Failure Risk of Spray Devices

Both dynamic spray devices and static spray balls can fail through mechanical malfunction or blockage. Process controls or instrument monitoring (such as flow meters and rotation speed sensors) must be used to ensure consistent cleaning performance.

Analogy: Household Dishwasher vs. Industrial CIP

A household dishwasher has fixed spray arms and temperature settings, but you would never connect a pot directly to the dishwasher. CIP lets the cleaning solution "flow through the inside of the pot", circulating and cleaning directly inside the equipment without disassembly.

CDMO in Practice: Standardizing Cleaning Equipment Configuration

In a multi-suite production facility, it is advisable for every line to use the same model of parts washer and CIP system. This not only reduces validation cost but also allows operators to move seamlessly between lines.

Cleaning Equipment Location and Selection

Cleaning equipment should be located to minimize impact of mechanical systems and maintenance activities on the cleanroom environment. For example, a pass-through type parts washer can be installed to allow access to the mechanical sections from CNC or mechanical space. Drains should be located in a mechanical area, when possible, due to their high moisture levels and potential to introduce contamination.

Specific considerations for selection of cleaning equipment include:

  • Types of equipment and components that require cleaning
  • Product characteristics/unique cleaning requirements
  • Cycle times and impact on capacity
  • Demand on water systems as well as heating and cooling systems
  • Location in facility
  • Use of and need for detergents
  • Local requirements for capture and treatment of rinse water

Interpretation and Application

Separating the Cleanroom from the Mechanical Area

Where to place cleaning equipment is an important facility design decision. The core principle: put the parts that generate noise, humidity, and maintenance needs outside the cleanroom, so that only the clean operating face faces the clean area.

Contamination Risk of Drains

Drains are a known contamination risk point in cleanrooms because a high-humidity environment favors microbial growth. ISPE recommends locating drains in the mechanical area rather than inside the cleanroom, which is consistent with the EU GMP Annex 1 requirement that prohibits drains in Grade A/B areas.

Steam Sterilization

Steam Sterilization

Critical parts in an aseptic process, which are defined as parts, equipment, tools and utensils either in direct contact with sterile product or having the possibility to contaminate the product, should be subjected to a qualified sterilization process within a defined period prior to use.

Use of sterile articles, components, or equipment in aseptic fill/finish operations requires:

  1. Effective sterilization of the article
  2. Protection of the article from contamination during staging and transfer to the aseptic zone
  3. Transfer into the aseptic zone

Several sterilization methods are available:

  • Gamma irradiation
  • E-beam irradiation
  • Ethylene Oxide (EtO)
  • Dry heat
  • Moist heat

The two available methods for moist heat (or steam) sterilization are autoclaving or SIP. These cycles are generally qualified according to the overkill approach, requiring a minimum F0 of 12 minutes.

When qualifying a steam sterilization process, the following should be verified:

  • Steam quality at point of delivery (dryness, superheat, non-condensable gases)
  • Preparation/wrapping of articles to be sterilized (autoclave only)
  • Effective removal of air from porous loads or wrapped articles (autoclave) or from all points in the system (SIP)
  • Effective removal of condensate from the system during the cycle
  • Appropriate design of the sterilizing cycle (pre-vacuum pulses, F0 requirements, post-vacuum drying)
  • Temperature mapping (minimum F0 delivered at all locations)
  • Orientation/equipment configuration
  • Minimum and maximum loads (autoclave only) and load mapping
  • Determination of worst case conditions
  • Ability to inactivate biological challenge (Geobacillus stearothermophilus, 1.0 x 106 minimum population)

Interpretation and Application

Three Steps of Sterilization: Sterilize, Protect, Transfer

Sterilization is not as simple as "putting items in the autoclave". The complete sterilization process has three stages: effective sterilization, contamination-protected storage, and safe transfer into the aseptic area. If any one step fails, the whole sterilization is invalidated.

The Meaning of the F0 Value

F0 is the standard unit for measuring the effectiveness of moist heat sterilization, expressed as the equivalent sterilization time (in minutes) at 121.1°C. The overkill approach requires a minimum F0 of 12 minutes, ensuring complete sterilization even under worst-case conditions.

Steam Quality: A Frequently Overlooked Critical Factor

Steam dryness, superheat, and non-condensable gas content directly affect sterilization effectiveness. Wet steam contains too much water and leaves the load wet, while superheated steam reduces heat transfer efficiency. Steam quality should be tested regularly, especially for new facilities or after changes to the steam system.

Analogy: The Oven and the Autoclave

An autoclave is like an oven: you need to ensure uniform temperature (temperature mapping), place the food in the right position (load pattern), preheat sufficiently (air removal), and use a thermometer to confirm it is cooked through (biological indicators).

Exercise: Sterilization Validation Planning

Your CDMO is to validate a new double-door autoclave. List the following:

  • The load types to be validated (at least three)
  • The maximum and minimum configuration for each load
  • How to determine the worst-case temperature location

Autoclave Process Design

Effective removal of air from wrapped articles and porous loads is required for good sterilization efficacy. Autoclaves should be properly maintained and checked at regular intervals for vacuum integrity (leak rate). Use of an air removal test (e.g., Bowie-Dick, DART, Lantor Cube) at a regular interval is also recommended.

Autoclave sterilization process design should consider the packaging/wrapping of articles:

  • Packaging/wrapping should be designed to promote effective air removal, steam penetration, and condensate removal during sterilization.
  • Packaging and wrapping may be a manual operation; effective training is required to ensure consistent and reproducible preparation of articles.
  • Packaging/wrapping materials should provide an effective microbiological barrier to maintain sterility during cool down and staging.
  • The packaging/wrapping should allow for successive improvement steps during transfer of the articles to areas of higher cleanliness.
  • Permeability of the packaging/wrapping as required for sterilization may impact selection of subsequent improvement steps.

Sterilized articles should be securely staged and transferred to the aseptic processing zone. Considerations for secure transfer include:

  • Technologies such as Rapid Transfer Ports (RTPs) or automated VHP airlocks for secure transfer across the RABS/isolator boundary
  • For isolator-based facilities, autoclaves may be unloaded into an ISO 8/Grade C area
  • In RABS-based facilities, autoclaves are generally unloaded into an ISO 5/Grade A area

The number and size of autoclaves should be designed to support production operations, considering types of equipment, number of cycles, cycle time, and impact of routine testing on availability.

Interpretation and Application

The Importance of Air Removal Testing

Air is the greatest enemy of steam sterilization. The thermal conductivity of air is far lower than that of saturated steam, so if air remains in the load, the temperature in that area will not reach the sterilization requirement. The Bowie-Dick test or the DART test is a routine tool for verifying air removal.

Packaging Design: Balancing Sterilization and Sterile Protection

Packaging must meet two conflicting requirements at once: it must let steam penetrate during sterilization (breathability) and block microorganisms after sterilization (barrier property). Multi-layer packaging designs (such as a double-layer breather bag) let operators remove the outer layers one at a time during transfer.

RTP vs. VHP Airlock: Choosing a Transfer Technology

  • RTP (rapid transfer port): suited to isolator technology, achieving aseptic transfer through a mechanical seal
  • VHP airlock: an automated airlock that uses hydrogen peroxide sterilization, suited to RABS and isolators

Both are superior to the traditional method of manually spraying disinfectant.

CDMO in Practice: Autoclave Capacity Planning

The autoclave is often the capacity bottleneck in sterile manufacturing. At the design stage, evaluate thoroughly the number of sterilization cycles needed per day, the time of each cycle (including heat-up, hold, and drying), and the time taken by routine testing, to ensure it does not become a production bottleneck.

Sterilize-In-Place (SIP)

Sterilize-In-Place (SIP)

The term SIP is commonly used to refer to both:

  • Sterilization of large scale fixed holding vessels and fill line process piping
  • Sterilization of smaller portable vessels at a dedicated SIP (or CIP/SIP) process station

Product compounding/filtration/transfer/holding systems can be designed as completely closed systems, due to advances in aseptic fluid transfer and material addition technologies (e.g., tubing welders, aseptic connectors, closed addition devices). This allows installation in areas of lower cleanliness (e.g., ISO 8/Grade C, Grade D or CNC zones).

When installed in aseptic areas, systems should be designed to minimize impact of mechanical and control elements and steam/condensate release in the process area. This may be accomplished via use of "half-wall" or split systems that segregate the process side of the equipment from the mechanical side.

Design considerations for effective SIP include:

  • Air removal: Pre-vacuum steps or gravity displacement; leak rate assessment on regular basis; proper steam trap design; multiple steam injection points for large systems
  • Sterilization of vent filters: Avoid compromising filter integrity at elevated temperatures; limit flow across filters; use multiple steam injection points for large systems
  • Condensate drainage: System should drain condensate quickly from all portions; use steam traps and orifices; avoid group trapping of drain legs
  • Drying and cool down: Use 0.2 µm sterile filtered air or nitrogen; avoid exceeding differential pressure rating of filters at elevated temperatures; maintain overpressure until time of use

Calibrated temperature sensors (RTD, thermocouples) and pressure sensors are required for system control and monitoring. Temperature sensors should be installed at potential cold spot locations. Comparison of system pressure and temperature can verify presence of saturated steam.

Interpretation and Application

Two Application Scenarios for SIP

  • Fixed system SIP: large tanks and line piping are sterilized directly with steam, with no disassembly
  • Mobile SIP (Steam Out of Place): small vessels are taken to a dedicated CIP/SIP station for sterilization

The Transformative Significance of Closed Systems

With the maturing of tube welders, sterile connectors, and closed addition devices, process systems can be designed as fully closed systems. This means sterility can be maintained even when installed in an ISO 8 or CNC area, greatly reducing reliance on higher-grade cleanrooms.

Analogy: The Half Wall, Separating Front of House from Back of House

A "half wall" or split-body design is like the kitchen pass-through window of a restaurant: you see only the clean serving side, while the stoves, piping, and water heaters are hidden behind. In an SIP system, the steam valves, condensate drainage, and control components are all placed on the mechanical side, leaving only the sterile process path on the clean side.

Four Major SIP Design Challenges

  1. Air removal: piping systems are easier to air-purge than autoclaves (there is no porous load), but large systems need multiple steam injection points and door sequence control
  2. Vent filter protection: at high temperature the pressure resistance of the filter drops significantly, so flow across the filter must be limited
  3. Condensate drainage: avoid group trapping, which leads to uneven condensate drainage
  4. Drying and cooling: use 0.2 µm sterile-filtered air or nitrogen and maintain positive pressure until use

Exercise: Temperature Sensor Layout

You are to plan the temperature sensor layout for an SIP system consisting of a compounding tank, two filtration lines, and a filling tank:

  • Where are the potential cold spots? (Hint: the ends of independent flow paths)
  • Which locations need sensors to detect steam trap failure?
  • How can the comparison of pressure and temperature be used to confirm the presence of saturated steam?

Other Sterilization Methods

Other Sterilization Methods

The use of fumigants—for example, hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), chlorine dioxide (ClO2), and nitrogen dioxide (NO2)—for room and equipment surface decontamination should consider that, in order to be effective, they need to be able to directly contact target surfaces in adequate concentrations.

Fumigation is generally not required to maintain aseptic conditions in a facility; however, in some cases it can provide a useful add-on process. Considerations include:

  • VHP: Usually used to decontaminate the interior of barrier isolators.
  • Gamma irradiation: Usually used for sterilization of single-use technology, as well as selected ready-to-use elastomeric components such as syringe plungers. Cycles should be validated and under routine dose auditing.
  • Ethylene oxide (EtO): Usually used for sterilization of ready-to-fill pre-nested components such as syringes, vials, and cartridges and ophthalmic containers.

Interpretation and Application

Limitations of Fumigation

The fumigant must come into "direct contact" with the target surface at a sufficient concentration to be effective. This means shielded surfaces (such as the inner side of stacked loads) may not be adequately fumigated. This is also why fumigation cannot replace routine cleaning and disinfection procedures.

CDMO in Practice: Supply Chain Management for Outsourced Sterilization

Because gamma irradiation and EtO sterilization are usually outsourced, a CDMO needs to pay attention to the storage conditions and location of components after sterilization, shelf-life management (typically two years), and the supplier's dose audit program. All of these should be included in the regular supplier management process.

Section Summary — Chapter 3d: Process Equipment (3.2.10–end)

Key Concepts

  • Cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization form the three-layer defense for sterile manufacturing facilities and equipment
  • Disinfectants must be sterile, properly labeled, expiry-dated, and rotated; terminology (disinfection vs. sanitization) must be standardized
  • Critical parts require documented risk assessment, dirty hold times, clean hold times, and qualified cleaning processes
  • Single-use systems eliminate cleaning validation and cross-contamination risk, but require lengthy implementation timelines and cross-functional effort
  • Unidirectional equipment flow with pass-through washers/autoclaves prevents clean/dirty cross-contamination
  • CIP design requires elimination of dead legs, adequate flow rates, complete drainability, and appropriate surface finishes (Ra values)
  • Steam sterilization (autoclave and SIP) requires effective air removal, condensate drainage, temperature mapping, and F0 ≥ 12 min (overkill approach)
  • SIP systems benefit from closed system design and half-wall installation to segregate process from mechanical areas
  • VHP, gamma irradiation, and EtO serve specific niches; fumigation supplements but does not replace routine cleaning/disinfection

Key Takeaways

  • Cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization are the three lines of defense in sterile manufacturing, and equipment design must consider all three from the very beginning
  • Critical parts (product-contact surfaces) require risk assessment, dirty/clean hold time management, and cleaning validation
  • Single-use systems are a powerful tool for a CDMO, but their implementation timeline is longer than the facility design and must be started early
  • Equipment flow must be unidirectional, with dirty and clean kept strictly separate, which is especially important in a CDMO multi-product facility
  • Key CIP design points: eliminate dead legs, adequate flow velocity, complete drainability, appropriate surface roughness
  • Steam sterilization (autoclave + SIP) requires F0 ≥ 12 minutes, and validation of air removal, condensate drainage, temperature recording, and biological indicators
  • Large SIP systems use closed designs and half-wall installation to reduce the impact on the cleanroom
  • VHP, gamma irradiation, and EtO each have their own application scenarios, and a CDMO needs to manage the outsourced sterilization supply chain and shelf life
