4.4 Room Function 4.4.2 Changing Rooms 4.4.3 Bulk Storage 4.5 Surface Finishes Table 4.2 4.5.2 Room Finishes 4.6 Transfer Zones 4.6.1 Improvement Step 4.6.2 Sequential Transitions 4.6.3 Airlock Design 4.6.4 Pass Boxes
4.4

4.4 Room Function

Room Function Categories | p. 92-93

4.4.1 Room Function

Facility areas are divided into five general functional categories:

  • Areas for aseptic processing of product or components
  • Areas immediately adjacent to the above, comprised of material/personnel airlocks
  • Preparation areas closely related to the aseptic processing area
  • Areas immediately adjacent to the above, comprising material airlocks, personnel clean change, inspection, and other associated areas ("pharmaceutical" areas)
  • General ancillary/support functions, including warehousing, offices, plant utilities, and circulation areas with no protection requirements other than, perhaps, a factory change/uniform for unclassified areas

The Five Functional Categories of Rooms

ISPE divides a sterile facility into five levels, from the aseptic processing core at the center to the general support areas at the outer edge. Understanding this five-layer structure is the basis for laying out a cleanroom facility.

Key concept: five rings of protection, from the inside out

  • Ring 1: Aseptic processing core (Grade A/B) - the area where product is directly exposed
  • Ring 2: Adjacent airlocks and personnel/material transition areas
  • Ring 3: Preparation areas (solution preparation, washing, assembly)
  • Ring 4: Pharmaceutical areas (testing, clean changing, material staging)
  • Ring 5: General support areas (warehouse, offices, utilities)

Analogy: the onion

Picture the whole facility as an onion: every layer is a barrier. The closer you get to the center (the aseptic core), the stricter the environmental control, and every layer you cross must go through a "transition station" (an airlock or changing room). This is why the facility layout has to be planned from the core outward.

4.4

4.4.2 Changing Rooms

Changing Room Design | p. 93

4.4.2 Changing Rooms

Changing rooms should be designed to accommodate the gowning philosophy and changing regimes determined by process operations. They should be arranged to support procedures which prevent the ingress of outside environmental contaminant. Personnel should pass from facility changing rooms (where street clothes are replaced with facility uniforms) to clean environment or aseptic changing rooms in a logical progression.

Changing rooms into open process aseptic areas (including RABS) should, where possible, have separate ingress/egress routes to prevent chemical or bio-contamination of clean garments. Clean and aseptic processing change areas can be sequential and in separate rooms. HVAC and personnel movements should be controlled.

Changing facilities can range from CNC or Grade D to ISO 7/Grade B or higher, so the changing area standards and finishes should be appropriate for the highest cleanliness processing area into which it opens. The flow and storage of gowning materials should also be considered in the design.

Personal showering and toilet facilities should not be directly connected to classified cleanroom locker room or gowning areas.

Key Points for Changing Room Design

Four Principles of Changing Room Design

  • Logical progression: Personnel move from the general changing room (changing into plant garments) step by step into the clean changing room (donning cleanroom garments), completing gowning in stages.
  • Separate ingress and egress: Changing rooms leading into aseptic areas (including RABS) should, where possible, have separate entry and exit routes to avoid contaminating clean garments.
  • Grade matching: The environmental control standard of a changing room should match the highest cleanliness grade it leads to.
  • Isolated toilets: Showers and toilets must not open directly into classified cleanrooms or gowning areas.

Practical Reminder

Separation of ingress and egress in changing rooms is a common audit finding. Many older plants share one corridor for both because of space constraints. If physical separation is not possible, at a minimum an SOP should allow only one-way traffic at a time (either gowning or de-gowning), with HVAC positive-pressure airflow as a compensating measure.

4.4

4.4.3 Bulk Storage Areas

Bulk Storage Areas | p. 93

4.4.3 Bulk Storage Areas

Bulk storage areas within warehouses are generally remote from the clean core. Some intermediate, product, and components storage may be required within the preparation and aseptic processing areas. Storage within these areas should have dedicated floor space and may need special HVAC provisions.

Bulk Storage Area Design

Bulk material storage areas are normally located well away from the clean core. However, some intermediates, finished products or components may need to be held temporarily in the preparation area or the aseptic processing area. Such holding areas need dedicated space and may need special HVAC design (such as temperature and humidity control).

Analogy: holding ingredients in a kitchen

The big warehouse is like the walk-in cooler at the back of a restaurant (far from the cooking area), but the kitchen usually also needs a small under-counter fridge for ingredients about to be used. The holding area inside a cleanroom is that "under-counter fridge": small, tightly controlled, and holding only the materials that are about to go into the process.

4.5

4.5 Surface Finishes and Materials of Construction

Surface Finishes and Materials of Construction | p. 93-94

4.5.1 Architectural Detailing

In detailing the architectural aspects of cleanrooms, key factors which should be addressed include:

  • The principal function of the room is to provide an enclosure to contain the defined activity and its associated equipment.
  • Finish materials should be non-shedding, non-porous, and resistant to sustaining microbial growth.
  • Surfaces should be smooth and easy to clean, with minimal ledges and joints. Corners at walls, ceilings, and floors should be coved with a sufficient radius to facilitate cleaning and minimize areas that are difficult to access, particularly near the product and process equipment.
  • Finishes should be able to withstand repeated cleaning and sanitization with various chemicals and resist surface oxidization.
  • Attention should be given to these issues when detailing any interface between the facility and the equipment and services.
  • Wall protection and guarding to prevent mechanical failure should be considered to maintain the integrity of the finishes and minimize damage or premature wearing.

Door hardware should be carefully considered for ease of cleaning. "Hands off" proximity sensors and openers should be installed, where possible. Normally, doors should swing towards higher room pressures, to assist in maintaining differential pressurization. Fire regulations governing escape in an emergency, however, usually take precedence, requiring door closers of sufficient force to overcome the pressure. Door interlocks should have emergency override features in case of fire.

A risk assessment should be made when doors swing into ISO 7/Grade B or higher areas as these doors may contaminate the aseptic area, having been exposed to lower classified areas.

The goal of architectural detailing is to help protect the product by providing finishes which can withstand cleaning and sanitization requirements, providing details which minimize horizontal ledges and provide tight seals at penetration points or where different systems are integrated.

Higher quality, robust finishes can evoke an environment of cleanliness and control, where lesser finishes which do not hold up as well to use and cleaning can make a facility look dated and in need of repair. Higher quality finishes demonstrate a dedication to quality to inspectors.

Architectural Detail Design

Six Principles for Cleanroom Surface Finishes

  • Non-shedding: The material does not release particles
  • Non-porous: The surface does not absorb liquids or microorganisms
  • Antimicrobial: The surface does not favor microbial attachment and growth
  • Easy to clean: Smooth surfaces, minimal joints, coved corners
  • Chemical resistance: Withstands repeated cleaning and disinfection without oxidation or corrosion
  • Impact resistance: Impact protection should be considered, especially in high-traffic areas

Door Design - the Pressure Differential versus Fire Safety Dilemma

Doors should open toward the higher-pressure side to maintain the pressure differential. Fire regulations, however, require doors to open in the direction of escape. The two requirements often conflict, especially in areas of Grade B and above. The usual solution is to fit door closers strong enough to overcome the pressure differential, together with an emergency door-release override.

Analogy: choosing surface finishes is like choosing a waterproof phone case

Choosing cleanroom surface finishes is like choosing a protective phone case: you need it to be waterproof (non-porous), shockproof (impact resistant), easy to wipe (easy to clean) and not flake (non-shedding). The higher the cleanroom grade, the more expensive the "phone", and the higher the specification of protection it needs.

Audit Perspective: Appearance Is Quality

ISPE specifically notes that a high-quality finish can convey a commitment to quality to auditors. Conversely, peeling old walls or rusty door frames lead auditors to doubt the management standard of the whole facility. This is not just a matter of appearance; it is a demonstration of GMP culture.

T4.2

Table 4.2: Architectural Materials and Finishes Guide

Materials and Finishes Guidance Table | p. 94-97

Table 4.2 — Floors

Table 4.2 — Interior Walls

Table 4.2 — Ceilings

Table 4.2 — Junctions, Doors, Hardware, Lighting, Sprinklers, Penetrations

Key Points from Table 4.2

Quick Logic for Material Grades

As the area classification rises from unclassified to Grade A, material requirements step up clearly:

  • Floors: sealed concrete → epoxy/vinyl → welded-seam vinyl with coved skirting → no drains
  • Walls: latex-painted gypsum board → metal panels/glazed tile → chemical-resistant coating → seamless, coved corners, corrosion resistant
  • Ceilings: suspended ceiling → FRP/metal panels → sealed, flush-mounted → HEPA filter array (UAF)
  • Doors: standard hardware → epoxy-coated metal → all stainless steel + touch-free sensors

Unique Requirements for Grade A

  • Drains and sinks are not permitted (Floor drains and sinks are not permitted)
  • The ceiling consists of an array of HEPA/ULPA filters providing unidirectional airflow (UAF)
  • Fire sprinklers must be a special design that does not disturb the UAF
  • All door hardware is recessed with touch-free actuators

Analogy: from a home kitchen to an operating theater

An unclassified area is like a kitchen at home: tile floors and painted walls are enough. Grade C/D is like a restaurant back kitchen, needing stainless steel counters and washable floors. Grade A is like an operating theater: the ceiling is the laminar-flow air outlet, every corner is coved, and there is not a single drain in the floor. With every step up in grade, you move closer to the ultimate standard of "no dead corners, nowhere for dirt to hide".

Common Audit Finding: Mold on Gypsum Board

Note 2 of Table 4.2 specifically warns that gypsum board carries a risk of mold in areas of high humidity or frequent cleaning and disinfection. If it must be used, choose glass-faced or antimicrobial gypsum board. This is the material issue most easily overlooked in new plant design and most often problematic in older plants.

4.5

4.5.2 Room Finishes

Room Surface Specifications | p. 98

4.5.2 Room Finishes

While specifying room finishes for cleanrooms, key factors which should be addressed include:

  • The nature of the process performed in the room should be considered. Manufacturing or preparation activity in an ISO 8/Grade C room places more demands on housekeeping, cleaning, disinfection, and environmental monitoring than if an aseptic processing isolator were placed in the same room.
  • The balance of installation costs against maintainability and ease with which repair or replacement can be performed.
  • Finishes should allow for the ease of installation of building services, grilles, controls/switches, and piped penetrations.
  • Finishes should accommodate integration of fixtures such as CCTV, intercom panels, key pads, telephones, sprinkler heads and covers, and emergency showers.
  • Wall or floor mounted wall protection is recommended in high traffic areas.
  • Fire protection aspects should be accommodated: surface flame spread, fire resistant construction (doors and vision panels), detectors, sprinkler heads, and alarm sounders.
  • Air tightness of room fabric, particularly around door openings and sprinkler heads, and the choice of finish materials that are not adversely affected by sanitizing chemicals.
  • All wall penetrations (electrical outlets, data ports, fire extinguisher cabinets, etc.) should be sealed to maintain air pressure control and prevent pest infiltration.
  • Electrically conductive and grounded flooring should be considered in areas where explosion control is required.
  • Method and frequency of cleaning, cleaning agents, and details such as equipment surface fixings and floor drains should be considered. Floor drains are not permitted inside the aseptic processing area. In other areas, floor drains should be minimized with concave, minimum 2" air break on process drain lines. Back flow preventers and trap controllers should be utilized.

Key Points for Selecting Room Surface Specifications

Decision Factors in Selecting Surface Specifications

  • Process requirements: Within the same room grade, open processing versus isolator operation makes a huge difference to surface requirements
  • Installation vs. maintenance cost: Material selection must balance initial installation cost against long-term ease of maintenance and replacement
  • System integration: Walls must accommodate CCTV, intercoms, access control, fire sprinklers and many other devices
  • Airtightness: All openings, including door frames, sprinklers and penetrations, must be sealed to maintain pressure differential control
  • Explosion protection: Areas with solvents should consider anti-static conductive flooring

Drain Control - a Microbial Risk Hot Spot

Drains are a high-risk point for microbial contamination in cleanrooms. ISPE's position is very clear:

  • Aseptic area: drains are completely prohibited
  • Preparation and other areas: drains should be minimized, and must use a recessed design, an air break of at least 2 inches, backflow preventers and trap controllers

Microbial backsplash/backflow from drains is one of the common causes of sterility test failures and batch rejection.

Thought Exercise

Your Grade C preparation area currently uses an epoxy floor with a drain for wash-down. In the last two consecutive environmental monitoring runs, microbial counts near the drain were high. Which corrective measures would you consider?

  • Increase the cleaning and disinfection frequency of the drain
  • Install a backflow preventer and a trap monitor
  • Assess whether the number of drains can be reduced or their locations reconfigured
  • Fit a sealing cover over the drain, opened only during draining
4.6

4.6 Transfer Zones

Transfer Zones (Airlock Systems) | p. 98-99

4.6 Transfer Zones

Transfer zones and airlocks into and out of cleanroom areas should provide suitable transition for materials, personnel, equipment and waste. Airlocks are used to maintain pressure differentials between areas of differing classifications and to provide a controlled environment for the transfer of materials or the transition/gowning of personnel between classified areas.

Personnel and material (including components, raw materials, equipment and waste) require airlocks to enter and exit areas of different classifications. The staging and movement of personnel and materials should be designed to minimize errors, maintain gowning room hygiene, and minimize the risk of cross-contamination. Airlocks should be appropriately sized and environmentally controlled depending upon the activity occurring within the airlock.

Overview of Transfer Zones

The Three Functions of an Airlock

  • Maintain pressure differential: Acts as a buffer space between areas of different grades, so that opening a door does not immediately collapse the pressure gradient
  • Provide a transition environment: Gowning of personnel and cleaning and disinfection of materials, the "improvement steps", are completed here
  • Reduce cross-contamination risk: Through mechanisms such as door interlocks and one-way flow, ensure that lower-grade air does not enter higher-grade areas

Analogy: the submarine pressure chamber

An airlock is like the pressure chamber on a submarine: you cannot walk straight from the sea into the submarine; you must first enter the chamber, close the outer door, adjust the pressure, and then open the inner door. A cleanroom airlock works on the same concept: close the door → carry out cleaning/gowning → wait for the pressure differential to recover → open the other door. The two doors must never be open at the same time.

4.6

4.6.1 Improvement Step

Improvement Step | p. 99

4.6.1 Improvement Step

There is an expectation that when personnel and materials transition from a lower area classification to a higher area classification that an improvement step occurs.

For materials, the improvement step can be a cleaning and/or sanitization activity:

  • Depending on the cleanliness of the intended area, it can consist of removing an outer cover or wrapping, a manual wipe down, or fumigation/decontamination.
  • A transition line is recommended for airlocks moving into ISO 8/Grade C and higher areas. Materials should be transferred over the line after they have been cleaned/sanitized.
  • For materials going into a CNC or Grade D space, cleaning can take place outside of the Grade D airlock.

For personnel, the improvement step can include putting on an additional layer of protective clothing.

Improvement Step - Every Grade Crossing Must Be an "Upgrade"

Core Rule of the "Improvement Step"

When moving from a lower-grade area to a higher-grade area, a specific action that raises cleanliness (an improvement step) must be carried out:

  • Materials: remove outer packaging / wipe-down disinfection / fumigation decontamination
  • Personnel: put on an additional layer of protective garments

Transition Line

A clearly visible "transition line" should be set up inside the airlock - materials may cross it only after cleaning and disinfection are complete. This is a simple but highly effective contamination control measure. For airlocks of ISO 8/Grade C and higher, ISPE explicitly recommends providing a transition line.

In practice, the transition line can be a conspicuous strip of colored tape or an inlaid marking on the floor. Some facilities even use different floor colors to distinguish the "dirty side" from the "clean side".

Analogy: the airport security line

It is like passing through airport security: luggage (materials) goes through the X-ray machine (disinfection), and people take off their coats and pass through the metal detector (change into protective garments). The areas before and after the security line have different control levels, and you cannot carry anything unchecked across that line.

4.6

4.6.2 Sequential Transitions

Sequential Transitions | p. 99

4.6.2 Sequential Transitions

Airlock transitions should occur one grade at a time when transitioning from lower to higher (cleaner) classifications, for both personnel and materials. When exiting, it is often acceptable to step down in classification. Although, when exiting from an ISO 7/Grade B production room, an ISO 7/Grade B exit airlock is preferred to protect the critical area.

An airlock should be provided for transitioning from an unclassified environment into CNC or Grade D.

ISO 5/Grade A environments may only be accessed from ISO 7/Grade B environments. Airlocks are generally not provided between ISO 5/Grade A and ISO 7/Grade B; however, clear visual indications and physical barriers should be provided so that the boundary between these environments can be seen and understood by personnel.

ISO 7/Grade B environments should be accessed from ISO 8/Grade C, through airlocks. There should be separate entry airlocks for personnel and materials for entry to ISO 7/Grade B from ISO 8/Grade C rooms. The entry airlock into an ISO 7/Grade B aseptic area should demonstrate ISO 7 "at rest" conditions in the location where the final stages of gowning occurs.

Regular access to mechanical rooms should be from unclassified areas, or provisions should be made to accommodate required airlocks and gowning.

Key Rules for Sequential Transitions

Grade Transition Pathway

On entry, you must step up one grade at a time:

Unclassified → CNC/Grade D → ISO 8/Grade C → ISO 7/Grade B → ISO 5/Grade A

  • Each "→" represents an airlock transition
  • No skipping grades (for example, you may not go directly from Grade D to Grade B)
  • On exit, grades may be skipped, but a Grade B exit is still recommended to have a Grade B airlock to protect the core area

The Special Relationship Between Grade A and Grade B

There is usually no airlock between Grade A and Grade B (because Grade A sits inside the Grade B environment), but there must be:

  • Clear visual indication (such as floor markings or color differentiation)
  • Physical barriers (such as RABS panels or suspended curtains)

When entering Grade B from Grade C, separate airlocks for personnel and materials must be provided. The final gowning stage of a Grade B personnel airlock must meet ISO 7 "at-rest" conditions.

Quick Self-Test

A technician needs to go from the warehouse (unclassified) into a Grade B aseptic filling room. List all the airlocks and gowning steps he must pass through:

  1. Unclassified → Grade D airlock (change into plant garments)
  2. Grade D → Grade C personnel airlock (put on first-layer cleanroom garments)
  3. Grade C → Grade B personnel airlock (put on full sterile garments + gloves + goggles; final gowning area meets ISO 7 at-rest)
  4. Grade B → Grade A: no airlock, but with visual markings and physical barriers
4.6

4.6.3 Airlock Design Philosophies

Airlock Design Strategy | p. 99-101

4.6.3 Airlock Design Philosophies

Airflow direction is generally from higher grade to lower grade. A higher grade room or airlock should be positive to a lower grade room or airlock. Airlock doors should be interlocked or alarmed to prevent both sets of doors from being opened simultaneously, to control the ingress of potential contaminates to the cleaner zones.

Alternate airlock pressurization schemes are often required for containment or the mitigation of cross-contamination between different products. A risk assessment should be performed on such airlocks to evaluate the risk of product contamination versus the potential for cross-contamination or the requirements for containment.

Basic Principles of Airlock Design

Airlock Pressure Differentials and Door Interlocks

  • Airflow direction: From higher grade to lower grade (positive pressure pushing outward)
  • Pressure differential maintenance: The airlock itself should be kept at positive pressure relative to the lower-grade side
  • Door interlock: The two doors must not be open at the same time; use a mechanical interlock or an electronic interlock with alarm

Containment vs. Protection - Exceptions to Pressure Direction

When "containment" is needed, the pressure differential direction may be reversed. For example, when handling highly active or highly toxic products, the airlock must be kept at negative pressure relative to the product area to prevent hazardous substances from escaping. A risk assessment is then required to weigh:

  • Product contamination risk (ingress from outside)
  • Cross-contamination risk (between products)
  • Operator safety (escape of hazardous substances)

4.6.3.1 Personnel Airlocks (PAL)

4.6.3.1 Personnel Airlocks (PAL) from Lower Grade to Higher Grade

Unidirectional flow is suggested for ISO 8/Grade C and higher personnel airlocks (i.e., personnel should not gown and de-gown in the same PAL). If a single airlock is provided, procedures should be established to prevent simultaneous gowning and de-gowning.

PAL considerations include:

  • PALs should have clearly defined changing areas, adequate garment storage, dressing mirrors, and access control.
  • Step-over benches should be used in ISO 8/Grade C and ISO 7/Grade B PALs to put on shoe covers, boot covers, etc.
  • Toilet rooms should not be directly accessed from locker rooms or transfer zones where personnel will change for entry into ISO 8/Grade C or higher areas.
  • Hand washing sinks should be limited to CNC or Grade D areas.
  • Hand sanitizing gels and solutions should be used in higher (cleaner) classifications.

Personnel Airlock (PAL) Design

Five Elements of PAL Design

  • One-way flow: Entry and exit should use different routes (Grade C and above)
  • Step-over bench: Used in Grade C and Grade B PALs for putting on shoe covers, dividing the clean side from the dirty side
  • Gowning mirror: Lets personnel check the completeness of their own gowning
  • Access control: Ensures that only personnel trained in gowning can enter
  • Handwashing facilities: Handwashing sinks only in Grade D and below; Grade C and above use alcohol-based hand sanitizer

Why Can't Higher-Grade Areas Have Sinks?

Sinks are a breeding ground for microorganisms: water, organic matter and warmth together make an ideal culture environment. Drain lines can also harbor waterborne organisms such as Pseudomonas. ISPE therefore specifies that areas of Grade C and above use hand sanitizer instead of water washing. This also echoes the principle in 4.5.2 that there should be no drains in aseptic areas.

Analogy: the step-over bench is like a shoe store fitting bench

The step-over bench works like a fitting bench in a shoe store: you sit down, take off your street shoes and leave them on the "dirty side" of the bench, then swing your feet across to the "clean side" and put on cleanroom shoe covers. This simple physical separation ensures that contaminants on the floor are not carried into the clean area on the soles of shoes.

4.6.3.2 Material Airlocks (MAL)

4.6.3.2 Material Airlocks (MAL) from Lower Grade to Higher Grade

Airlocks should be sized appropriately to allow materials to be staged in the airlocks during disinfectant dwell times and to allow personnel adequate space for movement without compromising the materials or airflows.

Personnel gowning is allowed in a material airlock exclusively to allow personnel access to higher grade airlocks to support the movement of material. Personnel may not enter the production suite through this path.

A transition line should be established when an improvement step takes place within the airlock. Transition across the line requires an improvement activity, either unwrapping or wiping of all materials.

For sequential, adjacent MALs, personnel on the entry side of a MAL may pass through the MAL to the entry side of the higher grade MAL for the purpose of facilitating material movement. For example, CNC or Grade D personnel can go to the entry side of the ISO 8/Grade C MAL (without crossing the transition line).

Note: Manual transfers into ISO 7/Grade B are often inferior to automated sterilization systems or decontamination chambers; these should be used where practical. Decontamination should allow for the required dwell time to assure the effectiveness of disinfection for manual transfers.

Material Airlock (MAL) Design

Unique Design Requirements of a MAL

  • Space and size: Must be able to hold materials during the disinfectant dwell time, while leaving personnel enough room to work
  • Transition line: A transition line is set up inside the MAL; materials may cross it only after being wiped down or de-packaged
  • Personnel restriction: Personnel may gown inside the MAL (only to assist with moving materials), but must not enter the production area via the MAL route
  • Sequential passage: Lower-grade personnel may enter the entry side (dirty side) of the MAL, but must not cross the transition line

Automated vs. Manual Transfer

ISPE explicitly states that manually passing materials into Grade B is generally less reliable than automated sterilization systems or decontamination chambers. Where feasible, an automated solution (such as a VHP decontamination pass-through chamber or a tunnel oven) is recommended. If manual transfer is still required, you must ensure the disinfectant has sufficient contact time (dwell time) to achieve effective disinfection.

4.6.3.3 & 4.6.3.4 Same Grade / Exit Airlocks

4.6.3.3 PAL or MAL within the Same Grade

No additional gowning is required when moving between areas of the same grade, except where required for personnel protection or material containment.

4.6.3.4 Exit Airlocks from Higher Grade to Lower Grade

Generally, personnel and materials can share exit airlocks. Separate personnel and material exit airlocks are preferred at higher classifications where the de-gowning activity is substantial and in areas of high material movement activity.

Separate airlocks must be provided when there is a dwell time associated with material decontamination using chemical disinfectants.

Same-Grade Passage and Exit Airlocks

Same-Grade Passage

Moving between areas of the same grade requires no additional gowning. However, additional measures are still needed where personnel protection (such as for highly active drugs) or material protection (to prevent cross-contamination) is involved.

Exit Airlock Design Principles

  • In principle, personnel and materials may share an exit airlock
  • Separation is recommended for higher-grade areas, because the de-gowning procedure is complex and material traffic is heavy
  • Where materials require chemical disinfection with a dwell time requirement, separate airlocks must be provided

Exit Design Is Often Overlooked

Many facilities focus on the "entrance" in design and neglect contamination control at the "exit". The exit is also a risk point: particles released during de-gowning, the handling of waste materials, and airflow disturbance when doors are opened can all affect the environmental integrity of the higher-grade area.

4.6

4.6.4 Pass Boxes

Pass Boxes | p. 100-101

4.6.4 Pass Boxes

Pass boxes (also known as pass-through boxes or transfer hatches) may be used in lieu of material airlocks for smaller materials, equipment, product containers, waste, samples, etc.

The materials and construction should be compatible with the cleaning regime and consistent with the standards of the room(s) they are located in.

For detailed information about pass boxes, refer to Chapters 5 and 11.

Pass Box

Pass Box vs. Material Airlock

  • Pass box (Pass Box / Pass-Through): Used for small items (samples, containers, waste, etc.); smaller in size and usually built into the wall
  • Material airlock (MAL): Used for large equipment and whole batches of material, and requires personnel to enter and operate
  • Both must have door interlocks, so that the two doors cannot be opened at the same time
  • The construction materials and finishes of a pass box must meet the grade requirements of the room in which it is located

Analogy: the bank pneumatic tube

A pass box is like the pneumatic tube at a bank drive-through: you put your documents in, close the door on your side, and the teller opens the other side to take them out. The doors at both ends are never open at the same time, and the item is transferred inside a closed passage. The difference is that a cleanroom pass box may also have a built-in UV lamp or HEPA filter to further reduce contamination risk.

Integrated Exercise: Design a Grade C to Grade B Transfer Scheme

Your facility needs to transfer the following three types of items from Grade C into a Grade B aseptic filling room. Choose a suitable transfer method for each type:

  1. Environmental monitoring settle plates (small) - suited to a pass box, whose interior can be wiped and disinfected
  2. Stainless steel filling parts (medium, require sterilization) - an automated decontamination pass-through chamber or a tunnel dry-heat sterilizer is recommended
  3. Full pallets of glass vials (large batch) - require a material airlock (MAL), with a transition line and a wipe-down disinfection procedure

Section Summary

  • Five functional zones: Sterile facilities are organized from the aseptic core outward through preparation, pharmaceutical, and support zones, each requiring progressively less stringent controls.
  • Changing room design: Ingress/egress separation, logical gowning progression, grade-matched finishes, and isolation from toilet facilities are essential.
  • Surface finishes escalate by grade: From standard construction (unclassified) to seamless, non-porous, coved, stainless steel finishes (Grade A), with no drains permitted in aseptic areas.
  • Transfer zones maintain contamination barriers: Airlocks use pressure differentials, door interlocks, and improvement steps (cleaning/gowning) to prevent contamination ingress.
  • Sequential one-grade-at-a-time transitions: Entry must progress one classification step at a time; Grade A is accessed only from Grade B without a separate airlock but with clear visual/physical barriers.
  • PAL vs. MAL vs. Pass Box: Personnel and material airlocks serve different functions; pass boxes replace MALs for smaller items; all require door interlocks and grade-appropriate construction.
3c

Chapter 3c: 4c. Architecture (4.7–4.8)

p101-p106

ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 3 (3rd Ed.) | p101 – p106

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the design principles for support areas (gowning rooms, equipment prep, parts washing, buffer preparation, component staging) and their role in maintaining cleanroom integrity
  • Explain why technical support areas should remain separate and unclassified, and how service chases minimize contamination risk
  • Interpret five concept diagrams (Figures 4.4–4.8) showing functional adjacencies for different manufacturing configurations: small/large scale, RABS/isolator, aseptic/terminally sterilized
  • Apply the unidirectional flow principle to material and personnel movement in facility layout
  • Differentiate between segregation by physical barrier, procedural control, and time separation
4.7 Support Areas

Original Text

Technical support areas for the cleanrooms should be proximal to minimize service runs, but kept separate in unclassified areas.

Process support areas should be isolated from the aseptic area. If necessary, they can be adjacent, with vision panels and transfer hatches, and should generally be unclassified. Access would normally be provided by the facility corridor.

Services to equipment, such as autoclaves, may be provided by using a service chase (ideally accessed from outside the production areas).

Autoclaves, tunnels, and washers with access from two sides may have mechanical support rooms accessible from clean areas. Access should be from the less clean of the two areas, with tight seals on the critical side. Such service areas should be kept at pressures negative to the areas to which they connect.

The location of clean utility and CIP/SIP systems should consider the proximity to utility users and serviceability from unclassified areas. Locating these systems above or below the production area may be desirable.

Walkable ceilings can be an optimal solution for the overhead maintenance of cleanrooms. Regulated companies may prohibit access above processing areas during production, as traffic can dislodge particles.

Trainer's Analysis

Core Concept: The Role of Support Areas

Support areas are the "logistics supply chain" of the cleanroom. ISPE divides them into two categories:

  • Technical Support areas: electrical/mechanical maintenance and equipment back-end services; these should remain unclassified and separate from the cleanroom
  • Process Support areas: buffer preparation, parts washing, component staging, etc.; these may be adjacent to the aseptic area but must be segregated from it

Key principle: close but separate. Keep piping and transport distances short while preventing contamination from flowing back.

Analogy: The Support Spaces Around an Operating Room

Picture a hospital operating room. The room itself is the highest-grade clean area, but it needs support spaces around it: an instrument sterilization room (parts washing), a drug preparation area (buffer preparation), a changing area (gowning rooms), and a maintenance access route for equipment.

None of these spaces needs the same air quality as the operating room, but they must be adjacent to it for quick support, and at the same time segregated so that outside contamination cannot get in. The logic for pharmaceutical support areas is exactly the same.

Key Point: Pressure Strategy for Double-Sided Equipment

For equipment that spans two areas, such as autoclaves, tunnels (depyrogenation tunnels), and washers, the maintenance side must follow two rules:

  1. Access from the lower-grade side, so that maintenance personnel do not need to pass through higher-grade areas
  2. Keep the maintenance side at negative pressure, so that air flows "from clean to less clean" and particles cannot flow back from the maintenance corridor into the production area

This is a direct application of the Annex 1 pressure cascade principle at the equipment level.

Walkable Ceiling

A walkable ceiling lets maintenance personnel reach the HEPA filters, light fittings, and sensors of the cleanroom from above, without entering the cleanroom itself.

Restriction: no access during production. Vibration from walking could cause particles to penetrate the ceiling seals and fall into the cleanroom. This is why many companies schedule ceiling maintenance between batches or during shutdowns.

4.7 Support Areas — Design Summary Table

Original Text — Summary

The overarching principle: support areas should be close enough to serve the cleanroom efficiently, but separated enough to prevent contamination. Physical barriers, pressure differentials, and procedural controls are the three tools to achieve this balance.

Trainer's Analysis

Analogy: Front of House and Back of House in a Restaurant

Every high-end restaurant has a strict separation between the front of house (dining area) and the back of house (kitchen, dishwashing room, storage). The back of house must be close to the front for fast service, but cooking fumes, noise, and dirty dishes must never flow back into the dining area.

Pharmaceutical support areas are the "back of house" of the cleanroom:

  • Parts washing area = dishwashing room
  • Buffer preparation = food prep area
  • Service chase = staff circulation route
  • Walkable ceiling = rooftop maintenance access

Review Questions

  1. Your facility has an autoclave that spans between a Grade C filling support room and an unclassified maintenance corridor. Which side should maintenance personnel access it from, and what pressure differential should the maintenance side maintain relative to Grade C?
  2. A CIP skid is currently located inside the Grade D production area. Based on Section 4.7 guidance, would you recommend relocating it? What are the pros and cons?

Practical Application: Support Area Layout Checklist

  • Is the maintenance side of all double-sided equipment (autoclaves, washers) kept at negative pressure?
  • Can the service chase be accessed from outside the production area?
  • Can CIP/SIP systems be maintained from an unclassified area?
  • Is maintenance above the cleanroom ceiling excluded from production time?
  • Do process support areas communicate with the aseptic area through vision panels and transfer hatches?
4.8 Concept Diagrams — Overview

Original Text

Figure 4.4, Figure 4.5, Figure 4.6, Figure 4.7, and Figure 4.8 provide a graphic approach to the concepts discussed in this chapter. These figures are an approach to functional adjacencies and are not layouts or floor plans.

The five concept diagrams cover the following configurations:

  • Figure 4.4 — Small Scale Open System Aseptic Fill with RABS
  • Figure 4.5 — Small Scale Open System Aseptic Fill with Isolators
  • Figure 4.6 — Large Scale Open System Aseptic Fill with RABS
  • Figure 4.7 — Large Scale Open System Aseptic Fill with Isolators
  • Figure 4.8 — Large Scale Open Filling for Terminally Sterilized Product with RABS

Trainer's Analysis

Core Concept: Concept Diagrams vs. Floor Plans

ISPE stresses that these are functional adjacency diagrams, not actual floor plans. They answer the question "which rooms should be next to each other?" rather than "how big are the rooms?"

The value of this approach is that the functional logic (material flow, personnel flow, segregation needs) is settled first, before detailed architectural design begins. Many facility design failures originate from skipping the functional adjacency analysis and drawing floor plans straight away.

Key Point: How the Five Diagrams Are Classified

ISPE uses two dimensions to divide aseptic manufacturing facilities into five typical configurations:

Once you understand these dimensions, you can quickly identify which concept diagram is closest to your facility and use it as the basis for detailed design.

Figure 4.4: Small Scale Open System Aseptic Fill with RABS

Original Text

Notes for Figure 4.4:

  • All processes are open. Compounding is not prepared aseptically. Product is sterile filtered to the filling area. LP/GAAS is used to minimize bioburden.
  • The Parts Wash and Compounding rooms contain open processes with product exposure and should be segregated from other areas. Separate PAL In and PAL Out rooms are provided for the Compounding room, to prevent contamination of clean gowning supplies during de-gowning.
  • The airlocks into the Compounding room can also prevent the transportation of residual product into the corridor and allow for concurrent formulation and filling of multiple products.
  • Dirty parts and utensils are transferred to the Pre-Wash room through the Process Corridor. The Pre-Wash room can be a CNC or Grade D area, provided the final wash/rinse occurs within the pass-through washer which can be unloaded in an ISO 8/Grade C area.
  • The Process Corridor is a shared concurrent path for all non-product exposed items and personnel.
  • If waste cannot be considered closed, then it is an open system and segregation can be provided by procedural means or by transporting waste across the Process Corridor during "off hours" — this is segregation achieved by time separation.

Component transport notes:

  • Transportation of components shall be within RTP canisters or other closed transfer devices which can be docked with the RABS barrier system.

Trainer's Analysis

Key Features of a Small-Scale RABS Facility

This is the most basic aseptic filling configuration, suited to small CDMOs or clinical trial manufacture. Core features:

  • Fully open process: the product is exposed in a non-closed environment, so environmental control is critical
  • Non-sterile preparation: the preparation room does not need a sterile grade, but it must be segregated to prevent cross-contamination
  • Sterile filtration as a critical control point: the product passes through sterilizing filtration before entering the filling area
  • RTP closed-container transfer: components enter the RABS in sealed containers

Key Point: Time Separation

Where physical segregation is not feasible (for example, waste must pass through the process corridor), ISPE allows "time separation": open waste is moved during non-production periods (off hours). This is not an ideal solution, but it is a practical compromise in small facilities with limited space.

If waste contaminates the corridor, cleaning must be completed before production resumes. This means validated cleaning procedures and release criteria are needed.

Analogy: Managing a Shared Corridor

The process corridor is like a public corridor in a hospital: medical staff, visitors, and carts all use the same route. But surgical instruments are transported in sealed carts, and medical waste is removed by designated staff at set times.

The pharmaceutical process corridor follows the same logic: non-exposed items share it, exposed items are transported sealed, and waste is separated by time.

Figure 4.5: Small Scale Open System Aseptic Fill with Isolators

Original Text

Notes for Figure 4.5:

  • Open aseptic processes occur within isolators.
  • The Parts Wash room contains an open process with product exposure and should be a separate room.
  • A Compounding room directly connected to the Filling Suite is for a single product or campaign basis. Compounding of one product and filling for another product cannot be performed simultaneously.
  • The Process Corridor is a shared concurrent path for all non-product exposed items and personnel. It is primarily used to connect personnel from the locker rooms to the ISO 8/Grade C production suite and to transfer materials into the same suite.
  • Having the corridor eliminates the complicated procedures frequently involved with multiple in-line airlocks and allows for proper transitioning through areas of increasing cleanliness.
  • Product containers, stoppers, and caps are either pre-sterilized and ready-to-use, or are batch processed within RTP containers. Pre-wrapped ready-to-use components can be transferred into the isolator via VHP decontamination airlocks built into the isolator.
  • This figure shows the capping process inside the ISO 5/Grade A isolator. Therefore, caps should be sterilized.

Trainer's Analysis

Key Point: The Process Corridor Eliminates Multiple Airlocks

ISPE notes that an important benefit of the process corridor is that it replaces in-line airlocks. In a traditional design, personnel may have to pass through three or four airlocks between the gowning area and the production area, each with its own pressure differential control and procedural requirements.

A well-designed process corridor lets personnel transition naturally through spaces of progressively increasing cleanliness, which simplifies procedures and reduces the risk of human error.

Analogy: The Limitation of Campaign Manufacturing

A design in which "the preparation room connects directly to the filling suite" is like a restaurant with only one prep area. If you prepare steak today, you cannot prepare seafood at the same time, or you get cross-contamination. You must finish one product, clean, and only then start the next. That is campaign manufacturing.

Key Differences Between the Isolator and RABS Configurations

Comparing Figure 4.4 (RABS) with Figure 4.5 (isolator):

Isolators provide higher product protection but sacrifice operational flexibility.

Figure 4.6: Large Scale Open System Aseptic Fill with RABS

Original Text

Notes for Figure 4.6:

  • All processes are open and, therefore, unidirectional flows are provided for the exposed product areas. Compounding is not performed aseptically. Product is sterile filtered to the filling area and aseptic connectors are used.
  • RABS barrier technology is used along with RTP containers for material transfers to minimize manual handling of exposed and sterilized components and reduce the ISO 5/Grade A zones.
  • Automated loading and unloading of the lyophilizer (LYO) eliminates manual handling of filled, partially stoppered vials.
  • The Parts Wash and Compounding rooms contain open processes with product exposure and should be segregated. Separate PAL In and PAL Out rooms are provided for the Compounding room.
  • Dirty parts and utensils are transferred to the Pre-Wash room through the Process Corridor. The Pre-Wash can be a CNC or Grade D area, provided the final wash/rinse occurs within the pass-through washer.
  • This figure assumes the use of ready-to-sterilize stoppers which are sterilized in the pass-through autoclave.
  • The VHP chamber should be utilized to bring items that cannot be autoclaved into the ISO 7/Grade B areas.

Trainer's Analysis

Upgraded Design for Large-Scale RABS

In moving from Figure 4.4 (small scale) to Figure 4.6 (large scale), ISPE adds several key design features:

  • Unidirectional flow: in all product exposure areas, materials and personnel move in one consistent direction, with no backtracking
  • Aseptic connectors: replace open piping connections to reduce exposure risk
  • Automated freeze dryer loading: eliminates the risk of manually handling partially stoppered vials
  • VHP pass-through: handles items that cannot be autoclaved

Key Point: Why Must Large-Scale Facilities Use Unidirectional Flow?

Small facilities can share a path through a process corridor because traffic of people and materials is low and can be managed through procedural controls. In large facilities, traffic is high, and the cross-contamination risk of shared two-way paths rises sharply.

For this reason, ISPE explicitly requires unidirectional flow in large-scale configurations: clean materials move only toward higher grades, and soiled materials move only toward lower grades. This is the concrete practice of separating "material flow" and "personnel flow".

Review Questions

  1. Figure 4.6 mentions the use of "ready-to-sterilize stoppers" that are sterilized in a pass-through autoclave. What would change in the facility layout if you switched to pre-sterilized ready-to-use (RTU) stoppers instead?
  2. Why does ISPE recommend automated LYO loading/unloading for large-scale facilities but not necessarily for small-scale? What risk does manual handling introduce?
Figure 4.7: Large Scale Open System Aseptic Fill with Isolators

Original Text

Notes for Figure 4.7:

  • All processes are closed except for Parts Wash. Filling and stoppering are performed in isolators.
  • The Parts Wash room contains an open process with product exposure and should be segregated from other areas. The bidirectional entry airlock to the Pre-Wash room is provided to allow personnel to over-gown upon entering and de-gown upon exiting to prevent the transportation of exposed product into the Process Corridor.
  • The Process Corridor is a shared concurrent path for all non-product exposed items and personnel.
  • If waste cannot be considered closed, segregation can be provided by temporal means or by transporting waste during "off hours" to the MAL Out.
  • The product transitions from the ISO 5/Grade A isolator to crimping under LP/GAAS. Capping can occur within a RABS within the ISO 8/Grade C environment and the caps do not need to be sterile.
  • Particulates generated by crimping are prevented from entering the isolator by the positive pressure of the isolator and the exiting airflow at the mousehole.
  • This figure shows the option of having capping inside the filling room instead of outside in a Grade D room.

Trainer's Analysis

Isolators + Large Scale: The Highest Level of Protection

Figure 4.7 represents the highest-protection configuration for aseptic filling. Key features:

  • Almost fully closed process: only parts washing is an open process
  • Isolator positive pressure protection: even though capping generates particles, the positive pressure inside the isolator and the outflow of air at the opening (mousehole) prevent particles from flowing back
  • Capping is performed inside a RABS in an ISO 8/Grade C environment, because at this point the vials are fully stoppered and the caps do not need to be sterile

Analogy: The Mousehole Concept

A mousehole is a small opening between the isolator and the outside environment that lets product containers pass through. Think of a ventilation opening in a building: air is always blowing outward, so dust cannot blow in from outside.

The isolator mousehole uses the same principle: positive pressure inside the isolator keeps air flowing out through the mousehole, preventing particles from the capping area from entering the aseptic filling area.

Key Point: Bidirectional Airlock

The bidirectional airlock in the pre-wash area is cleverly designed: personnel put on an over-gown when entering and remove it when leaving. The aim is to ensure that gowns that have touched exposed product are not carried into the process corridor, avoiding cross-contamination from product residues.

This is an important detail of personnel flow management: it is not only about controlling where people go, but also what they carry on them.

Figure 4.8: Large Scale Open Filling for Terminally Sterilized Product with RABS

Original Text

Notes for Figure 4.8:

  • All processes are open. Filling is performed within a RABS under LP/GAAS. Compounding is not produced aseptically or sterile filtered.
  • The Parts Wash and Compounding rooms contain open processes with product exposure and should be segregated. The bidirectional entry airlock into the Pre-Wash room prevents the transportation of exposed product into the Production Hallway.
  • Only one product can be made at a time.
  • The Process Corridor is a common concurrent path for all non-product exposed items and personnel.
  • If waste cannot be considered closed, segregation by temporal means or transport during "off hours" to the MAL Out.
  • Gowning into the ISO 8/Grade C area is unidirectional so the personnel exiting the area do not contaminate the gowning supplies of those who enter the production areas.

Trainer's Analysis

Key Point: Terminal Sterilization Does Not Mean Relaxed Environmental Control

Although terminal sterilization provides an additional safety net, ISPE still requires:

  • Filling takes place in a RABS with LP/GAAS
  • Open process areas need segregation
  • Gowning flow is unidirectional
  • Only one product at a time is manufactured

This reflects the modern regulatory trend: even for terminally sterilized products, pre-fill bioburden should be minimized as far as possible to ensure the sterility assurance level (SAL).

Analogy: One-Way Gowning Flow

Think of a swimming pool changing facility: before entering the pool you go through the shower route (put on swimwear, shower), and after leaving the pool you use a separate exit (rinse, change back into street clothes). If entry and exit used the same path, dripping swimmers would dirty the clean area for those about to enter.

The one-way design of pharmaceutical gowning rooms works on exactly the same principle: people entering do not cross paths with people leaving in the gowning area, so clean gowning supplies are not contaminated.

Terminal Sterilization vs. Aseptic Filling: The Fundamental Difference in Facility Design

Figure 4.8 is the only terminally sterilized configuration, and it differs in essence from the aseptic filling of the previous four diagrams:

Cross-Diagram Comparison — Five Configurations at a Glance

Original Text — Synthesis

Common themes across all five diagrams:

  • Parts Wash rooms with open product exposure must always be segregated
  • Process Corridor serves as shared concurrent path for non-exposed items
  • Waste handling requires either closed containment or time separation
  • RTP canisters or closed transfer devices are required for all component transport
  • PAL In/Out separation prevents gowning contamination

Trainer's Analysis

Design Principles Common to All Five Diagrams

Whichever configuration is chosen, the core design principles ISPE emphasizes remain the same:

  1. Segregate open processes: any room where product is exposed needs separate segregation
  2. Sealed transfer: all component movement between clean areas must take place in closed containers
  3. Separate gowning flows: entry and exit gowning paths are separate, to avoid contaminating clean gowning supplies
  4. Waste management: sealed or time-separated, one or the other
  5. Shared process corridor: but only for non-exposed items and personnel

Practical Application: Choose Your Facility Configuration

You are planning a new aseptic filling facility. Based on the following scenarios, decide which concept diagram fits best:

  1. Annual output of 5 million vials of injectables; the product is heat-stable and can withstand terminal sterilization → ?
  2. Annual output of 100,000 vials of a biologic; heat-labile, requires aseptic filling, limited budget → ?
  3. Annual output of 20 million vials of large-volume parenterals, requiring freeze drying and the highest level of product protection → ?

(Hint: consider the three dimensions of scale, product characteristics, and barrier technology choice)

Review Questions

  1. Why does using isolators allow a lower background classification (ISO 8/Grade C) compared to RABS (ISO 7/Grade B)? What risk trade-off is being made?
  2. All five diagrams mention the Process Corridor as a "shared concurrent path." Under what circumstances would you need to abandon the shared corridor concept and implement fully segregated corridors?
  3. Figure 4.8 (terminally sterilized) is the only configuration that explicitly states "only one product can be made at a time." Why is concurrent production feasible in aseptic configurations (Figs 4.4, 4.6) but not here?
Section Summary

Key Takeaways

Section 4.7 — Support Areas

  • Technical support areas should be proximal to cleanrooms but unclassified and separated
  • Process support areas (compounding, parts wash, buffer prep) should be isolated from aseptic areas, with vision panels and transfer hatches if adjacent
  • Dual-access equipment (autoclaves, washers, tunnels) should be serviced from the less clean side, with the service area at negative pressure
  • Clean utility and CIP/SIP systems should be serviceable from unclassified areas
  • Walkable ceilings enable overhead maintenance without entering cleanrooms, but access must be prohibited during production

Section 4.8 — Concept Diagrams

  • Five concept diagrams illustrate functional adjacencies (not floor plans) for small/large scale facilities using RABS or isolators for aseptic or terminally sterilized products
  • All configurations share common principles: segregation of open processes, closed material transfer, unidirectional gowning, and waste management by containment or time separation
  • Isolators permit lower background classification than RABS due to superior barrier integrity
  • Large-scale facilities require unidirectional flow for product-exposed areas
  • The Process Corridor concept reduces airlock complexity while maintaining contamination control

Key Takeaways

4.7 Support Areas — Key Points

  • Technical support areas (electrical/mechanical maintenance) should be close to the cleanroom but remain unclassified and physically separate
  • Process support areas (preparation, parts washing, buffer preparation) must be segregated from the aseptic area
  • Double-sided equipment is maintained from the lower-grade side, and the maintenance side is kept at negative pressure
  • CIP/SIP systems are best located above or below the production area, so they can be maintained from an unclassified area
  • No access to the walkable ceiling during production

4.8 Concept Diagrams — Key Points

  • The five concept diagrams cover typical configurations across small/large scale, RABS/isolator, and aseptic filling/terminal sterilization
  • All configurations share: segregation of open processes, closed transfer, unidirectional gowning, and sealed or time-separated waste
  • Because of their high barrier integrity, isolators allow a lower background environment grade
  • Large-scale facilities must implement unidirectional flow
  • The process corridor concept simplifies the traditional multiple-airlock design

5.1

Introduction — Scope & Role of HVAC

Pages 107–108

5.1.1 Scope

This chapter deals with creating a suitable environment for the processing of sterile products, including sterile bulks and terminally sterilized products. Biopharmaceutical bulk facilities are covered in the ISPE Baseline Guide: Biopharmaceutical Manufacturing Facilities (Second Edition), but further HVAC details for classified manufacturing space are considered in this Guide.

ISPE has chosen a new harmonized nomenclature for space classification that bridges the differing cleanliness classifications, focusing on the US FDA guidance, EU Annex 1, ISO 14644-1, and ISPE legacy grading systems (see Table 5.3).

For further information, refer to the ISPE Good Practice Guide: Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning, ISPE Baseline Guide: Biopharmaceutical Manufacturing Facilities (Second Edition), and Chapter 11 of this Guide.

5.1.1 Scope

This chapter addresses how to create a suitable environment for the manufacture of sterile products, including sterile bulk active ingredients and terminally sterilized products. Biopharmaceutical bulk drug substance facilities are covered in the ISPE Biopharmaceutical Manufacturing Facilities Guide, but the HVAC details for classified manufacturing spaces are discussed further in this Guide.

Key Point

ISPE has adopted a new harmonized nomenclature to unify cleanroom classifications across regions, combining US FDA guidance, EU Annex 1, ISO 14644-1 and the earlier ISPE classification system (see Table 5.3).

For further information, see the ISPE HVAC Good Practice Guide, the ISPE Biopharmaceutical Manufacturing Facilities Guide and Chapter 11 of this Guide.

5.1.2 The Role of HVAC

The role of HVAC in sterile product facilities is primarily to ensure that the processing environment does not negatively impact product quality. The product and process should be understood, to assess the level of environmental control necessary to reliably make product. The environmental control provided by HVAC typically impacts a very limited number of Critical Process Parameters (CPPs). The critical environmental parameters associated with sterile product quality can include:

  • Airborne particulates (both viable and non-viable, which may contaminate the product)
  • Temperature (which may affect product stability and operator comfort/cleanliness)
  • Humidity (which impacts microbial growth, operator comfort and cleanliness, static electricity, and may impact some products)
  • Relative pressurization (which may impact the ingress and egress of airborne gases and particles)
  • Gaseous contaminants and oxygen concentration (which may impact operator health/safety)
  • Airborne product aerosols (which may impact operator health/safety and cross-contamination risk)

The control of airborne particulates is usually associated with HVAC for sterile manufacturing. HVAC can also indirectly affect surface contamination by limiting the deposition of airborne particulates, but it has limited use in removing deposited (surface) contaminants, due to the high velocities typically required to overcome surface attractions.

Advanced aseptic processing techniques (such as isolators, BFS, single-use technologies, etc.) have influenced the importance of airborne particulate control required in facilities. These advanced technologies are intended to provide enhanced separation of the processing environment from the room environment (and personnel). This separation improves sterility assurance and decreases the impact of room conditions on product quality. Therefore, lower space classifications and HVAC environmental controls may be required, depending on the level of separation provided.

5.1.2 Role of HVAC

The main role of HVAC (heating, ventilation and air conditioning) in a sterile pharmaceutical facility is to ensure that the manufacturing environment does not adversely affect product quality. The product and process must be well understood in order to assess the level of environmental control needed for reliable manufacture. The environmental control provided by HVAC typically affects only a small number of critical process parameters (CPPs).

Six Critical Environmental Parameters

  • Airborne particulates (viable and non-viable, which can contaminate the product)
  • Temperature (affects product stability and operator comfort)
  • Humidity (affects microbial growth, static electricity and some products)
  • Relative pressure (affects the movement of air and particles into and out of a space)
  • Gaseous contaminants and oxygen concentration (affect operator health)
  • Product aerosols (affect health and cross-contamination risk)

Analogy

Think of the HVAC system as the cleanroom's "respiratory system": it continuously supplies clean air and removes contaminants to keep the room environment "healthy". However, HVAC cannot remove surface contamination, because very high air velocities (3,000-5,000 ft/min) would be needed to overcome surface adhesion forces.

Advanced Technology Impact

Advanced aseptic processing technologies such as isolators, BFS and single-use systems provide enhanced separation between the process environment and the room environment. This separation improves sterility assurance and reduces the influence of room conditions on the product, and may therefore allow a lower room classification and less demanding HVAC controls.

Temperature & Humidity Impact on Product

The temperature and humidity of the room can impact the product in four ways:

  • The comfort of operators present in the room can be affected, and therefore impact the number of particles (viable) shed by them. A high degree of protective gowning is usually employed to minimize contamination from operators, but cooler room temperatures and lower relative humidity may be needed to keep operators comfortable with this added gowning.
  • Heat sensitive products (especially large molecules) may need to be processed or stored at temperatures well below those required for comfort.
  • Hygroscopic (or moisture reactive) products may need to be processed at lower relative humidity than is required for health and safety.
  • The temperature and relative humidity of a space significantly impact the growth of microorganisms and can impact the hygiene of a facility.

Four Effects of Temperature and Humidity on the Product

Four Impact Pathways

  • Operator comfort: Higher temperatures increase the number of particles shed by operators. Lower temperature and humidity help personnel who wear heavy protective garments to stay comfortable.
  • Heat-sensitive products: Large-molecule drugs in particular may need to be manufactured or stored at temperatures well below those comfortable for people.
  • Hygroscopic products: May need to be manufactured at a relative humidity lower than that required for health and safety.
  • Microbial control: Temperature and relative humidity significantly affect microbial growth and facility hygiene.
5.1.3

HVAC and Particulate Control for Product Quality

Pages 109–111

5.1.3 HVAC and Particulate Control for Product Quality

HVAC systems control particulates by applying filtration of varying efficiencies to incoming and recirculating airstreams. For the most critical environments (ISO 5/Grade A, ISO 6, ISO 7/Grade B, ISO 8/Grade C), FDA guidance suggests that one layer of HEPA filtration of at least 99.97% efficiency at 0.3 μm particle diameter should be applied (similar to EU filter designation H13). While not required, HEPA filters with 99.99% efficiency (similar to EU filter designation H14) or Ultra Low Penetration Air (ULPA) filters may also be applied to provide enhanced particulate matter control and to comply with integrity testing to a limit of 0.01% penetration as suggested by the FDA.

This filter is typically fitted at the boundary to the room (terminal) to separate the HVAC system from the critical environment, although it is not stipulated in regulations.

EU filter designation F9/MERV 14-15 filtration may achieve ISO 8/Grade C classification at particle sizes ≥ 0.5 μm (depending on room internal particle generation), making this level of filtration suitable for lower class environments (such as Grade D or CNC) or for pre-filtration of air prior to final HEPA filtration.

Regulated companies may employ two or more HEPA filters in series in the most critical environments. This practice may be justified in cases where highly potent products may be present in recirculated air.

Exhaust and return grilles are generally not fitted with filters, but these may be added to protect ductwork and the outside environment where an aerosol of a highly potent or sensitizing product is present or for biosafety level (BSL) above BSL-2.

5.1.3 HVAC and Particulate Control

HEPA Filtration Hierarchy

  • HEPA 99.97% (H13): The minimum recommended by FDA, applicable to ISO 5 through ISO 8
  • HEPA 99.99% (H14): Provides enhanced particulate control and meets the integrity test requirement of 0.01% penetration
  • ULPA filters: Used for critical applications that require higher cleanliness
  • F9/MERV 14-15: Can achieve ISO 8 (≥ 0.5 μm); suitable for lower classifications or as pre-filters

Terminal Filter Placement

HEPA filters are normally installed at the room boundary (terminal position), separating the HVAC system from the critical environment. Although this arrangement is not mandated by regulation, terminal filters are strongly recommended for ISO 7/Grade B and higher classifications, and are common in ISO 8/Grade C systems.

Dual HEPA in Series

In the most critical environments, two or more HEPA filters may be installed in series, particularly where highly potent product may be present in the return air. However, the ISPE HVAC Guide recommends MERV 13/14 filters as an alternative.

Particles in the Critical Area

Particles generated inside the critical area, where sterile product or materials are exposed, may be composed of:

  • The product itself
  • Particles from the process equipment
  • Particles from containers/closures
  • Particles from operators

The difference between particles from these different sources should be understood. Particles of product are not a contaminant and steps should be taken to exclude these during space qualification or environmental monitoring. Particles generated by equipment, materials, or personnel are of concern.

The HVAC system can control particulates within the critical area by providing a flow of clean, nearly particle free air to displace these potential contaminants and sweep them out of the critical area. This unidirectional flow of air from the source, through the critical zone, to a less clean area, and without recirculation back into the critical zone should maintain ISO 5/Grade A conditions and establish LP/GAAS zones.

Particles generated outside the critical zone (i.e., in the room) should be kept out of the critical zone, especially viable particles from operators. This is generally accomplished by use of displacing unidirectional flow and physical barriers. The concentration of particulate within areas outside the critical zone is typically controlled by dilution of airborne particulate with a flow of clean, nearly particle free air.

Particles in Critical Areas

Four Particle Sources

  • The product itself: Not considered a contaminant and should be excluded when monitoring
  • Process equipment: A source of contamination of concern
  • Containers/closures: A source of contamination of concern
  • Operators: The largest source of particulate contamination

Two Control Strategies

Strategy 1, unidirectional airflow displacement: Within the critical area (ISO 5/Grade A), unidirectional airflow (UAF) sweeps from the HEPA filters across the critical area toward less clean areas, carrying contaminants away.

Strategy 2, dilution mixing: Outside the critical area (ISO 7/Grade B, ISO 8/Grade C), particle concentration is diluted with large volumes of clean air. The dilution calculation should be based on the particle generation rate ("source strength").

Air Change Rate (ACR)

Traditionally, the industry has used the Air Change Rate (ACR), expressed in Air Changes per Hour (ACH) to specify the desired diluting airflow. The target ACR has historically been correlated to a specific cleanliness level; however, industry standards such as ISO 14664-4 and IEST-RP-CC012 no longer provide minimum ACH tables and are shifting towards a scientific evaluation utilizing dilution calculations and computer modeling.

While FDA guidance states that a value of 20 ACH is typically acceptable for ISO 8 (0.5 μm, "in operation"), this Guide recommends using ACH as a planning tool and suggests using the following parameters as acceptance criteria for cleanrooms: room particulate, viable concentration, or other empirical measures of room performance (such as recovery, as outlined in ISO 14644-3).

Air Change Rate (ACR / ACH)

Industry Shift

The traditional practice was to specify dilution airflow in air changes per hour (ACH) and link it to a particular cleanliness class. However, standards such as ISO 14644-4 and IEST-RP-CC012 no longer provide minimum ACH tables and have moved toward science-based dilution calculations and computer modeling.

Recommended Approach

FDA suggests 20 ACH as a reference value for ISO 8, but this Guide recommends using ACH only as a planning tool, with the actual acceptance criteria based on:

  • Room particle counts
  • Viable microbial concentration
  • Other empirical performance indicators (such as recovery tests)
5.1.4

Maintaining Environmental Classification

Pages 110–111

5.1.4 Maintaining Environmental Classification

The airborne particulate concentration in a room is the result of a balance of competing factors:

Particles entering the room:

  • Internal activities (particle generation into the space from personnel and processes)
  • Particles entering at the interfaces to outside spaces
  • Particles entering through the HVAC system

Particles retained within the room:

  • Containment devices
  • Adhesion or deposition of airborne particles on surfaces

Particles leaving the room:

  • Returns
  • Effectiveness of airflow patterns in the room and/or unidirectional flow
  • Exhaust of particles from their source

Quantity of air diluting the particles

A good design should include specific controls to address all of these factors:

  • Equipment should be designed for minimal particulate release into the cleanroom. Particle generating components should be fully enclosed and provided with filtered ventilation or remotely mounted outside the clean space.
  • Personnel should be properly gowned in a properly ventilated gowning room.
  • Particles entering at the interfaces should be controlled by air pressure differences, mass flow across openings, or airlocks and pass-through boxes.
  • Particles entering through HVAC should be appropriately filtered.
  • Wherever possible, ensure that generated particles cannot be disseminated through the room by use of containment barriers and exhaust.
  • Ensure rapid removal of particles from the room via evenly distributed low returns, effective airflow patterns, exhaust at source, and adequate dilution air quantity.

In ISO 7/Grade B and ISO 8/Grade C rooms, dilution of airborne particles using high airflow rates of clean supply air is common. Within these rooms, areas of unidirectional flow (e.g., UFH) can be used to create conventional ISO 5/Grade A areas or areas of LP/GAAS.

Historically, unidirectional air has been introduced at nominally 0.45 m/s (90 ft/min) ± 20%, although other velocities (as low as 0.20 m/s / 40 ft/min) may create more favorable airflow patterns. The velocity employed should be periodically verified as consistent with velocities found at the time of airflow visualization.

5.1.4 Maintaining the Environmental Classification

Particle Balance Model

The particle concentration in a room is the result of a balance between several competing factors:

  • Entry: Generation by personnel and process, infiltration through external interfaces, HVAC supply air
  • Retention: Containment devices, surface deposition and adhesion
  • Exit: Return air grilles, efficiency of the airflow pattern, source extraction
  • Dilution: The diluting effect of the air volume

Design Control Principles

  • Equipment should fully enclose particle-generating parts or be fitted with filtered ventilation
  • Personnel should gown correctly in appropriately ventilated changing rooms
  • Interfaces should be controlled using pressure differentials, mass flow or airlocks/pass-through hatches
  • HVAC supply air should be appropriately filtered
  • Use containment barriers and extraction to prevent particle dispersion
  • Use evenly distributed return air grilles, an effective airflow pattern and sufficient dilution air volume

UAF Velocity

Historically, unidirectional airflow velocity has been 0.45 m/s (90 ft/min) ± 20%, but lower velocities (down to 0.20 m/s / 40 ft/min) may produce a better airflow pattern. Velocity should be verified periodically, usually together with filter integrity testing (FIT).

5.1.5

Environmental Classification and Monitoring: Occupancy States

Pages 111–113

"In Operation" State

Both the US FDA and EU require that sterile manufacturing cleanrooms should be designed and tested to ensure proper cleanliness while "in operation". Operational, or "in operation", is defined in ISO 14644-1, Section 3.3 as "agreed condition where the cleanroom or clean zone is functioning in the specified manner, with equipment operating and with the specified number of personnel present".

It is recommended that pharmaceutical "in operation" (also referred to as "dynamic") complies with this ISO definition, with HVAC in operation, including local protection devices, with product or simulated product present, with process equipment running, and the specified number of operating and support personnel performing appropriate tasks.

Regulations require that monitoring of the "in operation" particle counts be continuous during aseptic operations. EU regulations require that this be undertaken with a fixed system within Grade A space. The FDA prefers this approach for ISO 5, but allows for portable equipment. The ISO 7/Grade B space surrounding ISO 5/Grade A space should also be monitored "in operation".

"In Operation" State

"In Operation" Definition

Per ISO 14644-1 clause 3.3, "in operation" means that the cleanroom or clean zone is functioning in the specified manner, with equipment operating and the specified number of personnel present.

For pharmaceutical use, "in operation" is recommended to include: HVAC running, local protection devices active, product or simulated product present, process equipment operating, and operating and support personnel performing appropriate tasks.

Monitoring Requirements

  • EU: Grade A spaces require continuous monitoring of "in operation" particle counts with a fixed system
  • FDA: A fixed system is preferred for ISO 5, but portable equipment is permitted
  • Spaces surrounding ISO 7/Grade B should also be monitored "in operation"

"At Rest" State

In addition to designing for "in operation" conditions, design should account for an "at rest" datum condition to meet EU requirements. "At rest" is defined in ISO 14644-1, Section 3.3 as "condition where the cleanroom or clean zone is complete with equipment installed and operating in a manner agreed upon, but with no personnel present".
