Chapter 4c: 5c. HVAC (5.8–5.10)

p137-p142

ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 3 (3rd Ed.) | p137 – p142

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the rationale for continuous vs. periodic monitoring of HVAC parameters (particle counts, differential pressure, temperature, humidity) and how each contributes to sterility assurance
  • Know the recommended test frequencies for HEPA filter integrity testing, airflow pattern analysis, recovery time testing, and open door testing
  • Describe the role of Environmental Monitoring Systems (EMS) and their compliance with 21 CFR Part 11
  • Explain the IQ/OQ/PQ approach for HVAC qualification, including airflow visualization (smoke studies) and recovery testing
  • Identify critical considerations for differential pressure monitoring: sensor placement, accuracy, reference points, and alarm management
  • Understand HVAC cleaning, maintenance philosophy, and HEPA filter integrity testing as ongoing operational requirements
5.8 Monitoring — HVAC Monitoring

Original Text

It is not possible to assess product sterility on-line. The level of sterility assurance required for sterile products means it is unlikely that random sampling of the finished product will detect any sterility failure resulting from processing.

Such techniques as particle counting (per ISO 14644-2), active and “at rest” air sampling, surface sampling, and personnel sampling provide useful data. Even with this essential and informative data, final product sterility cannot be assured. Hence, aseptic operations rely upon validated procedures carried out in strictly controlled environments for all critical stages to minimize potential product risk.

Certain environmental parameters may be considered critical. These parameters should be monitored and documented, but it is not always possible to do so continuously. Aseptic manufacturing HVAC should have a robust design to minimize potential problems, and a well-considered and qualified monitoring/documenting program.

Parameters that are often continuously or frequently monitored include:

  • Temperature
  • Humidity
  • Differential pressure (DP) between air classes where a contamination path exists
  • Airflow volume rate (volume/time) — continuous monitoring is optional
  • Airborne non-viable particle levels
  • Grade A air supply velocity at 100–150 mm below the filter face — continuous monitoring is optional

Typically, periodic requalification may repeat some tests carried out as part of the original equipment qualification, such as:

  • Integrity testing of terminal HEPA filters
  • Confirming airflow or air change rates
  • Checking ISO 5/Grade A and LP/GAAS velocities at a defined distance proximal to the work surface and below the filter face (typically 300 mm above vial, 100–150 mm below filter)
  • Checking ISO 5/Grade A and LP/GAAS airflow patterns
  • Checking airflow patterns at the interface between ISO 5/Grade A and ISO 7/Grade B as well as between ISO 7/Grade B and surrounding areas
  • Recording room airflow patterns (optional in ISO 7/Grade B and ISO 8/Grade C)
  • Confirming room recovery time
  • Open door testing (confirming how long a door can remain open without need for an alarm)
  • Checking operator product exposure levels
  • Airborne non-viable particle levels (classification)
  • Shut down and restart testing
  • Reduced flow rate testing
  • Verification of impact of loss of HVAC on environmental control (time before triple clean is required)
"Airflow pattern analysis (visualization) outside of the Grade A zone may be undertaken as a qualification activity or as an engineering study."

Teaching Notes

Core Concept: Why Product Testing Alone Is Not Enough

The sterility assurance level (SAL) of a sterile product is normally required to reach 10-6, meaning no more than one non-sterile unit in a million. In practice, you can almost never detect contamination in the finished product by random sampling.

The quality assurance logic of sterile manufacturing is therefore process-oriented rather than result-oriented: we monitor environmental conditions to ensure the process stays in a state of control, rather than testing the product for sterility after the fact.

This is the fundamental reason HVAC monitoring matters so much: it is the cornerstone of process control.

Continuous Monitoring vs. Periodic Monitoring

ISPE divides monitoring into two broad categories:

  • Continuous monitoring: temperature, humidity, differential pressure, particle counts. These parameters change quickly, so abnormalities must be detected in real time.
  • Periodic requalification: HEPA integrity testing, airflow pattern analysis, recovery time testing. These are deeper, systematic verifications of system performance.

Continuous monitoring tells you "Is it normal right now?"; periodic requalification tells you "Is the system fundamentally sound?"

Analogy

Daily health tracking vs. the annual physical:

Continuous monitoring is like the smartwatch you wear every day, constantly tracking heart rate, blood oxygen, and body temperature. As soon as a value looks abnormal, it alerts you.

Periodic requalification is like the annual comprehensive check-up, with in-depth examinations such as X-rays, blood tests, and an ECG.

You would not skip your annual physical just because your watch shows normal readings every day; likewise, you would not skip HEPA integrity testing just because differential pressure is within specification every day. The two complement each other, and neither can be dropped.

Key Point: The Requalification Test List

ISPE lists 13 periodic requalification tests. For CDMO operations, the most critical ones are:

  • HEPA filter integrity testing — a single leaking HEPA filter can contaminate an entire area
  • Airflow pattern analysis (smoke studies) — confirms that unidirectional flow is actually present and undisturbed
  • Recovery time testing — how quickly a cleanroom returns to its classification standard after a contamination event
  • Open door testing — confirms how long a door can be open without causing the environment to go out of control

These items bear directly on whether a deviation investigation must be initiated.

5.8.2 Typical Frequencies for Testing

Original Text

The test frequency for each test depends upon plant operating experience, the process/equipment qualification findings, and regulatory expectations. It may also vary from area to area. Considerations for testing frequencies are as follows:

  • Room airborne particles should be checked frequently as established by the EM plan. Use of automated continuous particle monitoring is recommended. Automated particle monitoring systems provide extensive relevant data on the state of the environment and are generally more reliable than manual monitoring.
  • Integrity testing of terminal HEPA filters should typically be performed twice per year in aseptic fill environments and once every year or two in less critical areas. The rationale for the testing frequency should be supported by ongoing data.
  • Checking ISO 5/Grade A and LP/GAAS velocities and uniformity at the filter face should be performed when integrity testing the HEPA filters.
  • Checking room airflow patterns is usually performed at HVAC qualification, but may be justified when room equipment layouts change.
  • The need for retesting ISO 5/Grade A and LP/GAAS patterns should be assessed whenever the process physically changes (such as new or relocated equipment) or when operator procedures change; otherwise, the frequency should be every 3 to 5 years.
  • Determining how long a door may remain open should be performed at qualification and every 3 to 5 years thereafter.
  • Confirmation of recovery time (EU) should be performed at qualification. There is no fixed requirement for re-verification frequency; this should be determined by risk assessment.
  • Parameters such as operator product exposure levels should be tested frequently for reasons other than GMP.

Teaching Notes

Why Is HEPA Integrity Testing (DOP/PAO) So Critical?

DOP/PAO integrity testing (aerosol challenge testing with dioctyl phthalate or poly-alpha olefin) is the only reliable method to verify that a HEPA filter does not leak.

A leaking HEPA filter will not necessarily show up in differential pressure monitoring: the differential pressure may remain normal even though large numbers of particles are passing through. This is why ISPE recommends testing aseptic filling areas twice a year.

Common leak locations:

  • Pinholes or tears in the filter media itself
  • The gasket between the filter frame and the ceiling grid
  • Cracks or deformation in the frame itself

A leak at any of these points can let outside particles enter the Grade A area directly, which amounts to losing the last line of defense.

Analogy: Regular Inspection of a Bulletproof Vest

A HEPA filter is like the "bulletproof vest" of the aseptic area. Even if it feels fine when you wear it (normal differential pressure), you still need to inspect it regularly for wear and cracks (DOP/PAO testing).

A vest that looks intact but whose internal fibers have degraded may fail completely when hit by a bullet (a particle). In the same way, a HEPA filter that looks normal but has a tiny leak may be unable to protect the product when faced with the real particle challenge of a production environment.

5.8.3–5.8.4 Environmental Monitoring Systems & Typical EMS Monitoring

Original Text

5.8.3 Environmental Monitoring Systems

From an engineering perspective, automated environmental monitoring should provide feedback on the HVAC system’s overall performance. It should highlight lack of performance in an individual system or room and notify the occupants of the condition.

An automated Environmental Monitoring System (EMS) is recommended to provide a GMP record of critical environmental parameters. Automated monitoring systems should comply with US FDA 21 CFR Part 11 and be subject to validation to assure the accuracy of the readings and records produced by the system.

EU Annex 1 requires that HVAC monitoring systems notify occupants when the HVAC has failed. The monitoring system should notify the occupants when any critical parameter is out of specified range for more than a predetermined period of time. The system should be equipped with colored warning lights to indicate the state of the HVAC system.

5.8.4 Typical EMS Monitoring for Aseptic HVAC

Differential Pressures

All DPs within a sterile area environmental cascade should be continuously measured, indicated, recorded, and alarmed. It may be advisable to select a representative number of particular DP measurements as key indicators of overall HVAC system “health.”

Additional considerations for monitoring of DPs include:

  • Monitor DP across airlocks; DP should not go to zero as long as one door in the contamination path remains closed.
  • DP sensors can be employed to detect door opening and control the time that doors remain open.
  • Only one DP sensor is needed per room, but it should be located to minimize impact of air currents at the sensor.
  • The monitoring system should document the duration of an unexpected loss (reduction) in pressure differential.
  • Reversed direction of airflow across a door is undesirable and should only occur for brief intervals.
  • The accuracy of differential measurement devices is critical. For control to ± 2.5 Pa, an accuracy of 0.25 Pa is desirable.
  • The reference point selected for DP measurements is critical. If measurements are made to a central reference, this reference point should be located in a large stable space.

Airflow to Rooms

While continuous measurement of airflow is not required, assurance of a consistent airflow supply is an indirect indicator of the ability to dilute contaminants and of room environmental control. Airflow monitoring is usually continuous since an airflow volume/velocity monitor is often installed to adjust fan delivery to compensate for air filter loading.

If a variable airflow scheme (such as idle airflow setback) is utilized, room airflow measurement is recommended. These schemes typically are not implemented until 15–20 minutes after cessation of use to allow for recovery.

Temperature and Humidity

Temperature and humidity for rooms with critical operations should be monitored to ensure control of operator comfort, product temperature, humidity requirements, and bioburden. Monitoring and data collection at short intervals (minutes instead of seconds) should provide adequate data without creating data overload.

The accuracy of temperature and humidity instruments is critical. Platinum RTD are preferred for temperature reading and capacitance sensors are preferred for RH.

Airborne Particle Count (Total or Non-viable)

In critical zones (e.g., ISO 5/Grade A and at ISO 5/Grade A to ISO 7/Grade B interface), the use of automated continuous particle monitoring is recommended. Automated particle monitoring systems provide extensive relevant data on the state of the environment and are generally more reliable than manual monitoring.

Teaching Notes

The Three Main Functions of an EMS

An environmental monitoring system (EMS) does more than "record data"; it plays three key roles:

  1. Real-time feedback: continuously monitors the overall performance of the HVAC system and notifies you immediately when a problem arises
  2. GMP records: meets the electronic record requirements of 21 CFR Part 11, including audit trails, electronic signatures, and data integrity protection
  3. Alarm management: when a critical parameter goes out of specification, operators are notified by colored beacons and audible alarms

Key Details of Differential Pressure (DP) Monitoring

Differential pressure is one of the most important continuously monitored parameters for environmental control in aseptic areas. ISPE sets out several key requirements for DP monitoring:

  • Accuracy: for a control range of ±2.5 Pa, sensor accuracy must reach 0.25 Pa (that is, 10% of the control range)
  • Choice of reference point: choose a large, stable space as the reference point. The outdoors is a poor reference because wind speed is unstable; a mechanical room is also unsuitable because of its temperature-controlled ventilation
  • Airlock differential pressure: as long as one door along the contamination path remains closed, the differential pressure should not fall to zero
  • Reverse airflow: brief reverse airflow may occur when a door opens, but it should last only a very short time

Analogy: Differential Pressure Is Like the Water-Level Difference at a Dam

Imagine the aseptic area as a reservoir at a high elevation, and the outside environment as a river far below. Differential pressure is the difference in water level between the reservoir and the river. As long as that difference exists (positive pressure), water (air/particles) can only flow from high to low, and contaminants from outside cannot flow back into the aseptic area.

If the level difference drops to zero or even reverses, river water will flow back in. This is why a pressure reversal (reversed airflow) is regarded as a serious event.

A DP sensor is like the water gauge on the reservoir: it must be installed in a stable location unaffected by turbulence in order to give accurate readings.

Practical Points for Temperature, Humidity, and Particle Monitoring

  • Temperature sensors: platinum resistance temperature detectors (Platinum RTDs) are recommended for their high accuracy and stability
  • Humidity sensors: capacitance sensors are recommended for their fast response and durability
  • Data acquisition frequency: intervals of minutes are sufficient (seconds are not needed), which avoids data overload while still providing adequate resolution
  • Large rooms: perform temperature mapping to determine the most representative monitoring locations
  • Particle monitoring: for critical areas (ISO 5/Grade A), automated continuous particle counters are strongly recommended, as they are more reliable than manual monitoring
5.8.5 HVAC Controls (Building Automation System / Building Management System)

Original Text

When considering the HVAC control system, it is important to consider it as another service supporting environmental condition control. Automatic controllers may indirectly affect patient safety and product quality, but performance can be monitored by a qualified EMS. HVAC controls would not need to be qualified; HVAC field devices would only need to be qualified when HVAC control and environmental monitoring are shared.

HVAC automatic controls may be employed to control variables such as temperature and humidity. In more complex designs, other variables may also be controlled:

  • Room DP (especially where airflows to/from rooms are expected to vary)
  • Constant supply and extract fan volume control (to compensate for air filter loading)
  • Filter blinding condition (pressure drop) monitoring
  • Active room pressure control

During design, risk assessment should be performed to assess the positive and negative impacts of an automatic control system. Considerations include:

  • What would happen if constant fan volume control were not employed?
  • What would happen if an active pressure control system failed?
  • Does the system incorporate fail safe features?
  • Does the control design prevent catastrophic failures such as duct collapse and airflow reversals?
  • Are visible and audible alarms included to monitor environmental control changes?

Teaching Notes

BAS/BMS vs. EMS: Keep the Roles Clear

This is an easily confused concept, and ISPE draws a clear distinction:

  • BAS/BMS (building automation system): is responsible for controlling the HVAC, regulating temperature, humidity, airflow, and differential pressure. It is the executor.
  • EMS (environmental monitoring system): is responsible for monitoring and recording environmental parameters, producing GMP-compliant records. It is the supervisor.

Key principle: the BAS/BMS itself does not need to be validated (because the EMS can independently verify its performance), but if the BAS and EMS share field devices (such as the same sensor), those devices must be qualified.

This reflects a risk-based approach: only the parts that directly affect GMP records are validated.

Risk Assessment Questions at the Design Stage

The five risk assessment questions listed by ISPE all essentially ask the same thing: "If this control fails, what is the worst that can happen?"

The two most severe failure modes:

  • Duct collapse: can be caused by excessive negative pressure resulting from a fan control failure, and can bring down the entire HVAC system
  • Airflow reversals: contaminants flow from a lower-cleanliness area to a higher-cleanliness area, directly threatening product sterility

Fail-safe mechanisms must be built in at the design stage, for example, automatically opening a bypass when a fan fails, or automatically closing the supply air damper when differential pressure is too low.

Scenario Thinking

  1. During an audit, your site is asked: "Has the BAS been validated?" How would you answer, and on what basis?
  2. If the BAS and EMS share the same differential pressure sensor, how does the validation scope change, and why?
  3. An active pressure control system suddenly fails. Which environmental parameters would you expect to change, and how should you respond?
5.9 Qualification of HVAC Systems

Original Text

HVAC systems serving an aseptic manufacturing suite should be considered as a system which may affect patient safety and product quality. Qualification, testing, and commissioning, in line with GEP, should be considered.

For additional information, refer to ISPE Baseline Guide: Commissioning and Qualification [34]. Field qualification procedures are detailed in ISO 14644-3 (Cleanrooms and Associated Environments, Part 3 – Test Methods).

Teaching Notes

The IQ/OQ/PQ Framework for HVAC Qualification

Although ISPE gives only an overview in this section and refers to other guides, the standard HVAC qualification process is worth understanding in full:

  • IQ (installation qualification): verifies that the HVAC system is installed correctly according to design specifications. This includes confirming equipment model and serial numbers, checking piping connections, HEPA filter installation and seal integrity, electrical wiring, and control system configuration
  • OQ (operational qualification): verifies that the system operates correctly across its designed operating range. This includes airflow volume testing, differential pressure cascade verification, temperature and humidity control testing, alarm function testing, and failure mode testing
  • PQ (performance qualification): verifies the sustained performance of the system under actual production conditions. This includes airflow visualization (smoke studies), recovery time testing, particle classification testing, and HEPA integrity testing

Smoke Studies: The Core of Airflow Visualization

Airflow visualization is the most visually striking test in the PQ stage. By releasing smoke in critical areas, you can directly observe:

  • Whether the Grade A area truly maintains unidirectional flow
  • Whether the airflow is disturbed by operator interventions
  • The direction of airflow at the interface between Grade A and Grade B
  • Whether there is any turbulence or dead zone

Smoke study results are usually recorded on video as part of the qualification documentation. This is one of the documents most often requested for review during regulatory inspections.

Recovery Testing

Recovery time is the time a cleanroom needs to return to its classification standard after a contamination event.

EU Annex 1 requirements:

  • Grade A: recovery time should be less than 15 minutes (from the "at rest" state until the particle count meets the limit)
  • Grade B: recovery time should be less than 15-20 minutes

Recovery time directly reflects the air change capability and filtration efficiency of the HVAC system. The shorter the recovery time, the more robust the system, and the faster it can eliminate the effects of an abnormal event.

In practice, recovery testing usually simulates a contamination event by generating aerosol particles artificially, then measures how long the particle counter takes to return to baseline.

Analogy: The Self-Cleaning Ability of a Swimming Pool

Recovery time is like the self-cleaning ability of a swimming pool. If someone pours a bottle of ink into the pool (a contamination event), how long does the circulation and filtration system need to restore the water to clear and transparent (meet the classification standard)?

A pool with a powerful circulation pump and high-efficiency filters (high air change rate + HEPA) may clear up within minutes, while a pool with insufficient circulation may need several hours.

This is why air change rate and HEPA filtration efficiency are the two key factors determining recovery time.

5.10 Cleaning and Maintenance of HVAC Systems

Original Text

5.10.1 Air System Cleaning and Sanitization

  • Ductwork should be manufactured, inspected, and installed according to GEP.
  • To minimize potential for growth of bioburden within the duct, ductwork should be cleaned internally prior to assembly, and temporarily sealed after installation.
  • Periodic cleaning of duct systems is not normally required due to the performance of pre-filtration.
  • Fumigating production rooms may be desirable for control of microorganisms. The HVAC system should be specially designed to isolate rooms to allow fumigation without circulation of the agent to surrounding spaces. Room pressurization may need to be controlled to prevent migration of sanitizing agent.
  • Fumigating some or all of the system may be desirable where highly potent or pathogenic materials are handled. The system should be designed to allow fumigation through the HVAC system without circulation to surrounding spaces. HVAC system materials should be selected with this procedure in mind.

5.10.2 Maintenance Philosophy

  • As much of the system as possible should be accessible and maintained from outside the aseptic processing area.
  • When replacement of terminal air filters (and lighting) are expected to be more frequent than planned maintenance shutdowns, access to these items from outside the processing area should be considered.
  • Access should not require working directly on ceilings from above.
  • HVAC designers should understand the planned facility maintenance philosophy.
  • An effective and fast-response breakdown maintenance plan can minimize the economic impact of unplanned HVAC shutdowns.
  • HVAC maintenance personnel should be trained on the system and its effect on the product/process.
  • Critical components in systems which affect patient safety and product quality should be under quality change control.
  • Thoroughly investigate the impact of filter leaks to determine patient and product risk. Proper investigation of filter leaks can determine if contamination that penetrates HEPA filters has the potential to jeopardize patient safety.
  • Refer to ISO 14644-3 for suggested commissioning and retesting procedures.

Teaching Notes

Practical Principles for Duct Cleaning

A common misconception is that cleanroom ducts need to be cleaned regularly. ISPE states clearly: because of the effectiveness of pre-filtration, duct systems generally do not require periodic cleaning.

This rests on several preconditions:

  • The ducts were cleaned internally before installation
  • After installation they were temporarily sealed to keep construction dust out
  • The pre-filters and medium filters are working properly and capture the vast majority of particles

If these preconditions do not hold (for example, pre-filters have gone unchanged for a long time), dust may accumulate inside the ducts and microorganisms may even grow there.

HVAC Design Considerations for Fumigation

Fumigation is an effective means of controlling microorganisms, but it places special requirements on HVAC design:

  • Room isolation: the HVAC system must be able to completely isolate the room to be fumigated from other areas, preventing the fumigant from spreading
  • Pressure control: room pressure must be controlled during fumigation to prevent the fumigant from migrating into other spaces
  • Material compatibility: when handling highly toxic or pathogenic materials, HVAC system materials must withstand corrosion by the fumigant (such as VHP/formaldehyde)

Common fumigants: vaporized hydrogen peroxide (VHP), formaldehyde, and chlorine dioxide (ClO2).

Core Principle of the Maintenance Philosophy

The maintenance philosophy proposed by ISPE can be summed up in one core idea: "Perform maintenance from outside the clean area wherever possible."

This means the following must be considered at the design stage:

  • Walk-on ceiling: allows maintenance personnel to replace HEPA filters and light fixtures from the interstitial space above, without entering the cleanroom
  • Maintenance access design: the maintenance side of equipment faces a non-clean area or a technical corridor
  • Replacement frequency: if HEPA filters are replaced more often than planned shutdowns occur, external replacement access must be provided

Every entry into the clean area for maintenance brings contamination risk and lost production time, so a good design should minimize this need.

Investigating HEPA Filter Leaks

ISPE specifically stresses that the impact of a filter leak must be thoroughly investigated. This is not simply a matter of replacing the filter and moving on:

  • You need to determine when the leak began (looking back to the last passing DOP/PAO test)
  • You need to assess whether all production batches during the leak period were affected
  • You need to analyze whether the contaminants that passed through the HEPA filter have the potential to affect patient safety
  • You need to evaluate whether the scope of the environmental monitoring data review should be expanded

This is why the frequency of HEPA integrity testing and the completeness of its records matter so much: they determine the time window and scope of impact of a leak investigation.

Practical Application: Impact Assessment of a HEPA Leak

Suppose a leak is found in the Grade A HEPA filter in your aseptic filling area during the six-month DOP test. These are the key steps you need to carry out:

  1. Confirm the last passing date: look back to the date of the most recent passing DOP/PAO test
  2. List the affected batches: all batches filled in this area during that period
  3. Review EM data: check whether particle counts and microbial monitoring show any abnormal trends in that period
  4. Risk assessment: assess product risk based on the size and location of the leak and the EM data
  5. CAPA: replace the filter, analyze the root cause (aged gasket? improper installation? vibration damage?), and adjust the test frequency
Section Summary

Key Takeaways

Core Principles from Sections 5.8–5.10

  1. Sterility cannot be tested into the product. Environmental monitoring through validated HVAC systems is the primary assurance mechanism for aseptic manufacturing.
  2. Continuous monitoring + periodic requalification provide complementary assurance. Key continuous parameters: DP, temperature, humidity, particle counts. Key periodic tests: HEPA integrity (DOP/PAO), airflow visualization (smoke studies), recovery testing.
  3. HEPA filter integrity testing is the most critical periodic test. Recommended frequency: twice per year for aseptic fill areas. A leaking HEPA can compromise an entire zone without triggering DP alarms.
  4. DP monitoring accuracy and reference point selection are engineering decisions with direct GMP impact. Accuracy should be 10% of the control range; reference points must be in stable pressure zones.
  5. EMS must comply with 21 CFR Part 11 and be validated. BAS/BMS does not require qualification unless it shares field devices with EMS.
  6. HVAC maintenance should be performed from outside the aseptic area wherever possible, to minimize contamination risk from maintenance activities.
  7. HEPA filter leaks require thorough investigation — not just replacement, but retrospective assessment of all production batches since the last passing integrity test.

Key Takeaways

Core Points of Sections 5.8-5.10

  1. Sterility cannot be assured by finished-product testing. Environmental monitoring through a qualified HVAC system is the primary assurance mechanism in sterile manufacturing.
  2. Continuous monitoring + periodic requalification provide complementary assurance. Continuous monitoring: differential pressure, temperature, humidity, particles. Periodic testing: HEPA integrity (DOP/PAO), airflow visualization (smoke studies), recovery testing.
  3. HEPA filter integrity testing is the most critical periodic test. Twice a year is recommended for aseptic filling areas. A leaking HEPA filter can contaminate an entire area even when differential pressure is normal.
  4. The accuracy and reference point selection of differential pressure monitoring are engineering decisions that directly affect GMP. Accuracy should be 10% of the control range; the reference point must be in a pressure-stable area.
  5. The EMS must comply with 21 CFR Part 11 and be validated. The BAS/BMS does not need to be validated unless it shares field devices with the EMS.
  6. HVAC maintenance should be performed from outside the clean area wherever possible, to minimize the contamination risk from maintenance activities.
  7. HEPA filter leaks require thorough investigation — not just replacing the filter, but also looking back at all production batches since the last passing integrity test.

Comprehensive Review Questions

  1. List four critical HVAC parameters that require continuous monitoring in an aseptic filling area, and explain the monitoring purpose of each.
  2. Explain why DOP/PAO testing can find problems that differential pressure monitoring cannot detect. Give a specific scenario.
  3. Your site is designing a new aseptic area. What design approach would you recommend for HEPA filter replacement and maintenance, and on what basis?
  4. A quality staff member proposes reducing the HEPA integrity test frequency from twice a year to once a year to save costs. How would you evaluate this proposal, and what data would you need to support the decision?
  5. Explain how recovery testing is performed and why it is a key indicator for HVAC performance qualification.

Chapter 5: 6. Utility Systems

p143-p150

ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 3 (3rd Ed.) | p143 – p150

Learning Objectives

  1. Distinguish between Process Systems and Process Support Systems and understand the criteria for classification
  2. Understand the critical quality attributes of WFI, clean steam, and process gases in sterile manufacturing
  3. Identify key design considerations for utility distribution, filtration, and point-of-use requirements
  4. Recognize the importance of risk-based approaches to utility system qualification and sterile boundary definition
  5. Apply CDMO-relevant principles: utility capacity planning for multi-product facilities
6.1 Introduction

6.1 Introduction

Utility systems used in sterile facility operations may be categorized as either Process Systems or Process Support Systems. The sterile product manufacturer should review the various systems within the facility and determine their respective categories. This provides the basis for determining the design, construction, commissioning, verification, and documentation requirements for the system.

Process Systems are systems that:

  • Contact the product (as defined by the ASME BPE Standard as a surface that contacts raw materials, process materials, and/or product)
  • Contact materials or components which ultimately become part of the product
    • Process components include piping, fittings, valves, gaskets, vessels, pumps, filter housings, and instruments
  • Control contamination of surfaces that contact the product
  • Could otherwise directly affect product quality as determined through risk assessment (e.g., systems that prepare components and equipment for production)

Process Support Systems are systems that:

  • Do not contact the product or materials which ultimately become part of the product
  • Are generally site or building systems that are not specifically tailored to sterile manufacturing operations
  • Deal with an ancillary manufacturing process (e.g., waste disposal)
  • Do not explicitly affect product quality as determined through risk assessment

Examples of system categorization:

  • Purified water (depending on use), WFI, and clean steam are normally categorized as Process Systems.
  • Airflow of a depyrogenation tunnel or barrier isolator is generally a Process System since air contacts product contact components.
  • Compressed air and inert gases may be either Process or Process Support Systems, depending on use.
    • Sterile compressed air for post-SIP sterilization or pressure transfer of product to filling = Process System.
    • Compressed air used as instrument air without product contact = Process Support System.
  • Breathing air, chilled water, instrument air, potable water, and floor drains are normally Process Support Systems.

Systems should be defined with clear system boundaries, indicating the scope of the sections that are subject to more stringent testing and commissioning activities.

6.1 Introduction: Analysis

Core Concept: Process Systems vs. Process Support Systems

This chapter divides the utilities in a sterile facility into two categories:

  • Process Systems: systems that contact the product or affect product quality. They require rigorous design, construction, commissioning, and qualification.
  • Process Support Systems: auxiliary systems that do not contact the product. They need only be designed in accordance with Good Engineering Practice (GEP).

The key classification questions: Does the system contact the product? Does it affect product quality?

Real-Life Analogy: Water Sources in a Restaurant

Imagine a restaurant:

  • Process systems are like the purified water used in the kitchen: it goes directly into food preparation and must meet drinking-water standards.
  • Process support systems are like the tap water used to rinse the floor: it does not touch the food, so cleaning-grade water is enough.

But if the tap water accidentally splashes onto the ingredients, it creates a contamination risk. Likewise, a poorly designed process support system (for example, instrument air exhausting into an ISO 5 area) can also affect the product.

Key Point: Defining System Boundaries

ISPE stresses that clear system boundaries must be defined for every system. This determines:

  • Which parts require rigorous commissioning & qualification
  • Which parts need only follow GEP
  • The scope of documentation required

In a CDMO environment, the same compressed air line may serve both process and instrument purposes, so the two must be clearly separated at a system boundary.

6.2 Descriptions

6.2.1 Process Systems

Process Systems are considered to affect patient safety and product quality, and therefore, should be designed, constructed, commissioned, and verified to provide a service that meets a defined specification (considering product quality requirements) and prevents product contamination accordingly.

Design considerations for Process Systems:

  • Appropriate materials of construction for process contact surfaces that allow systems to be cleaned, sterilized if required, operated, and maintained
  • Appropriate materials of construction for non-product contact surfaces that could affect the particulate count within the cleanroom
  • Exposure to cleaning materials of the room
  • Access for removal or maintenance
  • Particulates generated from rotating parts of equipment exhausts which could affect the particulate count of the cleanroom
  • Control of the system in service, out of service, and returned to service cases
  • Functional use and operator interaction
  • Ergonomic functionality

For material selection, refer to the ASME BPE Standard. Selection of materials for fluid storage and distribution systems should consider the nature of the fluid being conveyed. For non-corrosive liquids and gases (such as nitrogen), typical materials include copper, plastics, and stainless steel.

Regulated companies should consider the type of cleaning agents and sterilants to be used and how those chemicals affect the surface of the equipment contacting the process. Each piping component and connection should be reviewed to determine how the system should be sterilized and whether the materials of construction are appropriate.

Service components and piping should be located outside the aseptic area, where possible. Surfaces inside the cleanroom should be sanitized or sterilized to meet or exceed allowable limits for bioburden.

Single-use systems should be designed to protect product integrity and prevent contamination from interrupted connections. Single-use systems and connections should be designed for routine operator interaction and functionality.

6.2.1 Process System Design Considerations

Core Concept: Eight Key Design Considerations for Process Systems

When designing a process system, review the following aspects systematically:

  1. Product-contact surface materials: cleanable, sterilizable, and resistant to operation and maintenance
  2. Non-contact surface materials: do not add to the particle count in the cleanroom
  3. Resistance to cleaning agents: able to withstand cleanroom cleaning chemicals
  4. Maintenance accessibility: easy to disassemble or repair
  5. Particle control: exhaust from rotating parts does not affect cleanliness
  6. Service state management: in operation, out of service, and return to service
  7. Operator interaction: functionality and human factors
  8. Human factors design: compliant with ergonomic principles

Key Point: Principles for Material Selection

  • Product-contact surfaces: select in accordance with ASME BPE, typically 316L stainless steel
  • Non-corrosive fluids (such as nitrogen): copper, plastic, or stainless steel may be used
  • The effect of cleaning agents and sterilants on surfaces must be considered
  • Piping and components should be located outside the sterile area wherever possible

CDMO Perspective: Single-Use Systems

For a CDMO, single-use systems are an important strategy for multi-product manufacturing:

  • Reduce cross-contamination risk: no cleaning validation needed between products
  • Reduce the complexity of shared equipment
  • However, connection integrity must be ensured: breached connections are a major source of contamination

6.2.2 Process Support Systems

Process Support Systems generally do not affect patient safety and product quality, and should be designed and constructed in compliance with GEP and applicable codes and standards. Such systems typically are not located within a cleanroom; therefore, the materials of construction depend upon service requirements.

If these services or their points-of-use need to be located in the aseptic area, the materials of construction should be:

  • Non-additive
  • Non-reactive
  • Non-absorptive
  • Able to withstand repeated sanitation with harsh chemicals

Care should also be taken to prevent accidental spills and possible contaminant release into the area (e.g., point of use or vent filters for an instrument air supply line where instrument air may vent into an ISO 5/Grade A critical zone).

Preventative maintenance and equipment integrity should be established at locations where the process can be impacted (e.g., process heat exchanger integrity, piping integrity, equipment seals between process and process support systems).

6.2.2 Process Support Systems

Core Concept: Material Requirements for Support Systems

Process support systems can usually be designed to GEP, but if their point of use is inside a sterile area, the materials must meet four requirements:

  • Non-additive: does not release substances into the environment
  • Non-reactive: does not react chemically with cleaning agents or the environment
  • Non-absorptive: does not absorb liquids or microorganisms
  • Disinfectant-resistant: able to withstand repeated, aggressive chemical disinfection

Key Point: Protection Against Accidental Leakage

Even a "non-process" system can cause contamination if it is poorly designed. Typical risk scenarios:

  • Instrument air exhausting into an ISO 5/Grade A area: a point-of-use filter must be fitted
  • Heat exchanger leakage: seal integrity between the process and support systems
  • Loose pipe connections: support fluid entering the process area

The preventive maintenance (PM) program must cover every interface point that could affect the process.

6.2.3 Common System Classifications

Table 6.1 provides general guidance on typical system classifications. A risk-based approach should be used to define the critical aspects of each system to determine the GMP importance and requirements for documentation, commissioning, and sterile boundary conditions.

Note: Poor design of sanitary plumbing drains and process drains or poor procedures can lead to contamination of cleanrooms due to back flow of liquids or vapors that lead to microbial ingress.

6.2.3 Interpreting Common System Classifications

Core Concept: Practical Use of the Classification Table

This table is the starting point for facility design, but the actual classification must be determined through risk assessment. Key observations:

  • WFI, clean steam, and process gases: always process systems (P), requiring full qualification
  • Purified water: depends on the intended use (final rinse = P; general rinse = PS)
  • Compressed air: may be P or PS, depending on whether it contacts the product
  • Drains: although marked PS, poor design can lead to microbial contamination of the cleanroom

Key Point: Filter Requirements

The filtration requirements for process gases are the most stringent in this table:

  • Pre-filtration: 5 μm, to control particles
  • Point-of-use filtration: 0.2 μm, to ensure sterility
  • Both filtration stages are indispensable: the first protects the system, the second protects the product

CDMO Perspective: The Economics of Multiple Classifications

A common CDMO decision for compressed air systems:

  • Multiple manufacturing lines: a dedicated process-grade compressed air system may be worthwhile
  • Few manufacturing uses: a support system with point-of-use filters and stainless steel piping is more economical
  • The decision depends on: the number of manufacturing points of use, product sensitivity, and facility size

6.2.4 Multiple Categorization

The design of systems that can be multi-categorized should be considered with regard to the cost/benefit derived from installing separate utility systems or distribution networks versus special treatment at points of use. Filters, with break tanks or non-return valves, are widespread applications.

For example, an oil-free compressed air system may be used as both a Process and a Process Support system. If there are many manufacturing uses, there may be economical justification for running separate compressed air systems throughout the facility. If there are only a few manufacturing uses, utilizing a Process Support system (with point of use filters and stainless steel piping after the filter at the manufacturing use points) may be the more economical design.

Due consideration should be given to the upstream piping materials to ensure the air quality is not compromised.

6.2.4 Multiple Classification Decisions

Real-Life Analogy: Tap Water vs. Water Purifier

It is like water use at home:

  • A whole-house water purification system (a dedicated process-grade system): higher cost but simple to manage
  • Or a purifier fitted to the kitchen tap (point-of-use filtration): lower cost but must be managed point by point

The choice depends on the "number of points of use" and the "quality requirement". Sterile manufacturing follows the same logic.

Exercise: How many compressed air systems does your facility need?

Suppose your CDMO facility has the following compressed air uses:

  1. Filling line drying: process use
  2. Sterilizer vacuum break: process use
  3. Door actuation cylinders: instrument use
  4. Control valve actuation: instrument use
  5. Product pressure transfer: process use

Points to consider: are 3 process uses enough to justify a dedicated system? How heavy is the management burden of a point-of-use approach?

6.3 Specific Service Considerations

6.3.1 Purified Water and Water for Injection (WFI)

Water used in the manufacture of sterile pharmaceutical parenteral products should meet USP WFI grade requirements or relevant pharmacopeia standard. Water used for cleaning product contact surfaces should be from a controlled source and meet WFI standards during the final rinse or rinses.

Water used to clean non-product contact surfaces should not increase the background flora within the facility.

For further information, refer to ISPE Baseline Guide: Water and Steam Systems (Second Edition) and ISPE Good Practice Guide: Approaches to Commissioning and Qualification of Pharmaceutical Water and Steam Systems (Second Edition).

6.3.1 Purified Water and Water for Injection

Core Concept: WFI, the Most Critical Utility

Water for Injection (WFI) is the most critical utility in sterile manufacturing because it:

  • Is used directly in product formulation
  • Is used for the final rinse of product-contact surfaces
  • Must remain sterile at the point of use

Tiers of water use:

  • Product manufacture → must meet USP WFI standards
  • Cleaning of product-contact surfaces → the final rinse must meet WFI standards
  • Cleaning of non-product-contact surfaces → must not increase the background bioburden in the facility

Key Point: WFI System Challenges for CDMOs

WFI challenges facing a CDMO:

  • Fluctuating demand: WFI consumption differs widely between products
  • Storage and distribution: the system must keep circulating to prevent microbial growth
  • Dead leg management: the dead leg length at every point of use must be minimized
  • Temperature control: usually circulated at above 80°C or sanitized periodically

6.3.2 Pure Steam or Clean Steam

Pure steam (also referred to as clean steam) is predominantly used for sterilization. Pure steam should be free of boiler additives and have no impurities beyond that of the purified water used in production. The condensed steam should meet WFI specifications and clean/pure steam should be made from a controlled source feed.

Design practices (such as sloping lines and minimizing steam traps) should eliminate potential microbial growth in condensate within the system. Process steam for sterilization should contain minimal superheat entering the autoclave.

Non-Condensable Gases (NCG) should be controlled by preheat/pretreatment of feed water or vented from the system, preferably at the steam generator. The values for NCGs, dryness fraction, and superheating of the steam supply should be periodically tested and controlled within specified limits where the steam is used for the direct sterilization of product contact equipment and components.

6.3.2 Clean Steam

Core Concept: Quality Requirements for Clean Steam

Clean steam is used mainly for SIP (sterilization in place). Its quality requirements:

  • Free of boiler additives
  • Condensate must meet WFI specifications
  • The feed water must be controlled
  • It should arrive at the sterilizer with minimal superheat

Key Point: Three Key Quality Parameters

When clean steam is used to sterilize product-contact equipment directly, the following must be tested regularly and controlled:

  1. Non-condensable gases (NCG): form air pockets that block steam penetration
  2. Dryness fraction: too much moisture reduces sterilization efficiency
  3. Superheat: superheated steam cannot transfer latent heat effectively

NCG can be controlled through feed water pretreatment or venting at the steam generator.

Real-Life Analogy: Steam as a "Hot Cleaning Agent"

Imagine cleaning clothes with steam:

  • The steam must be pure (no chemical additives)
  • It must be moist heat (dry steam has poor germicidal effect)
  • It must penetrate evenly (no air bubbles blocking it)

NCG is like air bubbles trapped in the fabric: steam cannot reach the areas isolated by the bubbles, so those areas are not sterilized.

6.3.3 Nitrogen and Other Process Gases

If process gas is to be used in an aseptic or sterile process, it should be sterile filtered at the point of use. The filter and downstream components need sterilization or sanitization, as well as in situ or off-line integrity testing on a regular basis. If the service is not used in an aseptic process, but is a Process Support utility, standard materials of construction may be used.

Process gas system design considerations:

  • Process gas quality should meet product requirements.
  • Filtration may be used for several reasons: particulate control, environmental protection, or microbial control. For pre-filtration, 5 μm or better is recommended. For aseptic or sterile applications, 0.2 μm filtration is required at point of use.
  • One 0.2 μm filter can be used at the system boundary for particulate control, and a second 0.2 μm filter at the process system boundary for microbial control.
  • The gas distribution system design should include sampling points. Sterile filtered points of use should also permit downstream aseptic sampling for physical and biological quality.
  • Back flow from other systems into process gas systems should be prevented.

6.3.3 Nitrogen and Process Gases

Core Concept: Dual Filtration Strategy

Filtration of process gases uses two lines of defense:

  • First 0.2 μm filter: located at the system boundary, for particle control and sampling
  • Second 0.2 μm filter: located at the process system boundary (point of use), for microbial control

The filters and the components downstream of them must:

  • Be sterilized or sanitized periodically
  • Undergo periodic integrity testing (in situ or off-line)

Key Point: Backflow Prevention

Material from other systems must be prevented from flowing back into the process gas system. Practical measures:

  • Install non-return valves
  • Maintain a positive pressure differential
  • Use break tanks

In a CDMO where multiple products share a gas system, backflow protection is especially important to avoid cross-contamination between products.

Practical Checklist: Process Gas Systems

  • Is a 0.2 μm sterilizing filter fitted at the point of use?
  • Has the filter integrity test frequency been defined?
  • Is there a downstream sterile sampling point?
  • Is a backflow prevention device installed?
  • Is the pre-filter (5 μm) in place?
  • Does the gas quality specification meet product requirements?

6.3.4 Compressed Air

Process Compressed Air

Compressed air (such as used for drying or transferring product, for vacuum break, or for inlets into sterilizers) should be treated as a process gas.

For determination of compressed air attributes, refer to ISO 8573-1, ICH Q8, ICH Q9, and site-specific guidelines. The site location of the system should support maintaining these attributes. Air intake should not be located near traffic, shipping/receiving lanes, or emission-producing equipment. Hydrocarbon contamination should be prevented and monitored.

Instrument Air

Properly designed and maintained systems should prevent instrument air from coming into contact with product; therefore, these systems may be designed in accordance with GEP. Instrument air should be vented away from ISO 5/Grade A areas, to preserve low particulate and microbial levels.

Breathing Air

Breathing air is a Process Support system important to operator safety. It should be labeled and easily identifiable. Maximum contaminant levels per OSHA and CSA standards:

6.3.4 Compressed Air Systems

Key Point: Location of the Air Intake

Compressed air quality starts at the air intake. It must be kept away from:

  • Traffic areas (vehicle exhaust)
  • Loading and unloading areas (dust)
  • Other exhaust-emitting equipment (chemicals)

Hydrocarbon contamination must be prevented and monitored. In facility siting, the intake location is a key design decision.

Real-Life Analogy: Three Types of Air Are Like Three Types of Water

  • Process compressed air is like bottled mineral water: it directly contacts the "food" and is of the highest quality
  • Instrument air is like hand-washing water: it is not ingested, but its quality still needs to be controlled
  • Breathing air is like air-conditioning filtration: it protects personnel safety

Core Concept: Three Uses of Compressed Air

Compressed air has three distinct uses in a sterile facility, each with a different classification:

6.3.5 Vents

Nitrogen, compressed air, instrument air, and other gases are vented at several locations during operation (e.g., pneumatically operated parts on filling lines). In the case where these gases are vented during an aseptic process, vents should be released to a non-critical area outside of the equipment. A risk assessment should be performed to assess venting locations.

6.3.5 Exhaust Design

Key Point: Risk Assessment of Exhaust Location

Pneumatic components (such as pneumatic valves on a filling line) release gas during operation. If this exhaust occurs within the sterile process:

  • The exhaust outlet must be directed to a non-critical area, away from the inside of the equipment
  • A risk assessment must be performed to confirm that the exhaust location is appropriate
  • Avoid exhaust entering ISO 5/Grade A areas directly

Many deviation events on filling lines can be traced to poorly located exhausts that allowed particles or microorganisms into the critical zone.

6.3.6 Heating and Cooling Systems

Heating and cooling systems (including cooling and chilled water, glycol systems, and heat transfer fluid systems) should not contact the product. It is usually a Process Support utility, but can directly affect the product.

Equipment used for indirect heat transfer should not leak into the atmosphere or the product. Selection of the heat transfer medium should consider the potential risk of leakage. Provisions should be made to monitor such system leakage through pressure testing and level monitoring.

Designers should consider that a heat transfer fluid that would leak from a tank jacket into a batch of formulated product would contaminate the batch, regardless of the properties of the fluid, so jacket integrity should be assured.

For temperature-sensitive products, the temperature of the heating/cooling medium may be a critical parameter if it is not possible to monitor the product temperature at the heat transfer surface.

6.3.6 Heating and Cooling Systems

Core Concept: The Risk of Indirect Contact

Although heating/cooling systems should not contact the product, they may:

  • Control the air temperature in a depyrogenation tunnel
  • Control the product temperature in process tanks
  • Contaminate an entire batch directly through a jacket leak

A leak monitoring mechanism must therefore be established: pressure testing and level monitoring.

Key Point: Jacket Integrity

ISPE states explicitly that regardless of the nature of the heat transfer medium, a leak from the jacket into the formulated product will contaminate the whole batch. This means:

  • Even with a "food-grade" heat transfer medium, a leak is still a cause for batch rejection
  • Jacket integrity testing is a key preventive maintenance item
  • Piping should not be routed above sterile processing areas

6.3.7 Facility Steam and Hot Water Systems

Facility steam and hot water systems should not be used in applications where there is exposure to the product. These systems should be designed using GEP.

Care should be taken in the selection of boiler additives, especially when facility steam is used for HVAC humidification. The location of condensate and pressure controlling systems should be in facility areas, not within cleanrooms. These devices should not be located above aseptic areas, in case of leakage.

6.3.8 Process Vacuum Systems

If a single vacuum source is used for a mixture of process uses, the contamination risk increases. Steps should be taken to prevent pressure reversals or reverse flow (e.g., non-return valves or fail-safe vacuum pump/pressure arrangements) and to prevent material dropping from the system into the process.

Sanitization or sterilization is recommended for points of use upstream (nearer to the process) of the local vacuum isolation valve. Appropriate steps should be designed to prevent possible cross-contamination.

6.3.9 Potable Water

Potable water should be designed with GEP. Proper labeling and identification of these services is required. Potable water should not be used in the aseptic processing area. The chemical and microbiological profiles should exceed drinking water standards. A risk assessment should determine if the local drinking water quality increases risk of chemical and microbial contamination events.

6.3.7-6.3.9 Facility Steam, Vacuum, and Potable Water

Core Concept: Layout Principles

There is one key principle for the layout of facility steam and condensate systems:

  • Condensate discharge and pressure control devices → place them in the mechanical area, not inside the cleanroom
  • These devices should not be located above sterile areas, to prevent the risk of leakage
  • If boiler additives are used for HVAC humidification, select them carefully (to avoid introducing chemical contaminants)

Key Point: Cross-Contamination Risk in Vacuum Systems

The risk of a shared vacuum source is the one most easily overlooked:

  • Pressure reversal: backflow may occur when the vacuum pump stops
  • Material backflow: material from other processes may enter through the vacuum system
  • Protective measures: non-return valves, fail-safe vacuum pump configuration, sterilization upstream of the point of use

In a CDMO, a vacuum system shared by multiple products is a common configuration and must have a rigorous cross-contamination protection design.

CDMO Perspective: Labeling Management for Potable Water

A potable water system looks simple, but it has two common problems in pharmaceutical facilities:

  • Labeling confusion: operators may mistakenly use potable water for process cleaning
  • Water quality risk: the local municipal water quality may introduce chemical or microbial risks

Correct pipe labeling and identification is the most basic yet most easily neglected GEP requirement.

6.3.10 Mechanical Seal Fluids

If a pump is used for product transfer, the seal fluid should be of the same quality standards as the product. Double mechanical seals or equivalent are preferred. Typically for aseptic facilities, sterile alcohol, USP purified water, or WFI is used as a seal fluid.

If the pump is not for product transfer (i.e., for a Process Support service), then vendor recommended fluids should be considered.

6.3.11 Drains

There are several types of drains that can be located within process space. The US FDA suggests that drains should not occur within ISO 5/Grade A, ISO 6, or ISO 7/Grade B spaces, but allows exceptions.

Drains within the process spaces should be minimized. Drains within a classified process space should be sealed and capped. Where possible, drains should be located within mechanical spaces instead of within process spaces.

Waste transfer lines should be sloped to gravity flow and should not vent gases into the process space. Cleanouts should be located within mechanical space. Drain points should be designed to prevent capillary action and should be free flowing.

For products produced for use in the EU, Annex 1 requires that any drain connected to a sterile area should have an air gap. For locations where splash or condensate would cause contamination concerns, the drain should be enclosed while maintaining the air gap.

Where drains are placed within maintenance space (usually uncontrolled, non-ventilated), the need for point ventilation or enhanced biological control should be evaluated.

6.3.10-6.3.11 Mechanical Seal Fluids and Drainage Systems

Core Concept: Mechanical Seal Fluids, Product-Grade Quality

For pumps used in product transfer, the quality standard of the seal fluid must be the same as that of the product:

  • Double mechanical seals are preferred
  • The seal fluid is usually sterile alcohol, USP purified water, or WFI
  • For non-product pumps, the seal fluid recommended by the supplier may be used

Reason: if the seal fluid leaks, it contacts the product directly. This is the last line of defense.

Key Point: Drainage Systems, an Underestimated Source of Contamination

Drainage systems are the most easily overlooked source of microbial contamination in cleanrooms:

  • FDA recommends that ISO 5/Grade A, ISO 6, and ISO 7/Grade B areas should not have drains
  • Where drains must exist: they should be sealed and capped
  • EU Annex 1 requires that drains connected to sterile areas have an air gap
  • Waste lines must be sloped for gravity flow and must not vent gas into the process space

Exercise: Drainage System Design Review

In a design review, you notice the following drain arrangements. Which need improvement?

  1. An uncapped drain in the ISO 7/Grade B corridor
  2. A drain connection with an air gap inside an isolator
  3. A cleaning drain in a mechanical space discharging directly into piping below the sterile area
  4. A sealed and capped floor drain in the filling room, maintained weekly

Hint: consider the FDA recommendations, the Annex 1 requirements, and the risk of microbial backflow.

Section Summary

Key Takeaways

  1. Dual classification system: Every utility must be classified as Process (P) or Process Support (PS) based on risk assessment, which determines design, qualification, and documentation requirements.
  2. WFI is the most critical utility in sterile manufacturing — it must meet pharmacopeial standards and be sterile at the point of use.
  3. Clean steam quality is defined by three parameters: NCG content, dryness fraction, and superheat — all must be periodically tested.
  4. Process gases require dual filtration: 5 μm pre-filtration plus 0.2 μm sterilizing-grade filtration at the point of use.
  5. System boundaries must be clearly defined to delineate qualification scope from GEP-only scope.
  6. Backflow prevention is essential across all shared utility systems — especially vacuum and compressed gas systems.
  7. Drains are underestimated contamination sources: minimize in classified areas, seal and cap when present, maintain air gaps per Annex 1.
  8. Location matters: condensate systems, pressure devices, and heat transfer piping should not be above aseptic areas.

Key Points Review

One-Sentence Summary

The core of utility system design is "classification determines the standard, risk determines the scope": use risk assessment to classify systems as process-grade (P) or support-grade (PS), and then determine the rigor of design, qualification, and documentation accordingly.

Key CDMO Applications

  • Capacity planning: multi-product manufacturing must consider peak demand for WFI, clean steam, and process gases
  • Cross-contamination protection: backflow protection design for shared vacuum and compressed gas systems
  • Economic decisions: dedicated systems vs. point-of-use treatment, decided by the number of manufacturing lines
  • Single-use strategy: an effective way to reduce cross-contamination risk from utilities
  • Change management: introducing a new product may change the classification of a utility, which must then be reassessed

Self-Check: Can You Answer These Questions?

  1. What is the difference in system classification between WFI and purified water?
  2. What are the three key quality parameters of clean steam?
  3. Why do process gases need two 0.2 μm filters?
  4. Why should drains not be present in ISO 5/Grade A areas?
  5. What unique challenges does a CDMO face in utility design?
