Chapter 6: 7–8. Electrical & Controls

p151-p166

ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 3 (3rd Ed.) | p151 – p156

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the GMP requirements for electrical equipment in cleanroom environments of different classifications (ISO 5 through ISO 8)
  • Recognize the importance of UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) and emergency power for critical control systems
  • Learn the design principles for cleanroom lighting: flush-mount fixtures, non-shedding materials, and airflow compatibility
  • Understand door interlock systems for airlocks and their role in maintaining pressure cascades
  • Grasp wiring principles: minimizing wall penetrations, sealing conduits, and preventing contamination pathways
  • Know when and why hazardous (ATEX) electrical classifications apply in sterile facilities
7.1 Introduction

Original Text

This chapter focuses on electrical services that may have GMP implications. It outlines the critical characteristics of systems appropriate to the manufacturing environment.

Instructor Analysis

Core Concept

The GMP role of electrical services: In a sterile manufacturing facility, the electrical system does not usually have a direct impact on product quality or patient safety. However, how electrical equipment is designed and installed affects cleanroom cleanability, seal integrity, and the ability to maintain pressure differentials.

The central question of this chapter is: how can electrical equipment provide the necessary functions without compromising cleanroom integrity?

Analogy

Power outlets in an operating room: Picture a hospital operating room. You cannot simply drill holes in the wall to run wires; every outlet and switch must be flush-mounted, cleanable and disinfectable, with no gaps where dirt can collect. Cleanroom electrical design follows exactly the same logic: the function must be there, but never at the expense of environmental quality.

7.2 General Requirements

Original Text

When designing, selecting, and installing electrical equipment within aseptic processing areas, GMP considerations are limited to ensuring that equipment is cleanable, ledge and crevice free, non-shedding, sealed, and compatible with sanitization agents.

The selection and installation of all electrical equipment and wiring should, at a minimum, be in accordance with applicable local codes. All electrical components and materials should be compatible with the manufacturing process and operations.

Although the criteria for equipment appear to be identical from ISO 5/Grade A to ISO 8/Grade C environments, the degree of these aspects may differ (e.g., equipment in ISO 5/Grade A environments will require a higher standard). Recessed electrical devices may help achieve the standard required in each of these areas.

Sealed components are specified, not only to alleviate the risk of contamination, but also to cope with the different pressure regimes of adjacent rooms. In ISO 5/Grade A environments, the term “sealed” refers to being hermetically sealed, whereas in ISO 8/Grade C environments, the term “sealed” refers to a high degree of protection against the ingress of water and dust.

Electrical equipment within ISO 5/Grade A environments should be kept to an absolute minimum. Any services that can achieve their function by being located in an adjacent room or area should be so located. For example, a light switch for the room could be located outside the access door in the corridor.

Regarding the manufacturing process, electrical services normally do not affect patient safety and product quality; however, for business continuity and ensuring uninterrupted product supply, these systems should be designed in accordance with GEP (Good Engineering Practice).

"Electrical equipment within ISO 5/Grade A environments should be kept to an absolute minimum. Any services that can achieve their function by being located in an adjacent room or area should be so located."

Table 7.1: Typical GMP Requirements for Electrical Systems

Instructor Analysis

Core Concept: The Five GMP Requirements for Electrical Equipment

All electrical equipment installed in sterile areas must meet five basic requirements:

  • Cleanable - smooth surfaces that can be wiped down with standard cleaning agents
  • Ledge & Crevice Free - no dead spots where microorganisms or particles can accumulate
  • Non-shedding - materials that do not release particles into the environment
  • Sealed - prevents air leakage that would affect pressure differentials and stops external contamination from entering
  • Compatible with Sanitization Agents - able to withstand sanitizing agents such as VHP, hydrogen peroxide and alcohol

Key Point: Different Levels of "Sealed"

The source text distinguishes between different levels of what "sealed" means:

  • ISO 5/Grade A - Hermetically Sealed: completely airtight, ensuring that unidirectional airflow is not disturbed
  • ISO 8/Grade C - High Protection against Ingress: protected against water and dust, equivalent to IP65 or higher

This distinction is very important in practice: every electrical component inside an ISO 5 area must be treated as part of the cleanroom envelope.

Analogy

Submarine vs. raincoat: The electrical sealing requirement for ISO 5 is like a submarine: absolutely airtight, with no tolerance for even the smallest leak. The requirement for ISO 8 is more like a good raincoat: it keeps out water and dust, but does not need to withstand a pressure difference the way a submarine does.

Key Point: The Principle of Minimization

"Subtractive thinking" in ISO 5 areas: In the highest-grade cleanrooms, the design question is not "how do we install the electrical equipment?" but "how do we avoid installing electrical equipment at all?" Whatever can be placed outside should be placed outside: light switches in the corridor, distribution panels in the plant room, and sensors mounted remotely wherever possible.

This is the most frequently overlooked principle in GMP electrical design. Many engineers are used to installing equipment where it is needed, instead of first asking, "Can this be moved outside?"

Practical Application

GEP principles: Although the electrical system does not directly affect product quality, it does affect business continuity. Under GEP (Good Engineering Practice), the design should consider redundant power supply, emergency generators, UPS protection and so on. The loss of production batches caused by a power failure can run into millions.

7.3 Control System Power

Original Text

The prevalence of digital controls in HVAC and process equipment requires strong consideration of reliable and continuous power to the control units. Considerations should be made with regard to:

  • How multiple power sources affect equipment (e.g., equipment may have multiple power sources, such as line voltage motors, or the control system may operate on Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) while the fan motor operates on three phase line voltage)
  • Providing for orderly shutdown or planned restarts on loss of main equipment power
  • Programming of the systems to prevent tripping of main breakers on simultaneous restart of all equipment
  • Power needs for associated instruments

Instructor Analysis

Core Concept: Control System Power

UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply): Modern sterile facilities rely heavily on digital control systems (BMS, SCADA, PLC). These controllers are extremely sensitive to power interruptions; even a brief power flicker can cause:

  • Loss or reset of control programs
  • Loss of HVAC control, with room pressure differentials collapsing
  • Interruption of process parameter records, creating GMP data integrity issues

Critical control systems must therefore be powered by a UPS, so that an Orderly Shutdown can be carried out, or monitoring maintained, when power is lost.

Analogy

Abrupt computer shutdown vs. orderly shutdown: Imagine you are working on an important report on your computer when the power suddenly fails, and all unsaved work is lost. A UPS is like fitting your computer with a big battery, giving you enough time after the outage to save your files and shut down properly. In a sterile facility, that "unsaved work" could be a production batch worth millions.

Key Point: The Risk of Simultaneous Restart

Breaker Trip Prevention: When power is restored, if all equipment starts at the same moment, the inrush current may exceed the capacity of the main breaker and trip it again. The system must be programmed for Staggered Restart to avoid this "second disaster".

This is especially important in CDMO plants: when the HVAC, chillers and filling equipment of several production lines start at the same time, the inrush current can be 5 to 8 times that of normal operation.

7.4 Power Distribution

Original Text

Both reliability and stability of the power supply are important.

The impact of surges, dips, or total power loss on the overall manufacturing process, HVAC/mechanical services, or individual equipment items, should be studied to determine risk and effects. Generally, the impact is economic (loss of production capacity). If these impacts are considerable, then a standby generator or UPS should be considered.

For HVAC systems, momentary power losses may be significant; impact could be mediated if there are provisions for fan rotation to continue and room pressures are maintained within acceptance criteria for short periods. The impact of any power loss potentially affecting the sterility of the product should be evaluated.

Power for monitoring of DP (differential pressure) is a critical issue, as loss of differential or the ability to monitor differential pressure during outages may result in significant product quality impact.

Consideration for UPS or emergency generators can be considered for critical processes, equipment, and systems that may provide, maintain, or record critical parameters as part of GMP operations.

Power quality is equally important as precision equipment has a narrow bandwidth to operate within. Special consideration should be given to:

  • Power factor correction
  • Phase balance
  • Harmonics from digital equipment

Instructor Analysis

Core Concept: The Two Requirements of the Distribution System

The distribution system must satisfy two aspects at the same time:

  • Reliability - uninterrupted power, ensuring production continuity
  • Stability - stable voltage and frequency, with no surges or dips

The special status of DP monitoring: The source text specifically stresses that the power supply to differential pressure monitoring is a "critical issue". The cleanroom pressure cascade is the core barrier against cross-contamination; if a power failure causes the loss of both the pressure differential and the ability to monitor it, there is no way to demonstrate that the product was not contaminated during the outage.

Key Point: HVAC Fan Inertia

Fan Rotation Continue: After a brief power loss, the inertia of the HVAC fans can keep air moving for a few seconds. If properly designed, this time may be enough to keep room pressure differentials within an acceptable range. This is why the source text says "impact could be mediated": not every brief power failure causes the pressure differential to collapse.

However, this must be confirmed through risk assessment: for how long can power be lost before the pressure differential is no longer acceptable? This is usually something to be tested during qualification.

Exercise

  1. If differential pressure monitoring loses power during a production batch, what investigation steps would you initiate? How would you determine if the batch is still acceptable?
  2. Your facility experiences a 3-second power dip. HVAC fans coast for 5 seconds. Is this sufficient to maintain cleanroom integrity? What data would you need to make this determination?
7.5 Lighting

Original Text

There should be good uniform lighting levels in all manufacturing areas. Minimum levels in the personnel work areas should be no less than 500 lux, one meter from the floor.

Light fixtures in manufacturing areas should:

  • Be designed and selected to be cleanable, non-shedding, ledge free, or sealed, as appropriate for the different classifications of areas
  • Be arranged to prevent accumulation of dust, and be air tight and sealed to ensure no foreign matter is released into the manufacturing environment
  • Be located so they are not directly above the work area when the manufacturing process is open to the room
  • Have sealing properties which can withstand water jet pressure in wash down areas
  • Be constructed of materials that are compatible with room cleaning agents, which may be corrosive (stainless steel or aluminum fixtures may be considered appropriate because they are non-shedding and resistive to corrosive environments)

In ISO 5/Grade A environments, recess mounted or teardrop fixtures may be appropriate. The installation of surface mounted lighting in unidirectional ISO 5/Grade A airflow zones may interfere with airflow patterns and should be avoided.

In ISO 7/Grade B environments, recess mounted fixtures are beneficial because they can be installed through the ceiling, with maintenance access provided from a walkable ceiling or floor (facility room) above.

Lamps or fixtures, maintained from within the room, may be changed on an annual basis to reduce the effects of unplanned disturbances to production due to occasional lamp failures. Considerations for lighting include:

  • Redundant lighting units
  • Upgraded light types (e.g., T-5 fluorescent or Light Emitting Diode (LED)) which allow for longer life and reduced maintenance intervention
  • Adjustable lighting (adjusted in lux output) for night time operation, as increased light levels have demonstrated to improve night time work performance — if increasing light output, consideration for product impact (photo stability) should be evaluated

If color rendition and intensity of lighting equipment used for inspection, cleaning, etc., is considered critical, appropriate provisions should be made.

Emergency lighting should be provided in accordance with applicable local codes. Combining emergency fixtures with normal fixtures helps to limit the amount of electrical equipment on ceilings or walls.

Since priority needs to be given to the HVAC systems (e.g., air supply diffusers) and services to process equipment, lighting fixtures cannot always be positioned to achieve ideal lighting distribution. Therefore, careful coordination of ceiling services should be considered at the design stage.

Instructor Analysis

Core Concept: Cleanroom Lighting Design Principles

Cleanroom lighting design must balance three objectives:

  • Sufficient brightness - at least 500 lux in work areas, ensuring safe and accurate operation by personnel
  • No loss of cleanliness - the fixtures themselves must not become a source of particles or microorganisms
  • No airflow disruption - especially in ISO 5 unidirectional airflow areas, where surface-mounted fixtures disturb laminar flow

Core Concept: Recessed vs. Surface-Mounted Fixtures

Recess Mounted / Flush-Mount Fixture:

  • The fixture is recessed into the ceiling, with its surface flush with the ceiling
  • It creates no protruding surfaces and does not disturb airflow
  • Maintenance can be carried out from the technical void above the ceiling, without entering the cleanroom
  • The preferred solution for ISO 5 and ISO 7 areas

Teardrop Fixture:

  • Streamlined design that reduces disturbance to airflow
  • Suitable for positions in ISO 5 areas where recessed installation is not possible

Analogy

Ceiling space is prime "real estate": Cleanroom ceiling space is like property in the city center: HVAC supply outlets, return grilles, HEPA filters, process equipment interfaces, light fixtures and fire sprinklers all compete for it. The source text reminds us that HVAC has the highest priority and lighting can only be fitted into whatever room is left. Coordinated planning of ceiling services must therefore be done at the design stage.

Key Point: Photo Stability Considerations

Photo Stability: Increasing light levels to improve night-shift performance is a good idea, but the effect of the light on the product must be assessed. Some drugs (especially biologics and certain small-molecule drugs) are light-sensitive, and excessively intense lighting may cause degradation.

This is a typical GMP cross-consideration: when improving one aspect (personnel performance), you must not overlook another (product quality).

Key Point: Preventive Maintenance Strategy

Annual Replacement: The source text suggests that light fixtures can be replaced on a scheduled annual basis instead of waiting for them to fail. This is because replacing a fixture inside a cleanroom requires:

  • Shutting down or pausing production
  • Possibly having maintenance staff gown up and enter the cleanroom
  • Cleaning and environmental recovery after the replacement

Planned maintenance is far less disruptive than unplanned maintenance. Using LED fixtures can extend the replacement cycle to several years, greatly reducing the number of maintenance interventions.

Exercise

  1. Why must surface-mounted lighting be avoided in ISO 5 unidirectional airflow zones? Describe the specific mechanism by which a protruding fixture disrupts laminar flow.
  2. Your facility has a product that is light-sensitive (ICH Q1B photostability testing required). How would you design the lighting in the filling room to balance operator visibility with product protection?
7.6 Hazardous Environments

Original Text

The selection and installation of electrical equipment within hazardous environments (due to dust or solvent vapor) should comply with applicable local codes. Classification of an area to require explosion proof electrical equipment is likely to be very rare, because of the high air change requirement and monitoring of the area; however, design should also take into consideration loss of HVAC fan rotation and reduction of room air changes (e.g., failure mode operations with regards to volatiles).

Hazardous area classification is not a GMP issue, but the class of room may affect the location of production equipment and it also may affect the selection of the electrical equipment. Some electrical equipment may suit a higher class of area in terms of cleanliness.

Electrical equipment within these areas should be kept to an absolute minimum. Any devices that can achieve their function while located in an adjacent room should be located externally and do not need to be classified.

Provisions should be made in these areas to dissipate possible static build-up on personnel, equipment, and materials. Conductive floors should be installed, if necessary.

Instructor Analysis

Core Concept: Explosion-Protected Environments

ATEX (explosion protection classification): When a cleanroom uses processes involving solvents (for example, ethanol in the compounding step of some injectables) or handles combustible dust, the area may require hazardous area classification.

However, the source text points out that in sterile facilities this is very rare, because:

  • The high air change rate in cleanrooms (20-60 or more per hour) quickly dilutes flammable vapors
  • The environmental monitoring system continuously detects abnormalities

Even so, the design must consider "what happens if the HVAC fans stop rotating?" This falls within the scope of Failure Mode Analysis.

Analogy

Gas stove vs. ventilated kitchen: Using a gas stove in a well-ventilated kitchen carries very little risk of a gas leak, because air movement dilutes any leakage. But if the extractor hood breaks down (equivalent to an HVAC failure), the gas could build up to a dangerous concentration. The high air change rate of a cleanroom is that "super extractor hood", but you still need to consider the scenario in which it fails.

Key Point: Static Protection

Static Build-up is a serious safety hazard in areas that use flammable solvents or handle powders. The source text requires:

  • Installing Conductive Floors to carry static charge to ground
  • Providing static dissipation measures for personnel, equipment and materials

In a CDMO setting, if you take on contract injectable projects involving organic solvents, these explosion-protection requirements must be built into the facility design.

7.7 Wiring

Original Text

If possible, wiring and wiring accessories should be hidden within the building fabric to improve cleanliness, particularly in higher classification areas. Recessed boxes also would be appropriate in these instances. The number of penetrations through walls, ceilings, or floors for services to equipment should be minimized.

Where wiring is installed on the surface, installation should minimize the accumulation of foreign matter and allow easy and effective cleaning.

Enclosing wiring in fully sealed conduit or trunking may improve the level of cleanliness and prevent air leakage from a classified room. Trunking, which is not sealed, may appear clean but act as a reservoir for contaminants. Sealing of conduits and trunking may be necessary to reduce the risk of contamination from outside and loss of air from pressurized rooms.

Lengths of wiring to mobile equipment should be kept to a minimum and should be kept off the floor.

Where necessary, as part of the process operations, wiring and glands should withstand washing.

Instructor Analysis

Core Concept: Managing Wiring Penetrations

Wiring Penetration is a major threat to cleanroom integrity. Every cable pathway through a wall, ceiling or floor is a potential:

  • Air leakage point - undermining room pressure differentials
  • Contamination pathway - external particles or microorganisms may travel along the conduit
  • Cleaning blind spot - penetrations are difficult to clean thoroughly

The source text therefore stresses that the number of penetrations must be minimized, and that all penetrations must be sealed.

Key Point: The Unseen Contamination Reservoir

The hidden risk of unsealed trunking: The source text makes a profound observation: unsealed trunking may look clean on the surface, but inside it is actually a Reservoir for Contaminants. Dust, particles and even microorganisms can accumulate inside the trunking and then be slowly released into the cleanroom by the airflow.

This is why the ISPE Guide requires trunking to be fully sealed: not just "looking sealed", but genuinely preventing the movement of air and particles.

Analogy

The leaking pipe analogy: Imagine a rusty water pipe inside the wall of your home. The wall looks intact on the surface, but the pipe has been leaking all along, slowly eroding the wall. An unsealed cable conduit is the "invisible leaking pipe" of a cleanroom: it looks fine on the outside, but it keeps letting uncontrolled air (and contaminants) move in and out of the cleanroom.

Practical Application

CDMO wiring best practices:

  • Plan all penetration locations at the design stage and reserve suitable cable routes
  • Use qualified penetration sealing systems (such as Roxtec or equivalent), with a pressure test record for every penetration point
  • Use ceiling-suspended cables or cable reels for mobile equipment, to avoid cables lying on the floor and making cleaning difficult
  • Include all sealing points in a periodic inspection program to maintain integrity over the long term
7.8 Door Interlocks

Original Text

Electrical interlocks for the doors of airlocks or changing rooms assist in maintaining pressure regimes and GMP practices. Alternatively, an audible local alarm could be generated to indicate if more than one airlock door is open at the same time. If interlocks are provided, override features should be included in case of emergency.

Additionally, provisions should include electronic access control for rooms that require restricted access for aseptic operations (e.g., ISO 5/Grade A). It is recommended that door interlocks are verified as part of facility commissioning/qualification per GEP.

Instructor Analysis

Core Concept: Door Interlock Systems

Door Interlock: An electrical control mechanism that ensures the two doors of an airlock cannot be open at the same time. It is a key line of defense in maintaining the cleanroom pressure cascade.

How it works:

  • When one door is open, the other is electrically locked and cannot be opened
  • The second door can be unlocked only after the first door is fully closed
  • If both doors are open at the same time (a fault condition), the system triggers an alarm

Analogy

The double doors of a bank vault: Like the entrance to a bank vault, you must first enter through the first door and wait for it to close before the second door will open. This ensures the vault is never directly exposed to the outside environment. The airlock interlock in a cleanroom follows exactly the same logic: it prevents a higher-grade area from being directly exposed to the air of a lower-grade area.

Key Point: Emergency Override

Override: The source text specifically stresses that a door interlock system must include an emergency override function. This is a basic Life Safety requirement: in a fire, chemical spill or other emergency, personnel must be able to evacuate quickly and must not be trapped by the interlock system.

This is a typical trade-off between GMP and safety: under normal conditions the interlock protects product quality, while in an emergency life safety takes priority.

Key Point: Electronic Access Control

Electronic Access Control is necessary in ISO 5 aseptic operation areas. Its purposes are to:

  • Restrict entry to personnel who have been trained and qualified in gowning
  • Record who enters and when, providing traceability
  • Prevent unauthorized persons from entering and potentially contaminating the sterile environment

The door interlock system should be verified during the Commissioning / Qualification phase of the facility, to confirm that its function meets the design requirements.

Exercise

  1. During a routine production run, an operator reports that both airlock doors opened simultaneously due to an interlock malfunction. What immediate actions do you take? How do you assess the impact on the in-process batch?
  2. Should the emergency override of door interlocks trigger an alarm and a log entry in the BMS? Why or why not?
7.9 Outlets and Miscellaneous Equipment

Original Text

Electrical components should be designed and selected to be:

  • Cleanable
  • Non-shedding
  • Ledge and crevice-free, or sealed
  • Appropriate to the classification (HVAC grade) of area

Fittings in process areas should be arranged to prevent accumulation of dust and be air tight and sealed, to ensure no foreign matter is released into the manufacturing environment. Recess mounting of fittings in these areas provides distinct benefits.

Aspirated fire detection, or systems able to detect fire within the HVAC extract systems for ISO 5/Grade A environments, may avoid installing conventional fire/smoke detection equipment within the room. Flashing lights, in place of conventional sounders, also may be beneficial. Additionally, source specific cleanroom appropriate sprinkler heads may be used for fire suppression systems.

Sealing membranes on loudspeaker systems located within ISO 5/Grade A and ISO 7/Grade B environments should be considered. A membrane in the wall between two adjoining rooms may provide acceptable voice communication between those rooms. Consideration for use of appropriate cleanable/sealed wireless communication should be given.

Insect light traps should be placed strategically outside of cleanroom areas to reduce contamination risks from flying insects.

Since sinks and drains are not permitted in aseptic processing areas (ISO 5/Grade A and ISO 7/Grade B), an electronically heated (bio-control) trap beneath sinks in ISO 8/Grade C environments could serve as an alternative to routine chemical sanitization.

Instructor Analysis

Core Concept: GMP Design of Miscellaneous Equipment

Besides lighting and power distribution, a cleanroom contains many "miscellaneous" items of electrical equipment that also need to meet GMP requirements. The source text lists several important categories:

  • Fire detection - Aspirated Fire Detection avoids the need to install conventional smoke detectors inside the cleanroom
  • Communication systems - speakers need a sealing membrane, or wireless communication can be used instead
  • Pest control - Insect Light Traps are placed outside the cleanroom perimeter
  • Drainage control - electrically heated bio-control traps under sinks in ISO 8 areas

Key Point: Aspirated Smoke Detection Systems

Aspirated Fire Detection: A system that continuously draws air from the monitored area to a remote detector. Its advantages are:

  • No equipment inside the cleanroom - the detector unit is installed in the technical area, and only small sampling pipes are inside the cleanroom
  • High sensitivity - smoke can be detected at a very early stage
  • Avoids false alarms - conventional smoke detectors may be triggered by the vapor from VHP sanitization

In ISO 5 areas, this is almost the only workable smoke detection solution.

Key Point: No Drains in Sterile Areas

Sinks and drains are not permitted in ISO 5 and ISO 7 areas: this is a basic GMP principle. Drainage systems are a breeding ground for microorganisms and a direct threat to the sterile environment.

In ISO 8/Grade C areas, however, sinks are necessary (for example, for hand washing). The source text recommends using an electrically heated Bio-control Trap under the sink, which uses heat to suppress microbial growth in the drain pipe as an alternative to chemical disinfection.

Analogy

The cleanroom as a "silent operating room": In an operating room, you would not install an ordinary household intercom; all communication equipment must be waterproof, disinfectable and non-shedding. The same applies to cleanroom speaker systems: with a sealing membrane fitted, sound can pass through, but air and particles cannot. The modern trend is to use cleanable, sealed wireless communication devices, eliminating the need for openings in the wall altogether.

Practical Application

CDMO facility planning checklist:

  • ISO 5 areas: aspirated fire detection + flashing light alarms (in place of buzzers) + sealed communication
  • ISO 7 areas: recessed fire detection + sealed speaker membranes + no-drain design
  • ISO 8 areas: standard smoke detection (with protection against VHP false alarms) + electrically heated drain traps + insect light traps on the perimeter
  • All areas: recessed or flush mounting, cleanable materials, and compatibility with sanitization agents

Section Summary

  • General Requirements: All electrical equipment in aseptic areas must be cleanable, ledge-free, non-shedding, sealed, and compatible with sanitization agents. ISO 5 areas require hermetic sealing and absolute minimization of installed equipment
  • Control System Power: UPS is essential for digital control systems (BMS, SCADA, PLC) to ensure orderly shutdown and data integrity during power loss. Staggered restart programming prevents breaker trips
  • Power Distribution: DP monitoring power is critical — loss of pressure monitoring during outages directly impacts product quality assessment. Power quality (harmonics, phase balance) matters for precision equipment
  • Lighting: Minimum 500 lux at work areas. Flush-mount (recess) fixtures mandatory in ISO 5 to avoid airflow disruption. LED preferred for reduced maintenance. Consider photo stability impact on light-sensitive products
  • Hazardous Environments: ATEX classification is rare in sterile facilities due to high air changes, but failure mode analysis (HVAC loss) is required. Static dissipation and conductive floors may be needed
  • Wiring: Minimize wall/ceiling penetrations, seal all conduits. Unsealed trunking is a hidden contamination reservoir. Mobile equipment cables must be kept off the floor
  • Door Interlocks: Airlock interlocks maintain pressure cascades. Emergency override is mandatory for life safety. Electronic access control required for ISO 5 areas. Verify during commissioning/qualification
  • Miscellaneous: Aspirated fire detection for ISO 5 (avoids in-room equipment). Sealed communication membranes. Insect traps outside cleanrooms. Bio-control heated traps for ISO 8 drains
ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 3 (3rd Ed.) | p157 – p166

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the role of C&I systems in sterile manufacturing and how they impact patient safety and product quality
  • Identify critical environmental process parameters (CPPs) and their monitoring requirements
  • Distinguish between active and passive control strategies for environmental parameters
  • Apply the hierarchy of Process Limits, Alert Limits, and Normal Operating Conditions
  • Understand instrument selection criteria: accuracy, location, and calibration
  • Evaluate HVAC control system choices: BMS/BAS vs. DCS/PLC/SCADA
  • Describe airborne particle counting configurations and monitoring considerations
