8.1 Introduction 8.2 CPPs – Environmental 8.2.3 Alert & Action Alarms 8.2.4 Limits Hierarchy 8.3 Instrumentation 8.4 Production Process Parameters 8.5 General Design Issues 8.6 HVAC Controls 8.6.2 Particle Counting Section Summary
8.1 Introduction — Control & Instrumentation Overview

Original Text

8.1 Introduction

This chapter considers the various functions of Control and Instrumentation (C&I) systems for sterile products manufacturing facilities and focuses on those facility and environment controls which affect patient safety and product quality. The objective is to provide design guidance for cost effective systems which can be qualified.

C&I systems are used in many facility related systems. They may be deemed to affect patient safety and product quality if they control, monitor, or record a CPP, or directly affect a CQA. Components of C&I systems may also be considered critical if they come into direct physical contact with the product.

The functions described may be combined within a single C&I system or be performed by several independent systems.

Specific design advice has been given where possible, but it is stressed that each application has different priorities and operational preferences that influence the adopted solution.

Designers should also consider other relevant design criteria, such as safety, reliability, data integrity, and design for maintenance.

Trainer's Analysis

Core concept: the role of the C&I system in a sterile facility

The control and instrumentation (C&I) system is the "nervous system" of a sterile manufacturing facility. It does three things:

  • Control: keeps parameters such as temperature, differential pressure, and humidity within the specified range
  • Monitor: measures continuously or periodically to confirm parameters are within limits
  • Record: retains the data for traceability and compliance review

Any subsystem that controls, monitors, or records a critical process parameter (CPP) or directly affects a critical quality attribute (CQA) is regarded as "potentially impacting patient safety and product quality."

Analogy: the nervous system of a sterile facility

Think of a sterile facility as a human body. HVAC is the respiratory system (supplying clean air), the water systems are the circulatory system (carrying purified water), and C&I is the nervous system: it senses the environment (sensors), carries signals (signal cables and networks), reacts (controllers adjust valves or motors), and keeps a memory (data records).

Without a nervous system, the body cannot hold a steady temperature. Without C&I, a sterile facility cannot hold cleanroom differential pressure, temperature, and particle levels either.

Key point: data integrity is one of the design criteria

This section explicitly lists data integrity as a design consideration. When selecting or designing a C&I system, it is not enough to measure accurately; the system must also ensure the data is retained and cannot be tampered with, which is essential to applying the ALCOA+ principles.

8.2 Critical Process Parameters — Environmental Conditions

Original Text

8.2.1 Environmental Conditions within the Production Area

The production of sterile products requires a clean classified work environment for open, exposed processes. Processes and products vary greatly. Specific environmental parameters should be considered, specified, monitored, and recorded, as discussed in Chapter 5.

Several requirements for particulate and microbiological cleanliness, differential pressure (DP), and airflow are required in the GMPs for typical process steps and unit operations.

If manufacture of several products is considered, the design team should ensure that the design accommodates the most demanding product requirements.

8.2.2 Monitoring and Documenting

CPPs should be monitored and documented.

Monitoring means that a parameter is continuously or periodically measured to ensure it is within its defined limits. This can be accomplished with either permanently installed, portable, or disposable instruments. When determining whether to monitor a CPP continuously or periodically, it is recommended to perform a comprehensive risk assessment and develop a mitigation plan to fully define the rationale.

Documented means that the parameter value (or evidence that the value is within control limits) is recorded at some predefined frequency for future reference. The frequency should be based on a documented rationale which reflects:

  • Consequences of manufacturing outside required (process) limits
  • Probability and frequency of temporary parameter control loss
  • Duration and frequency of activities such as process interventions

An active control system is deemed to have a control loop with direct feed-back or feed-forward. A passive control system is where a condition is monitored, and management action is implemented, if needed, to rectify the deviation in conditions.

When CPPs are monitored, the monitoring regime should, where possible, be established with alert and action limits. Alert limits provide early warning of a potential deviation enabling corrective or preventative measures to be taken prior to an action limit being reached; in some conditions, alarm condition delays may be appropriate.

Table 8.1: Typical Environmental Process Parameters

Airborne particle levels (viable and non-viable) reflect the effect of achieving and maintaining the control parameters in Table 8.1. Particle levels are also influenced by internal operations (personnel).

Trainer's Analysis

Core concept: active control vs. passive control

This is the most important classification framework in this section:

  • Active control: has a control loop with feedback or feedforward. Example: AHU supply air temperature control. When the sensor detects high temperature, the controller automatically opens the chilled water valve further.
  • Passive control: has no automatic loop. The condition is maintained by the design itself (for example a fixed airflow ratio or HEPA filters), and personnel intervene when there is a deviation.

Key principle: passive control systems are usually more reliable than active ones (fewer parts, less to fail), but once a deviation occurs they respond more slowly. For this reason the guide allows a "lower" monitoring frequency for passive control.

Key point: the debate over pressure control

Note a key recommendation in Table 8.1: the guide does not recommend using actuated control dampers to actively control differential pressure.

Reason: differential pressure is extremely sensitive to door openings and personnel movement. Active control dampers easily cause "pressure oscillation" between rooms: room A's pressure rises, room B's controller reacts by lowering it, and the result is unstable back-and-forth hunting.

Technical baseline: passive locked-in-position dampers + continuous monitoring. Simple and reliable.

Analogy: passive vs. active control

Passive control is like a drainage ditch built to a designed slope: water naturally flows the right way and no pump is needed. Periodic walk-throughs to confirm there is no blockage are enough.

Active control is like piping with a pump: it can control flow precisely, but when the pump fails the water stops flowing. It needs more frequent monitoring and maintenance.

Decision logic for monitoring frequency

"How often should we measure?" is not decided by gut feeling. ISPE proposes three evaluation factors:

  1. Consequence of deviation: how serious it is to manufacture outside the process limits (scrapped product? recall? patient risk?)
  2. Probability of loss of control: the reliability and complexity of the control system
  3. Frequency of intervention: how often activities that can disturb the parameter occur, such as operator actions and door openings

The higher the risk, the more frequent the monitoring. Differential pressure and temperature in grade A/B areas usually need continuous monitoring; grade C/D can use a lower frequency.

Practical application: multi-product design at a CDMO

This section reminds us that if one area will make several products, the design must meet the "most stringent product requirement." For a CDMO this means:

  • Take the narrowest temperature range among all products
  • Take the highest differential pressure classification requirement
  • The monitoring system must be able to switch alert limits between products

Design recommendation: build in a BMS parameter-switching function so operators can quickly load the matching limit configuration for each product batch.

8.2.3 Alert and Action Alarms

Original Text

8.2.3 Alert and Action Alarms

CPPs should remain within specified values. Where monitoring and documenting is necessary, the monitoring system should provide an:

  • Alert Alarm to indicate that the parameter has deviated from the normal operating range (i.e., outside the Normal Operating Conditions — a possible control problem)
  • Action Alarm to indicate that the parameter has deviated from Process Limits (i.e., may result in a product quality issue)

Alarms should latch and not self-cancel (i.e., the alarm remains active even after the condition has been corrected) until acknowledged by the user/operator. All alarm conditions should be documented and corrective actions recorded.

Where momentary parameter deviation outside specified limits is acceptable, appropriate time delay intervals can be incorporated into the alarm logic. These should be thoroughly tested, with the rationale documented as part of the system qualification.

Trainer's Analysis

Two-tier alarm architecture

This section establishes the standard alarm model for a GMP C&I system:

Action alarm: approaching the process limit
▼
Alert alarm: deviating from the normal operating range
▼
Normal operating conditions

Alert = early warning, giving you time to take preventive action. Action = the process limit is close to being reached or has been exceeded, and immediate response is required.

Key point: the alarm latching principle

Alarms that "latch and do not clear automatically" are a core GMP design requirement. Even after the deviating condition has returned to normal, the alarm stays active until the operator acknowledges it manually.

Why? It ensures every deviation is seen, assessed, and recorded by someone. If alarms cleared themselves, operators might never know a deviation had occurred, which is fatal for product quality decisions and deviation investigations.

Key point: the time delay trap

"Time delay" logic that tolerates brief excursions sounds reasonable (for example a momentary pressure dip when a door opens), but if set improperly it can hide real problems.

ISPE requires that delay logic be "thoroughly tested" and have a "documented rationale." At audit, the focus is often: what is the basis for the delay setting, and was it risk assessed?

8.2.4 Environmental Process Limits, Facility Design Limits, and Normal Operating Conditions

Original Text

8.2.4 Environmental Process Limits, Facility Design Limits, and Normal Operating Conditions

Environmental Process Limits are the upper and lower limits demanded by the production process(es). The Facility Design Limits are used to calculate HVAC facility or utility capacity, and are based upon a number of factors, such as:

  • Operator comfort
  • Energy conservation
  • Regulatory requirements
  • Process limits
  • What is technically and practically possible

Facility Design Limits should be set to operate within Normal Operating Conditions, where the extremes of these conditions are defined by the Alert Limits.

Example: Assume that Process Limits are 22°C ± 4°C (71.6°F ± 7.2°F). The HVAC system facility is designed to provide 22°C ± 2°C (71.6°F ± 3.6°F); however, control to within 22°C ± 1°C (71.6°F ± 1.8°F) is usual. Alert Limits can be set at a lower limit of 21°C (69.8°F) and an upper limit of 23°C (71.4°F), as deviation outside these conditions indicates a situation which may require investigation.

Figure 8.1: Alert and Alarm Limits illustrates this relationship.

Trainer's Analysis

Analogy: the speed limit on a highway

Imagine a highway with a 110 km/h speed limit (Process Limit). The car is designed to cruise at 100 km/h (Facility Design Limit). You normally drive at 95-105 km/h (Normal Operating Conditions). The dashboard lights a yellow warning at 105 km/h (Alert) and sounds an alarm above 110 km/h (Action Alarm).

Key point: every tier exists for a reason and none can be omitted. If you use the Process Limit directly as the Alert Limit, there is no room left for early warning.

Exercises for reflection

  1. If a product's process limit is 22°C ± 2°C (very narrow), and on a summer day with an outside temperature of 35°C the HVAC system can only control to ± 1.5°C, what problem does this indicate? How should it be solved?
  2. Why does ISPE stress that the "facility design limits" must consider both operator comfort and energy saving? How does this relate to product quality?

The four-tier limit architecture, from wide to narrow

This is the most important design concept in the chapter, explained tier by tier using temperature as the example:

The "white space" between tiers is the safety margin. In a well-designed system there is enough room between the tiers that a minor disturbance does not trigger an Action Alarm.

8.3 Instrumentation

Original Text

8.3.1 Physical Design

Instruments in process areas should be located to allow cleaning and sanitization of exposed surfaces and should be designed and installed to prevent accumulation of particulate matter. Computer screens and keyboards located in processing areas should be cleanable, such as by utilizing touch membrane technology.

Instruments in direct contact with the product, its components, or associated with a critical manufacturing process should be designed and installed to:

  • Prevent accumulation of any matter (including product)
  • Withstand required cleaning/sanitization processes and agents without degradation
  • Not present a contamination risk to the product or its components
  • Not be degraded (physically or in performance) by contact with the product

Many instruments have sensing elements remote from their data processing components. The use of such instruments allows isolation, separation, or remote location of the processing components. This may simplify cleaning and reduce contamination risk.

8.3.2 Performance: Accuracy

When assessing an instrument's accuracy, several factors should be considered:

  • Fitness for purpose
  • Instrument cost increases with accuracy
  • How misleading the instrument can be without threatening product quality
  • Higher accuracy instruments reduce the risk of manufacture under unsuitable conditions because of instrument drift

For each CPP, there are usually Process Limits within which a product should be produced. C&I systems should be designed to control conditions to a set point within the Process Limits, usually with a margin of safety or reserve.

An indicated value on an instrument is subject to uncertainty (i.e., subject to the instrument accuracy). For the true condition to remain within Process Limits at the indicated extremes of the Alert Limits, the instrument's accuracy should give a measurement whose uncertainty is no greater than the difference between the Process and Alert Limits. This difference defines the Instrument Permitted Limit.

Example: Process Limits are 22°C ± 2°C, Alert Limits are 22°C ± 1°C. At the extremes of the Alert Limits, the instrument should be accurate to at least ± 0.5°C to guarantee temperature remains within Process Limits.

8.3.3 Location

Instrument sensors measuring the critical process or environmental parameter(s) should be located at a point representative of the condition to be measured. Ease of calibration should also be considered.

Where separate sensors are used to control and monitor the same CPP, they should be co-located to ensure the parameter is equally measured.

8.3.4 Calibration

The calibration method and its cost should be considered when selecting any instrument. Comprehensive calibration guidance should be obtained from the suppliers before an instrument is chosen.

Trainer's Analysis

Four principles of physical instrument design

Instruments in sterile areas must not only "measure accurately" but also follow cleanroom design principles:

  1. Cleanable: smooth surfaces with no dead spots, able to withstand disinfectants
  2. No accumulation: installed so as to avoid horizontal recesses or crevices where dust can collect
  3. No contamination risk: product-contact parts are made of compatible materials
  4. Durable: not degraded by the product or cleaning agents

In practice, more and more instruments use a "remote sensing" design: only a small probe sits in the cleanroom while the electronics are in the technical interstitial space, greatly reducing cleaning difficulty and contamination risk.

Instrument permitted limit

This is an elegant design concept:

Instrument permitted limit = process limit - alert limit

Taking temperature as an example:

  • Process limit: 22°C ± 2°C → upper limit 24°C
  • Alert limit: 22°C ± 1°C → upper limit 23°C
  • Instrument permitted limit: 24 - 23 = 1°C
  • The instrument accuracy therefore needs to be at least ± 0.5°C

If a more accurate instrument is used (for example ± 0.1°C), there is a larger "drift margin" and the calibration interval can be extended, which saves money in the long run.

Key point: the accuracy vs. cost decision

The higher the accuracy, the more expensive the instrument, but it brings three benefits:

  • A larger drift allowance → calibration frequency can be reduced
  • Lower risk of manufacturing under inappropriate conditions
  • Fewer deviation events → lower investigation and scrap costs

ISPE recommends choosing high-accuracy instruments for critical support systems and allowing lower accuracy for non-critical systems. This is consistent with a risk-based design philosophy.

Key point: sensor co-location

When different sensors are used to "control" and to "monitor" the same CPP, the two must be installed at the same location. Otherwise the control sensor may read 21.5°C (normal) while the monitoring sensor, at a different location, reads 23.5°C (out of limits), causing confusion and an investigation burden.

Exercises for reflection

  1. One temperature sensor is installed at the return air grille (warmer) and another directly above the work surface (cooler). Which is better as the "representative measurement point"? Why?
  2. If calibration cost is one of the factors in selecting instruments, how would you choose between a high-accuracy sensor that is hard to calibrate in situ and a medium-accuracy sensor that is easy to calibrate?
8.4 Production Process Parameters

Original Text

8.4 Production Process Parameters

The number and diversity of production processes that can be used in sterile product manufacturing facilities are such that a comprehensive discussion of their parameters is not practical within the scope of this Guide.

Detailed knowledge of the production process in question and application of rigorous design and operation review methods are necessary to identify appropriate systems of control and monitoring. This can be achieved through detailed PAT (Process Analytical Technology) and application of process control to achieve proper parameters or conditions that mitigate product quality issues and avoid impact on patient safety.

Trainer's Analysis

Why is this section short? What it implies about design philosophy

This section is deliberately short because production process parameters (such as fill weight, stopper placement, and capping torque) vary by product and cannot be generalized. It does, however, convey two important messages:

  1. PAT is the preferred approach: use real-time analytical technology to monitor the process rather than relying on final testing
  2. Rigorous design review is required: the control and monitoring system for each production process must be tailored through risk assessment

Analogy: environmental parameters vs. process parameters

If the environmental parameters (temperature, differential pressure, particle counts) are the "stage lighting and air conditioning," then the process parameters (fill volume, stoppering depth, seal integrity) are "the actors' performance."

ISPE Vol.3 mainly designs the stage, which is environmental control. The actors' performance (process control) must be designed for the specific play (product), so this guide gives only the methodology (PAT + design review) and no specific parameters.

Practical application: common process parameters at a CDMO

Although this section does not list them, the following are common CPPs on a CDMO aseptic filling line:

  • Fill weight: typically within ± 2-5%, depending on dosage form and container
  • Stopper placement: stoppering height and tilt
  • Seal integrity: aluminum cap crimping torque
  • Fill speed: affects foaming and accuracy
  • Inert gas overlay: control of residual oxygen
8.5 General Design Issues

Original Text

8.5 General Design Issues

Computerized system lifecycle activities, such as specification, design, and verification should be scaled according to:

  • Potential for system to impact patient safety, product quality, and data integrity (risk assessment)
  • System complexity and novelty (architecture and categorization of system components)
  • Outcome of supplier assessment (supplier capability)

Refer to ISPE GAMP 5 for further details of these considerations and the scaling of lifecycle activities.

The following sections discuss cost effective separation of system functions (i.e., monitoring and control) and system choice in the context of typical supplier capabilities.

Trainer's Analysis

Core concept: the graded approach to the computerized system lifecycle

Not every C&I system needs the same level of rigor in validation. ISPE draws on the core idea of GAMP 5: a risk-based approach.

Three grading dimensions:

  • Degree of impact: if this system fails, will it affect patient safety? Will it affect data integrity?
  • Complexity: is it a simple single-loop controller, or a SCADA integrating several subsystems?
  • Supplier reliability: does the supplier have a sound quality management system? Does software development follow an SDLC?

High impact + high complexity + unqualified supplier = the most complete validation documentation is needed. Low impact + mature, simple system + well-known supplier = validation can be simplified.

Key point: separation of monitoring and control

This section implies an important design strategy: separate the "control" and "monitoring" functions onto different systems. For example:

  • Control: the BMS/BAS handles HVAC loop control
  • Monitoring: an independent environmental monitoring system (EMS) handles recording and alarms

Benefit: the monitoring system is independent of the control system and acts as a "second line of defense." If the control system fails, the monitoring system can still detect the deviation.

8.6 HVAC Control System Choice

Original Text

8.6.1 Control System Choice

Commercially available Building Management Systems/Building Automation Systems (BMS/BAS) are encouraged to be installed in all facilities to monitor critical facility control systems.

There may be some safety-critical systems that should utilize Distributed Control Systems (DCS) and Programmable Logic Controllers (PLC) with Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA); however, these are primarily targeted at controlling processes.

HVAC may be monitored and controlled using several control system types. Those designed specifically for HVAC include conventional controllers (typically single loop controls) and, more appropriately, BMS/BAS.

When specifying systems to control HVAC, the following should be considered:

  • HVAC's industrial nature in cleanroom applications may not justify use of PLC or DCS based solutions; however, personnel safety issues may justify their use.
  • Pharmaceutical HVAC can be controlled satisfactorily using HVAC industry control systems.

Where control is needed for a few simple systems, conventional controls may provide a marginal cost advantage. This advantage is offset by the fact that conventional controls cannot be integrated readily into any future BMS/BAS demanded by site development.

As the application scale, complexity, and remote monitoring demands increase, the use of BMS/BAS rapidly becomes more cost effective.

Monitoring of critical environmental parameters can be accomplished via the Process Control System, which should be qualified. The qualification of the BMS/BAS may then become simpler.

Trainer's Analysis

Key point: ISPE explicitly recommends BMS/BAS

The core message of this section is clear: use a BMS/BAS for HVAC; a DCS or PLC is not needed.

Reasons:

  • The "industrial nature" of pharmaceutical HVAC does not require the high-speed processing of a DCS/PLC
  • BMS/BAS is the native solution of the HVAC industry, with a mature supplier ecosystem
  • As the scale grows, the cost-effectiveness advantage of BMS/BAS becomes more and more obvious

Exception: where personnel safety is involved (such as toxic gas detection or emergency exhaust), a PLC/DCS may be needed.

Analogy: the logic of choosing a vehicle

Using a DCS to control HVAC is like driving a child to school in an F1 race car: performance far beyond the need, but high maintenance cost and complex operation.

A BMS/BAS is like a family SUV: it fully meets the need, is easy to maintain, and it is easy to add features later (such as navigation or parking sensors).

A traditional single-loop controller is like a bicycle: great for short distances, but it cannot take the whole family out.

Separation strategy for monitoring and control

ISPE proposes a clever simplification strategy:

  1. Use a validated process control system to "monitor" the critical environmental parameters
  2. The BMS/BAS is responsible only for "controlling" the HVAC
  3. Result: the qualification of the BMS/BAS can be simplified, because monitoring of the critical CPPs is already carried out by another validated system

This greatly reduces the validation scope and cost of the BMS/BAS without sacrificing compliance.

8.6.2 Airborne Particle Counting

Original Text

8.6.2 Airborne Particle Counting

The act of classification of a space environment, and of monitoring that environment "in operation", should be differentiated:

  • The method for formal classification is specified in ISO 14644-1. This standard defines the minimum number of sample locations, the minimum sample size at each location, the class limits, and the method for evaluation of data.
  • Note: In the context of sterile product manufacture, EU Annex 1 sets some class limits that are different from those found in FDA guidance and ISO 14644-1.
  • Monitoring may use similar instrumentation; in this case, specific critical or most important locations are determined from investigation and studies, and these are monitored to demonstrate the performance of critical parts of the controlled environment.

Particle counting instruments operate by taking a sample of the air and measuring the particle concentration by evaluation of scattered light in a special optical chamber. Such instruments can measure both the number and size of particles in the size range 0.1 µm to 5.0 µm.

Particle counting system configurations:

  • Single portable instruments: Located close to the environment being classified or monitored. Suitable for evaluating particles 0.1 µm to 5.0 µm. Used for both classification and monitoring.
  • Single fixed instruments with manifold: Connected to multiple sample locations via tubing arrays. Each location sampled in turn. Suitable only for 0.1 µm to 0.5 µm due to potential drop out of larger particles in transport tubing. Used for monitoring only.
  • Multiple miniature point-of-use counters: Each located close to a monitoring location, connected to a data acquisition system. Suitable for 0.1 µm to 5.0 µm. Used for monitoring only.

Major points to consider for particle monitoring systems:

  • Difficulty of correlating data from the relatively small number of sample points of a monitoring system compared to the larger number used for classification
  • Identifying the room "worst case" points and relating them to overall room conditions
  • Determination of an appropriate sampling frequency
  • Management and interpretation of potentially large amounts of data
  • Determination of alert and action levels
  • Procedures for excursion beyond alert and action levels
  • Re-evaluation of sample points if there is a change in room layout
  • Special attention to the distance between air collection point and counter: inner diameter of tubing, airflow throughput and turbulence (Reynolds numbers), particle drop-out impact, tubing material (surface roughness, electrostatic charge), geometry of flow paths (kinks, obstructions, sharp curves)

Where particle concentrations are very low, monitoring system alert and action levels may be better expressed using frequency (pattern) of seeing low counts rather than trying to discriminate between very low numbers.

2004 FDA Guidance: "Regular monitoring should be performed during each production shift. We recommend conducting nonviable particle monitoring with a remote counting system. These systems are capable of collecting more comprehensive data and are generally less invasive than portable particle counters."

2009 EU Annex 1: "For Grade A zone, particle monitoring should be undertaken for the full duration of critical processing, including equipment assembly, except where justified by contaminants in the process that would damage the particle counter or present a hazard... It is recommended that a similar system be used for Grade B zones although the sample frequency may be decreased."

Trainer's Analysis

Key point: tubing design is the hidden critical factor

A fixed manifold system can only measure 0.1-0.5 µm, because larger particles (≥ 0.5 µm) "drop out" in the transport tubing. Contributing factors include:

  • Tubing inner diameter: too narrow gives excessive flow velocity and turbulence
  • Tubing length: the longer it is, the more large particles are lost
  • Tubing material: inner wall roughness and static charge attract particles
  • Bends and obstructions: sharp bends are the main cause of particle loss

The design must calculate the Reynolds number to ensure the flow regime in the tubing is within an appropriate range.

Key point: differences between FDA and EU Annex 1

The two major regulations differ subtly in their particle monitoring requirements:

  • FDA: recommends monitoring each shift, and recommends remote counting systems (less intrusive, more comprehensive data)
  • EU Annex 1: grade A areas must be monitored for the full duration of critical processing (stricter), while grade B can be monitored less frequently

If the product is exported to both the US and Europe, the stricter standard of the two must be adopted, namely continuous monitoring of grade A for the full duration.

Analogy: expressing low counts as a "frequency"

When particle counts are extremely low (for example grade A areas often show 0 or 1 particles), looking at the raw number is meaningless: the difference between 0 and 1 has no statistical significance.

ISPE suggests using a "frequency mode" instead: for example, "≥ 1 particle detected in 5 of 100 samples" is more informative than "an average of 0.05 particles/m³." It is like judging whether an area is safe: you do not look at an "average crime rate of 0.001" but at "3 incidents in the past year, all late on weekend nights." The pattern means more than the number.

Exercises for reflection

  1. You are selecting a particle monitoring system for a new filling line. The line is inside a grade A isolator and must satisfy both FDA and EU Annex 1. Which system configuration would you choose? Why?
  2. If the sampling tubing of a manifold system is 15 meters from the particle counter to the farthest sampling point, what would you worry about? How would you verify that the tubing loss is acceptable?
  3. Why must sampling point locations be re-evaluated after a room layout change? Give a specific example.

Classification vs. monitoring: do not confuse them

This is a common point of confusion in regulatory audits:

Section Summary

Key Takeaways

Chapter 8 Summary

  1. C&I systems are the nervous system of sterile manufacturing facilities — they control, monitor, and record parameters that affect patient safety and product quality.
  2. Environmental CPPs (temperature, RH, differential pressure, particle count) can be managed through active or passive control strategies, each with different monitoring frequency requirements.
  3. Alert and Action alarms provide a two-tier warning system. Alarms must latch (not self-cancel) and any time delays must be justified and qualified.
  4. A clear hierarchy of limits (Process Limits > Facility Design Limits > Alert Limits > Normal Operating Conditions) ensures adequate safety margins at every level.
  5. Instrument selection must balance accuracy vs. cost, with the Instrument Permitted Limit defining the minimum acceptable accuracy. Sensors must be co-located when used for both control and monitoring of the same CPP.
  6. BMS/BAS is the recommended control system for HVAC in pharmaceutical facilities. DCS/PLC/SCADA should be reserved for safety-critical or complex process control applications.
  7. Airborne particle counting requires clear differentiation between classification (ISO 14644-1) and monitoring. System configuration must account for tubing losses, and both FDA and EU Annex 1 requirements must be met for global supply.

Key Takeaways

Chapter 8 Summary

  1. The control and instrumentation (C&I) system is the nervous system of a sterile facility: it controls, monitors, and records the parameters that affect patient safety and product quality.
  2. Environmental CPPs (temperature, humidity, differential pressure, particle counts) can be managed with active or passive control strategies, and the monitoring frequency varies with the strategy.
  3. Alert and Action alarms form a two-tier early warning system. Alarms must latch (not clear automatically), and time delays must have a sound rationale and be verified.
  4. The four-tier limit architecture (process limit > facility design limit > alert limit > normal operating conditions) ensures there is enough safety margin at every tier.
  5. Instrument selection must balance accuracy and cost, and the "instrument permitted limit" defines the minimum acceptable accuracy. Sensors that control and monitor the same CPP must be co-located.
  6. BMS/BAS is the recommended control system for pharmaceutical HVAC. DCS/PLC/SCADA should be reserved for safety-critical or complex process control.
  7. Airborne particle counting must distinguish "classification" (ISO 14644-1) from "monitoring." The system configuration must account for tubing loss, and supplying global markets requires meeting both FDA and EU Annex 1.

Key action items for CDMO operations

  • Confirm that every environmental CPP has a documented four-tier limit architecture
  • Review whether BMS alarms are latching and whether time delays have a documented basis
  • Assess whether instrument accuracy meets the "instrument permitted limit" requirement
  • Confirm the co-location status of control and monitoring sensors
  • Review whether the particle monitoring system meets both FDA and EU Annex 1 requirements
  • Confirm that tubing loss in manifold systems has been verified
7a

Chapter 7a: 9a. Barrier & Isolator (9.1–9.4)

p167-p178

ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 3 (3rd Ed.) | p167 – p178

Learning Objectives

  1. Understand why barrier technologies are preferred over conventional cleanrooms for aseptic processing
  2. Distinguish between oRABS, cRABS, and isolator systems with precise definitions
  3. Compare the three technologies across cost, flexibility, contamination control, and regulatory acceptance
  4. Apply a risk-based framework for choosing barrier technology for new or retrofitted facilities
  5. Recognize the EU Annex 1 (2022) direction toward isolators and cRABS

Section Navigation

9.1 Introduction 9.2 System Definitions 9.2.1 Isolators 9.2.2 RABS 9.3 System Comparisons 9.4 Factors to Consider
9.1

Introduction

p167 – p168

English — Original Content

For new and renovated aseptic processing facilities, barrier technologies, such as isolators and RABS, are usually preferred to protect the product. They are being increasingly used for aseptic filling. Isolators can provide a higher safety level and are typically used in new facility designs. RABS are usually used to upgrade existing facilities, when existing equipment needs to have better protection.

Both technologies can be applied to batches of all sizes, from small scale filling of clinical trial materials to large, automated, high speed processing lines. They can also be applied to research and development, quality control (sterility testing), and drug formulation. When the product is hazardous, isolators or RABS, with their reduced air overspill into a room, can help to protect the operator and the surrounding environment.

People are considered the greatest source of contamination in the manufacturing of sterile products. Over the past decades, substantial progress has been made in separating the operator from the critical areas within the aseptic manufacturing suite.

Physical separation, equipment integration, and the increasing use of automation in these systems can reduce the need for personnel involvement inside critical areas. Advantages of these technologies can, however, be counteracted by poor design and ineffective operator training. Ergonomic aspects are fundamental to the design concept and should be considered in conjunction with:

  • Mechanical movement (i.e., moving machine parts)
  • Safe material and product transfers in and out of the barrier
  • Cleanability
  • Ability to decontaminate the system
  • Appropriate background environment in which the system is to be operated

These decisions should be made on a risk-based approach, depending upon the application and specific system design.

Commentary

For new or renovated aseptic processing facilities, barrier technology (such as isolators and RABS) is generally the preferred way to protect the product, and its use in aseptic filling is increasing. Isolators provide a higher level of assurance and are typically used in new facility designs. RABS are more commonly used to upgrade existing facilities, giving better protection to existing equipment.

Both technologies suit a wide range of batch sizes, from filling small clinical trial materials to large, automated high-speed lines. They can also be applied in R&D, QC (sterility testing), and drug compounding. When the product is hazardous, an isolator or RABS helps protect operators and the surrounding environment by reducing the amount of air spilling into the room.

Core Concept: People Are the Biggest Source of Contamination

In sterile product manufacturing, personnel are regarded as the biggest source of contamination. Over the past several decades the industry has made major progress in separating operators from the critical zones of the aseptic suite, and barrier technology is the core means of achieving this.

Physical separation, equipment integration, and increased automation can reduce the need for personnel to be involved in critical zones. However, these benefits can be offset by poor design and ineffective operator training. Human factors engineering is fundamental to the design concept and must be considered together with the following:

  • Mechanical motion (i.e., moving machine parts)
  • Safe transfer of materials and product into and out of the barrier
  • Cleanability
  • Ability to decontaminate the system
  • The appropriate background environment in which the system operates

Practical Analogy

Think of barrier technology as an "aseptic kitchen": a conventional cleanroom is like an open kitchen where the cook (the operator) works in the same space; a RABS is like a kitchen with a glass partition, where the cook works through gloves; an isolator is like a fully sealed vending machine, where the food is prepared in a completely isolated environment.

9.2

System Definitions

p168 – p172

English — Original Content

The differences between the types of isolators and RABS used in pharmaceutical aseptic processing should be understood. Isolators and RABS can be broadly classified according to the type of separation they provide and the assurance of maintaining that separation, although there may be some overlap in the degrees of separation and operator protection.

Figure 9.1 (from ISO 14644-7) illustrates increasing levels of separation assurance moving from purely aerodynamic separation (as in a unidirectional airflow hood) to complete physical separation (as in a closed isolator).

Along the continuum of assurance of maintaining separation:

  • RABS tend to utilize physical separation and air overspill all around the barrier to separate personnel from the aseptic processing critical areas.
  • Isolators tend to rely on physical separation, positive pressure differentials and mouseholes with air overspill to provide the necessary level of separation and protection.

Where hazardous materials are aseptically processed:

  • RABS requires personnel to wear PPE and rooms to be fully segregated by airlocks to avoid spreading of product throughout the facility and into the environment.
  • Isolators maintain operator protection by technical measures, such as adequate differential pressure zones and the integrity of the isolator.
Commentary

It is essential to understand the differences between the various types of isolators and RABS used in pharmaceutical aseptic processing. Isolators and RABS can be broadly classified by the type of separation they provide and the degree of assurance with which that separation is maintained, although there may be some overlap in the level of separation and operator protection.

Continuum of Separation Assurance (Figure 9.1)

As shown in ISO 14644-7, the level of separation assurance runs from low to high:

Airflow separation (UAF hood) Physical + airflow (RABS) Full physical separation (sealed isolator)

Along this continuum of separation assurance:

  • RABS tend to use physical separation and air spillage around the barrier to separate personnel from the critical zone of the aseptic process.
  • Isolators rely on physical separation, positive pressure differentials, and mouseholes with air spillage to provide the required level of separation and protection.

Special Considerations for Hazardous Materials

When handling hazardous materials, a RABS requires personnel to wear PPE and the room to be fully separated by airlocks. An isolator maintains operator protection through technical measures (such as appropriate pressure differential zones and isolator integrity). This is why isolators are particularly favored for highly potent active pharmaceutical ingredients (HPAPIs).

9.2.1 Aseptic Isolators
English — Original Content

An aseptic isolator is described as a decontaminated unit which meets ISO 5/Grade A conditions on the inside and does not compromise these conditions over a specified period of time, by providing an uncompromised isolation of its interior from the surrounding environment.

9.2.1.1 Types of Isolators

Aseptic isolators can be either "open" or "closed", as defined in PDA TR 34, depending upon their operational state and may operate at positive or negative pressures with respect to the surrounding environment:

  • When "closed", isolators may exchange air with the surrounding environment only through microbial retentive filters.
  • When "open", isolators may transfer air directly to the surrounding environment through openings (e.g., mouseholes) that prevent the ingress of viable and non-viable particles.

1. Closed Isolators

Closed isolators are typically used for batch processes that do not require a high number of components. Material is placed inside the isolator before a decontamination cycle is performed, or material is transferred in via decontamination airlocks. Typical applications for a closed isolator are for a formulation process or for sterility testing.

2. Open Isolators

Open isolators are used in continuous process applications. Material is continuously transferred into the isolator via appropriate decontamination or sterilization devices. A differential pressure zoning concept guarantees a continuous airflow towards the surrounding environment to prevent particulate or microbiological ingress through transfer openings.

9.2.1.2 Considerations

The level of separation provided by isolators (both open and closed) allows for operating an isolator in an ISO 8/Grade C environment (Grade D or unclassified, but access controlled for sterility testing application), while providing ISO 5/Grade A conditions inside the isolator, after performing a surface decontamination.

A surface decontamination cycle is typically capable of six-log spore reduction. A surface decontamination cycle should be applied following any event when the enclosure is opened towards the surrounding environment.

The following should be considered for isolators:

  • Proper surface decontamination should be performed with a sporicidal agent (e.g., hydrogen peroxide).
  • Continuous positive pressure should be maintained inside the isolator.
  • Glove maintenance programs should ensure integrity and decontamination of gloves.
  • Transfer systems should ensure that the cleanliness of the isolator is not compromised.
  • Cleaning processes should ensure that all production remains are properly removed after a production batch, to a reproducible value allowing an efficient surface decontamination.
Commentary

Key Definition: Aseptic Isolator

An aseptic isolator is a decontaminated unit whose interior meets ISO 5/Grade A conditions and which, by providing uncompromised separation from the surrounding environment, does not jeopardize those conditions for a defined period of time.

9.2.1.1 Isolator Types

Aseptic isolators can be classified as "open" or "closed" according to their operating state (as defined in PDA TR 34), and can operate at positive or negative pressure relative to the surrounding environment:

  • "Closed" isolators exchange air with the surrounding environment only through microbe-retentive filters.
  • "Open" isolators transfer air directly to the surrounding environment through openings (such as mouseholes) that prevent the ingress of viable and non-viable particles.

9.2.1.2 Isolator Considerations

Important: The Advantage of a Downgraded Background Environment

The level of separation an isolator provides allows it to be operated in an ISO 8/Grade C environment (sterility testing applications can even be located in a Grade D or unclassified but access-controlled environment), while the interior of the isolator provides ISO 5/Grade A conditions after surface decontamination. This is a significant advantage over RABS, which require an ISO 7/Grade B background.

A surface decontamination cycle typically achieves a six-log spore reduction (i.e., a 99.9999% kill rate). A surface decontamination cycle should be performed whenever the isolator has been opened to the surrounding environment.

Key points to consider for isolators:

  • Appropriate surface decontamination using a sporicidal agent (such as hydrogen peroxide/VHP)
  • Maintaining continuous positive pressure inside the isolator
  • A glove maintenance program that ensures integrity and decontamination
  • Transfer systems must not compromise the cleanliness of the isolator
  • Cleaning processes that ensure all production residues are properly removed
9.2.2 Restricted Access Barrier Systems (RABS)
English — Original Content

A RABS is described as an aseptic processing system that provides an enclosed environment to house an aseptic processing line and supply it with ISO 5/Grade A unidirectional air. RABS utilize rigid wall enclosure design to provide a physical separation of the process. This rigid wall enclosure is decontaminated with sporicidal disinfectant and interventions are done using installed barrier gloves. RABS are rarely opened, except as appropriate.

RABS design provides a physical separation of the process through rigid doors and gloves, while keeping air overspill into the surrounding (or positive differential pressure versus the surrounding) as the main method of separation. RABS can provide ISO 5/Grade A environments on the inside and can be located in ISO 7/Grade B surroundings. RABS should be decontaminated with a sporicidal agent and operated within a fully disinfected surrounding ISO 7/Grade B cleanroom.

9.2.2.1 Types of RABS

Operations Perspective:

1. Open RABS (oRABS)

An open RABS is designed to operate with doors closed at all times, except in rare predefined circumstances when the doors of the enclosure can be opened to perform specific interventions.

2. Closed RABS (cRABS)

A closed RABS remains closed at all times during operation. The only acceptable intervention would be for machinery setup.

Airflow Design Perspective:

1. Active RABS with Air Overspill into the Room

An active RABS with air overspill into the room uses an integral HEPA filtered air supply providing UAF to the critical process and air overspill into the room below the critical process. RABS are not suitable for hazardous products, as they spill air into the surrounding area.

2. Passive RABS with Air Overspill to the Surrounding

In a passive RABS, the airflow to the critical area is provided by ceiling mounted HEPA filters and the bottom of the enclosure is open to the room to provide for airflow through the system.

3. Active RABS with Air Returns Through HEPA Filters

An active RABS with air returns through HEPA filters uses an integral HEPA filtered air supply providing UAF to the critical process. It also uses air return through HEPA filters to prevent hazardous product migrating to the surrounding or microbial contamination migrating into the RABS. This type of RABS can be suitable for hazardous products, based on a risk assessment.

9.2.2.2 Considerations

A formal risk management program should be established for RABS to ensure the effectiveness of the design in relation with the process, as well as the efficiency of the applied disinfection program.

The following should be considered for RABS:

  • Gloves and gauntlets attached to the glove ports should be sterile when installed. A glove monitoring program should ensure proper disinfection procedures and intervals, as well as glove exchange intervals.
  • Written procedures should describe what is done when an open door intervention (which should be rare) is performed.
    • Open door interventions should be documented, described in batch records, and followed by a disinfection step.
    • Open door interventions may require a line clearance, which should be documented in batch records.
  • Direct and indirect product contact parts and fluid pathways should be sterilized prior to filling of each batch.
  • Product contact equipment should be subject to sterilization.
  • Sterile components and supplies should be transferred to the RABS without exposing sterile surfaces to less clean environments, such as the use of RTPs or disinfection airlocks.
  • Robust disinfection of all non-product contact surfaces within the RABS should be performed with a suitable sporicidal agent before each batch or campaign.
  • The effectiveness of the overall disinfection program should be demonstrated and routinely evaluated as part of the environmental monitoring program.
Commentary

Key Definition: RABS (Restricted Access Barrier System)

A RABS is an aseptic processing system that provides an enclosed environment housing the aseptic processing line and supplied with ISO 5/Grade A unidirectional airflow. It uses a rigid-wall enclosure to provide physical separation, is decontaminated with sporicidal disinfectants, and interventions are carried out through installed barrier gloves.

Key difference: a RABS is located in an ISO 7/Grade B environment (rather than the Grade C/D of an isolator) and relies mainly on air spillage, rather than a positive pressure differential, to maintain separation.

9.2.2.1 RABS Types

Classified by mode of operation:

Classified by airflow design:

9.2.2.2 RABS Considerations

Strict Control of Door-Opening Interventions

A door-opening intervention is a significant event in RABS operation and must:

  • Be covered by a written procedure describing when and how it is performed
  • Be recorded in the batch record
  • Be followed by a disinfection step
  • Possibly require line clearance

EU Annex 1 (2022) is stricter on door-opening interventions and tends to treat a system that needs frequent door openings as not meeting the definition of a cRABS.

Other key RABS considerations:

  • Gloves and sleeves on the glove ports should be installed in a sterile state, and a glove monitoring program is required
  • Product-contact parts and fluid paths must be sterilized before each filling batch
  • Sterile components transferred into the RABS must not be exposed to a lower-cleanliness environment (use an RTP or a disinfected airlock)
  • Before each batch or campaign, all non-product-contact surfaces inside the RABS require robust sporicidal disinfection
  • The effectiveness of the disinfection program must be demonstrated and periodically evaluated as part of the environmental monitoring program
9.3

System Comparisons

p172 – p176

English — Original Content

In conventional aseptic filling operations, the filling equipment and gowned personnel operate together in a cleanroom environment. There is limited defined separation between the personnel and the production environment (e.g., flexible plastic curtains). The product and product contact exposure areas are locally protected in an ISO 5/Grade A environment.

Isolators and RABS utilize physical or aerodynamic methods (or both) to achieve separation between the inside of the containment and the surrounding environment. There are two primary differences between isolators and RABS:

Decontamination: Isolators are reproducibly decontaminated using an automated system (e.g., using VHP); such decontamination can be performed batch-wise. RABS are usually thoroughly manually disinfected. Alternatively, decontamination is performed by gassing or fogging processes together with the surrounding room. Typically, this cannot be performed batch-wise and manual disinfection may be used in conjunction with the room decontamination.

Pressure differentials: Isolators operate at an established pressure differential with respect to the surrounding environment, while RABS utilize air overspill without a defined pressure differential to achieve aerodynamic separation.

Table 9.1 contains points to be considered and highlights areas of differences among traditional cleanrooms, RABS, and isolator designs. Each system should be considered in terms of its intended use and the specific circumstances related to that use. All consideration points assume a proper design according to the latest standards of the respective technology. Poor design can have a negative impact (e.g., a poorly designed isolator can be less efficient than a well designed RABS).

Commentary

In a conventional aseptic filling operation, the filling equipment and gowned personnel work together in the same cleanroom environment, with only limited defined separation between personnel and the production environment (such as flexible plastic curtains).

The Importance of Design Quality

ISPE specifically emphasizes that a poorly designed isolator may be less effective than a well-designed RABS. Choosing the technology type is only the first step; the quality of the subsequent engineering design determines success or failure. This is also why ISPE positions this chapter as "points to consider" rather than a simple conclusion that "isolators are best".

Table 9.1: Points to Consider — Traditional Cleanrooms vs RABS vs Isolators

Table 9.1: Comparison of Design Considerations for Traditional Cleanrooms, RABS, and Isolators

9.4

Factors to Consider When Choosing

p176 – p179

9.4.1 Personnel Involvement with the Aseptic Process

English — Original Content

Isolator technology removes a major source of bio-contamination by eliminating direct operator intervention from the aseptic process, making it superior for aseptic/containment applications. RABS are superior to conventional manned cleanrooms for aseptic operation and can approach the superior separation provided by isolators if the doors remain closed.

Commentary

Isolator technology removes the main source of biological contamination by eliminating direct operator intervention in the aseptic process, which makes it superior for aseptic/sealed applications. A RABS is better for aseptic operations than a traditional cleanroom that personnel enter and, if the doors are kept closed, can approach the superior separation provided by an isolator.

CDMO Practical Perspective

For a CDMO, a cRABS (doors kept closed) can approach the separation level of an isolator, which makes it an important design decision point. If an existing facility cannot accommodate an isolator, a cRABS is a pragmatic and regulatory-acceptable choice.

9.4.2 Labor Efficiency Gains

English — Original Content

Isolators eliminate a confining gown, close fitting hood, and face mask, leading to improved operator comfort and cost savings in laundry and cleanroom clothing sterilization (each operator can consume 4 to 5 gown sets per day). Isolator systems require reduced gowning according to the lower grade surrounding room and allow the same operator to serve several different functions on the same line without re-gowning, affording greater labor utilization and significantly reducing gowning costs.

In general, access to the aseptic processing area is no longer restricted by sterile gowning and de-gowning procedures, therefore permitting controlled, multiple access routes.

RABS do not offer these advantages as the operators need to wear full aseptic gowns and are largely restricted to a single location/function.

Commentary

Isolators eliminate tight sterile gowns, snug hoods, and face masks, improving operator comfort and saving laundry and gown sterilization costs (each operator can use 4 to 5 gowns per day). Because the surrounding room is of a lower grade, isolator systems reduce gowning requirements and allow the same operator to serve multiple different functions on the same line without regowning.

Cost Comparison: Specifics

  • 4-5 gowns per operator per day → greatly reduced in an isolator environment
  • Operators can perform multiple functions without regowning → higher labor utilization
  • No longer constrained by aseptic gowning/degowning procedures → allows controlled multiple access paths

A RABS does not offer these advantages, because operators must wear full sterile gowns and are usually restricted to a single position/function.

9.4.3 Containment of Hazardous Product

English — Original Content

Isolators and active closed RABS with safe change HEPA filters in the air returns can be particularly useful for processing of chemically/biologically hazardous material when operated as closed systems from an operations and airflow perspective. RABS with air overspill to the room provide better separation than conventional cleanrooms but are not suitable if containment of hazardous materials is required.

Commentary

Isolators, and active closed RABS with safe-change HEPA-filtered return air, are particularly suitable for handling chemically/biologically hazardous materials when operated as closed systems. A RABS that spills air into the room provides better containment than a traditional cleanroom, but is not suitable where hazardous materials must be contained.

Decision Tree for Hazardous Products

  • Non-hazardous product → oRABS, cRABS, or isolator are all possible
  • Hazardous product + air-spillage RABS → not suitable
  • Hazardous product + active closed RABS (HEPA return air + safe-change filters) → feasible (risk assessment required)
  • Hazardous product + isolator → best choice

9.4.4 Setup Time and Facility Start-Up

English — Original Content

Enclosing the process inside an isolator means that some early construction and pre-delivery testing can be performed offsite, prior to installation, while the surrounding environmental room is being constructed. RABS start-up periods are closer to those for conventional cleanrooms, as critical facility environmental systems are required and control systems are less complex than for isolators.

Control systems can be designed integrally and placed into operation with the isolator, potentially shortening facility start-up time, since isolators are independent units. This can be improved when using isolator air handling concepts that operate without interface to the building HVAC and exhaust.

Commentary

Enclosing the process in an isolator means that some of the early construction and pre-delivery testing can be performed off-site before installation, while the surrounding room is being built. The start-up cycle for a RABS is close to that of a traditional cleanroom, because the critical facility environmental systems are required and the control system is simpler than that of an isolator.

Project Schedule Advantages

The stand-alone nature of an isolator brings project schedule advantages:

  • Off-site prefabrication and testing (FAT): most testing can be completed at the equipment supplier
  • Parallel construction: isolator prefabrication and building construction can proceed simultaneously
  • Independent air handling: an isolator air-handling concept that does not need to interface with the building HVAC further shortens start-up time

9.4.5 Capital Costs

English — Original Content

Isolator equipment cost usually is higher than conventional equipment and may offset initial capital cost savings gained by improved space utilization, compared to a conventional facility. RABS and associated processing considerations may be more expensive than conventional cleanrooms but are generally similar to isolators. Isolators may be the most cost-effective option for new construction. Individual cost analyses should be performed for RABS versus isolators. Consideration should be given to operational as well as capital costs, including the facility.

Commentary

Isolator equipment typically costs more than conventional equipment, and the initial capital cost savings from improved space utilization compared with a conventional facility may be offset. A RABS and its associated process considerations may be more expensive than a traditional cleanroom, but are usually similar to an isolator. For a new facility, an isolator may be the most cost-effective option.

Key Points of Cost Analysis

ISPE notes that a separate cost analysis of RABS versus isolators is needed, and that both operating and capital costs should be considered. Key conclusions:

  • Equipment cost: isolator > RABS ≈ conventional equipment
  • Total facility cost: isolator ≈ RABS (the space and air handling saved by the isolator offset the equipment price difference)
  • New facility: an isolator may be the most cost-effective option
  • Long-term operating cost: isolator is clearly lowest (about 75% less)

9.4.6 Operating Costs

English — Original Content

For most applications, the scaled down size of the aseptic process and associated air handling equipment, combined with the lower environmental class of the background room and reduced gowning and environmental monitoring requirements, results in significantly reduced operating costs for isolator systems. Operating costs for RABS designs are comparable to those for traditional cleanrooms, but the additional cost for maintaining and monitoring RABS gloves should also be considered.

Commentary

For most applications, the operating costs of an isolator system are significantly lower, thanks to the smaller size of the aseptic process and its associated air-handling equipment, a lower-grade background room, and reduced gowning and environmental monitoring needs. The operating costs of a RABS design are comparable to those of a traditional cleanroom, but the additional cost of maintaining and monitoring RABS gloves must also be considered.

9.4.7 Maintenance Access

English — Original Content

Maintenance access (from outside the critical environment) is possible with both isolator and RABS designs. It should be considered at the start of the design process. Given the freestanding nature of isolators, access may be superior and gowning requirements minimal.

A suitable glove management program should be established for both isolators and RABS, as gloves may become brittle over time.

Commentary

Both isolator and RABS designs can be maintained from outside the critical environment. This should be considered at the start of the design process. Given the self-contained nature of an isolator, its maintenance access may be superior, with minimal gowning requirements.

Both isolators and RABS should have an appropriate glove management program, because gloves can become brittle over time. Glove integrity testing is a key quality requirement for both systems.

9.4.8 Flexibility of the Equipment

English — Original Content

Isolator flexibility is increased by the reduced footprint of the ISO 5/Grade A area; there is also less facility area to clean between batches.

Various process equipment may be docked into isolator systems, via direct interfaces between the process equipment and isolator system.

Commentary

The flexibility of an isolator is increased by the smaller footprint of the ISO 5/Grade A zone, and less facility area needs to be cleaned between batches. Various process equipment can be docked to the isolator system through a direct interface between the process equipment and the isolator system.

CDMO Flexibility Considerations

For a CDMO, equipment flexibility is critical:

  • The modular docking capability of isolators allows rapid changeover of process equipment
  • A smaller Grade A zone means faster batch-to-batch changeover
  • In multi-product facilities, the enclosed nature of an isolator also helps prevent cross-contamination

9.4.9 Ergonomics

English — Original Content

The position of the glove ports, half-suits, and interfaces with the operator should be considered, as the aseptic method may suffer if the operator is uncomfortable. Efficient layouts should be developed for both isolators and RABS. Typically, an ergonomic mockup study is performed during the design phase of the project to ensure all process steps can be performed properly.

Commentary

The positions of the glove ports, half-suits, and operator interfaces should be carefully considered, because the aseptic technique may be compromised if the operator is uncomfortable. Both isolators and RABS should be developed with an efficient layout.

Ergonomic Mockup Study

An ergonomic mockup study is usually carried out during the project design phase to ensure that all process steps can be performed correctly. This is especially important for a CDMO, where operators must complete all interventions within the constraints of glove ports and half-suits. Poor design leads to:

  • Increased operator fatigue → higher error rate
  • Higher risk of glove/half-suit damage
  • More frequent process interruptions

9.4.10 Airflow within the Enclosure

English — Original Content

Airflow within the enclosure should be unidirectional at the product, container, or closure exposure points wherever product is exposed and according to GMP regulations.

The purpose of the UAF is to protect the product from viable and non-viable particles.

Turbulent flow might be applied in specific cases when required by the process, for example:

  • When the system design can guarantee that no particulates generated during the process can create an out of specification result
  • In quality control applications, such as sterility testing

The airflow can help to achieve faster decontamination cycles, especially to aerate decontamination agents at the end of a cycle. Poor airflow design can result in long decontamination cycles that can impact the productivity of the facility.

The impact of the airflow on the temperature distribution inside the enclosure should also be considered.

Commentary

Airflow within the enclosure should be unidirectional at the points where product, containers, or closures are exposed, wherever product is exposed, as required by GMP regulations. The purpose of UAF is to protect the product from viable and non-viable particles.

Turbulent flow may be used in specific circumstances, for example where the system design ensures that particles generated by the process cannot lead to out-of-limit results, or in QC applications such as sterility testing.

Productivity Impact of Airflow Design

Poor airflow design can lead to:

  • Longer decontamination cycles (especially the aeration/venting phase for the decontaminating agent at the end of the cycle)
  • Uneven temperature distribution inside the enclosure
  • Reduced facility productivity

Good airflow design speeds up decontamination cycles, especially the aeration/venting phase for the decontaminating agent.

9.4.11 Pressure Differential

English — Original Content

In an open RABS, the air overspill to the surroundings generates a dynamic barrier for contamination.

Isolators should be maintained at positive pressure relative to their surroundings in order to prevent ingress of any contamination from the external environment. The differential pressure levels are typically between 15 – 50 Pa to avoid ingress of contamination through transfer openings (such as mouseholes) and other potential openings.

Higher differential pressures provide better separation (air velocity should be ≥ 0.2 m/s according to ISO 14644-4). High differential pressures also generate high airflows between isolator chambers. This should be accounted for when specifying differential pressures, as airflows might compromise the UAF inside the enclosure or have an impact on the process itself (e.g., powder dosing, vial falling).

Reverse flow might be generated at mouseholes with high air velocity. The proper design can be shown with smoke studies.

When handling hazardous materials, a differential pressure concept should be established, using multiple differential pressure zones. The concept needs to ensure that the level of contamination escaping to the surrounding area is below any critical limits. One possibility is to add a higher pressure zone at the mousehole of the critical zone.

If out of specification results occur, a risk assessment should be performed to define necessary actions. Appropriate microbial monitoring results may prevent loss of a batch.

Commentary

In an open RABS, air spillage to the surroundings creates a dynamic contamination barrier.

Isolators should maintain a positive pressure relative to the surrounding environment to prevent the ingress of any contamination from the external environment. The pressure differential is typically between 15 and 50 Pa, to avoid contamination entering through transfer openings (such as mouseholes) and other potential openings.

Multiple Pressure Differential Zone Concept for Hazardous Materials

When handling hazardous materials, a pressure differential concept using multiple pressure zones should be established. One possibility is to add a higher-pressure zone at the mousehole of the critical zone, preventing airflow from this additional zone into the critical zone and avoiding contamination of the surrounding environment.

Trade-Offs in Pressure Differential Design

Per ISO 14644-4, air velocity should be ≥ 0.2 m/s. Proper design can be verified by smoke studies.

oRABS — Rare Door Opening
↓
Conventional Cleanroom — Becoming Unacceptable

Key definitions to remember:

  • oRABS: Doors closed at all times except in rare predefined circumstances for specific interventions
  • cRABS: Remains closed at all times during operation; only acceptable intervention is for machinery setup
  • Isolator: Decontaminated unit meeting ISO 5/Grade A providing uncompromised isolation from surrounding environment

Two primary differences between isolator and RABS:

  1. Decontamination: Isolators use automated, reproducible VHP cycles; RABS typically use manual disinfection
  2. Pressure: Isolators maintain defined pressure differential; RABS use air overspill without defined differential

Decision factors (9.4): Personnel involvement, labor efficiency, hazardous containment, setup time, capital costs, operating costs, maintenance access, flexibility, ergonomics, airflow design, and pressure differential.

Commentary: Key Takeaways

Key Points for CDMO Facility Design Decisions

This chapter is a core reference for CDMO facility design decisions. Key conclusions:

  1. New facility: isolators are strongly recommended; total cost may be similar, but operating cost is about 75% lower and regulatory acceptance is highest
  2. Retrofitting an existing facility: a cRABS is the pragmatic choice; with the doors kept closed, it can approach the separation level of an isolator
  3. Hazardous product handling: isolators are the first choice; active closed RABS (HEPA return air) are the alternative
  4. Traditional cleanrooms: increasingly unacceptable to regulators, and no longer regarded by the industry as the preferred option

Self-Assessment Questions

  1. What is the key difference between oRABS and cRABS in terms of operational interventions?
  2. In what grade of background environment can an isolator operate? What about a RABS?
  3. Why is an air-spillage RABS not suitable for handling hazardous products?
  4. Why can the operating cost of an isolator be about 75% lower than that of a traditional cleanroom? List at least three sources of savings.
  5. With the pressure differential set within the 15-50 Pa range, what are the potential risks of setting a higher pressure differential?

Link to EU Annex 1 (2022)

EU GMP Annex 1 (2022 revision) strongly pushes toward isolators and cRABS. Key provisions include:

  • A clear preference for barrier technology over traditional cleanrooms
  • Strict limits and documentation requirements for door-opening interventions
  • Emphasis on the reproducibility of automated decontamination
  • A requirement for risk-based selection of technology

The content of this chapter is highly consistent with Annex 1 and provides a practical basis for CDMO compliant design.

Chapter 7b: 9b. Barrier & Isolator (9.5–9.10)

ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 3 (3rd Ed.) | p179 – p188

Learning Objectives

  • Understand equipment design principles for isolator and RABS interiors, including ergonomics, transfer systems, and glove systems
  • Master the VHP decontamination cycle development process: cleaning, bio-decontamination, aeration, and validation with biological indicators
  • Apply environmental monitoring strategies specific to barrier systems
  • Evaluate leak rate testing methods and acceptance criteria for isolators
  • Implement preventive maintenance programs for gloves, seals, and HEPA filters
  • Recognize the importance of structured operator training for barrier system operations
9.5 Equipment Design for Inside an Isolator or RABS

Original Text

Equipment should be designed with the ergonomics of operating through glove ports in mind. The use of robotics or manipulators should be part of the design of isolators and RABS. This helps to minimize the potential for microbial contamination, by assuring better protection of the sterile product during aseptic processing. Considerations for equipment design inside an isolator or RABS include:

  • Format parts should be accessible via glove ports and the change should be designed as a one hand operation and tool-less, if possible.
  • Tools, such as forceps, should be used to separate the glove from the process.
  • Critical areas, where product is exposed to the surrounding, should not be covered with any parts or moving equipment, to allow proper UAF over the product.
  • Large components (e.g., stopper bowls) should be perforated to allow the airflow to penetrate as much as possible.
  • Obstructed surfaces should be avoided.
  • The interface of the equipment to the isolator should be gas tight. Penetrations (e.g., shafts and drives) should be sealed.
  • If the equipment requires shaft movements up and down through the base plate, such shafts should be protected by either a specific dynamic air barrier or bellows, to avoid ingress of contamination during operation.
  • Parts that undergo maintenance should be designed to be external to the ISO 5/Grade A environment.
  • The use of automated equipment should be considered, where feasible, to minimize human involvement within the controlled environment.
  • Half-suits may help operators to access equipment. Half-suits should be of good ergonomic design, cleanable, able to be decontaminated, and should undergo integrity testing.

For isolators and RABS that are decontaminated by gassing or fogging using sporicidal agents, the following should be considered for exposed equipment materials:

  • Chemical/corrosion resistance against decontamination agents used
  • No catalytic effect on decontamination agents
  • Potential impact on the decontamination efficiency of the surface structure of materials

The surface structure of materials can have an impact on the decontamination efficiency. Material studies should be performed to show the impact on the D-value of different surface materials. The results should be taken into consideration when validating decontamination efficiency inside an isolator.

The control system for the filling equipment should be configured to permit slow motion movement during decontamination of the isolator, to expose all the equipment surfaces to the decontamination agent.

Ergonomic design should allow access for all surfaces to be cleaned effectively, prior to gaseous surface decontamination. Before a decontamination cycle begins, the isolator should be mechanically clean (and dry, depending on the decontaminating agent). This may necessitate a manual cleaning and a drying step prior to decontamination.

Trainer Analysis

Core Concept: Equipment Design Principles Inside the Isolator

Ergonomics first: Every equipment operation must take into account the constraint of working through glove ports. Operators wear thick gloves with limited finger dexterity, so equipment must be designed as simply as possible; one-handed operation and tool-less format part changeover are the gold standard.

UAF (unidirectional airflow) protection: There must be no obstructions or moving equipment above the critical zone (where product is exposed), so that unidirectional airflow covers the product directly. This is the first line of defense for sterility assurance.

D-value: The time required to reduce the microbial population by 90% (1-log) under specific decontamination conditions. D-values differ by surface material; rough surfaces may make it harder for the decontaminating agent to reach the microorganisms.

Analogy

Imagine cooking in the kitchen while wearing thick ski gloves.
