This appendix provides supplementary engineering design information for sterile manufacturing HVAC systems, giving engineers practical calculation and design references.

Key Positioning

This appendix is a technical supplement to Chapter 5 (the main HVAC chapter), not a stand-alone document. It must be read together with Chapter 5 to fully understand the HVAC design requirements.

Further Reference

For more detailed HVAC engineering design information, refer to the ISPE GPG: HVAC specialist guide [28], which covers HVAC engineering in much greater depth.

11.2 Sources of Particulate Contamination

11.2.1 Internal Sources

Original Content (ISPE)

11.2.1 Internal Sources

Figure 11.1 gives an indication of particulates generated by personnel within a cleanroom.

Figure 11.1: Number of Particles Generated per Second and per Person

Figure 11.1 is but a single data point for the cleanroom designer; there have been numerous studies regarding human shedding and the impacts of proper gowning. The authors recommend reviewing current research and gowning manufacturer's data to establish the particle shedding rate to be used in calculations or modeling.

Development of a robust contamination assumption is a key step in cleanroom design.

To put this generation of particulates into perspective, the following example attempts to quantify the implications of personnel shedding on cleanroom classification.

Figure 11.2 and contamination estimates are provided to illustrate the impact of personnel to airborne contamination levels in cleanroom zones, particularly ISO 5/Grade A unidirectional airflow zones. The model considers the space immediately around an operator as the worst case within a clean zone.

Figure 11.2: Human Particle Generation — Consider the space around an operator as the worst case within a cleanroom.

Teaching Notes

Particle Shedding by Personnel

Particle Generation Rate

Personnel are the largest source of contamination in a cleanroom. The particle generation rate varies enormously with activity level:

  • Motionless: approx. 100,000 particles/minute
  • Head and arm movement: approx. 500,000 particles/minute
  • Walking: approx. 5,000,000 particles/minute
  • Fast walking: approx. 7,500,000-10,000,000 particles/minute

Using Particle Shedding Data

Figure 11.1 is only a single data point. In actual design you should:

  • Refer to multiple sets of study data
  • Take into account test reports from the garment manufacturer
  • Establish robust contamination assumptions as the basis of design
Design particle generation rate = f(number of personnel, activity level, garment type)

Analogy

Think of a person in a cleanroom as a "moving dust source". Standing still, they only leak dust slowly, but once they move it is like shaking a feather duster: the particle count jumps 50-100 times. This is why movements in the aseptic area must be slow and controlled.

Design Focus

Figure 11.2 models the space around the operator as the worst case. This is because particle concentration is highest close to personnel, and it is also the location where monitoring is most likely to exceed limits.

11.2.2 External Sources

Original Content (ISPE)

11.2.2 External Sources

Figure 11.3 provides typical particulate counts for fresh air. It is important that these figures be taken as a range, and that local site conditions of the facility are taken into consideration, in order to optimize the filtration design.

Although a HEPA filter is capable of capturing over 99.97% of particles (both larger and smaller than 0.3 μm), it is GEP to provide the system with pre-filters to capture larger particles representing most of the mass, therefore extending the life of the final HEPA filter.

Figure 11.3: Outdoor Air — Number of Particles

While Figure 11.3 provides an approximation of outdoor contamination levels, actual outdoor particulate levels are tracked by the EPA [64] in many areas. The EPA collects data for Particulate Matters (PM) in two size ranges, PM2.5 and PM10 (particles ≤ 2.5 or 10 μm in size); the most relevant to the cleanroom designer is PM2.5, which can serve as an indication of outdoor 0.5 μm particle concentration.

With proper filtration, the percentage of outside air has little impact on cleanroom performance.

Figure 11.4: Effect of Outdoor Air Percentage of Air Supply on Room Particle Concentration

Teaching Notes

Outside Air Particles and Filtration Strategy

HEPA Filter Efficiency

HEPA capture efficiency ≥ 99.97%  (for 0.3 µm MPPS particles)

Effective particle penetration = 1 - 0.9997 = 0.03%

Example: if outside air = 10,000,000 particles/m³
after the HEPA filter ≤ 3,000 particles/m³

Multi-Stage Filtration Strategy

Good Engineering Practice (GEP) calls for multi-stage filtration:

  • Coarse filter (G4/M5): captures large particles and protects the medium-efficiency filter
  • Medium-efficiency filter (F7/F9): captures fine particles and extends HEPA life
  • HEPA (H13/H14): final filtration, ensuring cleanliness

The coarse filter captures most of the dust mass and significantly extends the service life of the HEPA filter.

Using EPA PM2.5 Data

US EPA PM2.5 data can serve as a reference indicator for the 0.5 µm particle concentration in outside air. In heavily polluted areas (such as industrial zones or next to arterial roads), the number of pre-filtration stages should be increased and the filter replacement interval shortened.

Effect of Outside Air Fraction

The key conclusion of Figure 11.4: with appropriate filtration, the outside air fraction has little effect on cleanroom performance. This means:

  • Design effort should focus on filtration quality, not on reducing outside air
  • An adequate outside air volume remains important for ventilation and pressure differential control
  • The economic benefit of pre-filtration far outweighs the savings from reducing outside air

11.3 HVAC Design Principles

11.3.1 Dilution versus Displacement Designs

Original Content (ISPE)

11.3.1 Dilution versus Displacement Designs

Cleanroom design practice recognizes that environmental conditions equal to ISO 7/Grade B (10,000 particle/ft³) can be achieved, "in operation", by turbulent airflow dilution. Higher standards "in operation", such as ISO 5/Grade A (100 particle/ft³), are achieved by a displacement system.

In a displacement design, "dirty" air is displaced by "cleaner" air (i.e., UAF).

In a dilution design, "dirty" room air is mixed continuously with "clean" air to reduce the particulate load in the room air by turbulent air mixing.

Figure 11.5: Displacement or Dilution System Designs

The type of cleanroom design shown in Figure 11.5 using dilution is known as a "mixed flow" room. Turbulent air is used to maintain background conditions with islands of higher grade environment provided by small displacement systems, e.g., UAF units.

The inherent very high ACRs (hundreds per hour), high capital costs, and operating costs associated with displacement (UAF) cleanrooms are reserved for the highest risk ISO 5/Grade A pharmaceutical aseptic cleanrooms.

However, dilution design (turbulent airflow) also places high demands on HVAC system design, and room layout and operations should be taken into account in addition to providing adequate local UAF to protect critical areas. It is particularly important to identify areas of low air movement that may give rise to pockets of higher particle concentrations (for example, in room corners where impact of particles is low). Critical process operations should not be situated in these areas.

The use of high level return/exhaust is detrimental to acceptable airflow patterns in the room and is discouraged.

Teaching Notes

Core Differences Between the Two Ventilation Strategies

Dilution Ventilation

Principle: clean air is mixed turbulently with dirty room air, lowering the overall particle concentration.

  • Application: ISO 7/Grade B and below
  • Air change rate: typically 20-60 ACH
  • Cost: relatively low
  • Limitation: cannot achieve ISO 5

Displacement Ventilation

Principle: clean air is delivered as unidirectional airflow (UAF), pushing dirty air downward or outward.

  • Application: ISO 5/Grade A critical zones
  • Air change rate: hundreds of changes per hour
  • Cost: high capital and operating cost
  • Advantage: can achieve the highest cleanliness classification

Analogy: Clean Water and Dirty Water

Dilution ventilation: like continuously pouring clean water into a cloudy pool; after stirring and mixing, the whole pool becomes cleaner.

Displacement ventilation: like injecting clean water continuously at one end of the pool and pushing the dirty water out the other end, so the clean zone and the dirty zone stay clearly separated.

Mixed Flow Room

The most common design in practice is the "mixed flow" design: turbulent dilution maintains the background environment (e.g. ISO 7), while unidirectional airflow (UAF) devices at critical locations provide ISO 5 protection.

Warning: Dead Zones

A dilution system must identify areas with insufficient airflow (such as room corners), which can become "dead zones" with high particle concentration. Critical process operations must never be located in these positions.

High-level return grilles are not recommended, because they disrupt the airflow pattern in the room.

Original Content (ISPE)

UAF Hood Contribution to Room ACR

Note that airflow from a HEPA filtered UFH can also dilute room airborne particulates, in the same manner as supply air from the HVAC system. This airflow can increase the effective room air change rate (and speed recovery) and assist dilution.

For new HVAC installations, the minimum required air change rates may be achieved using only the supply HVAC system (discounting the effect of local hoods). It is not necessary for all the room supply airflow to pass through heating or cooling coils. It is only necessary to provide HEPA filtered air of sufficient volume, so local air handlers and hoods with filters may suffice.

Room recovery may be measured with or without UAF hoods operating.

Teaching Notes

Contribution of UAF Hoods to Room ACR

Calculating the Effective Air Change Rate

Effective ACR = HVAC supply ACR + UAF hood ACR contribution

Example:
  Room volume = 100 m³
  HVAC supply = 3,000 m³/hr → 30 ACH
  UAF hood discharge = 1,500 m³/hr → +15 ACH
  Effective ACR = 45 ACH

Design Principles

  • New designs should ensure that the HVAC system alone meets the minimum ACR
  • The UAF hood contribution is treated as an additional safety margin
  • Not all supply air needs to pass through the cooling/heating coils; HEPA filtration alone is sufficient
  • Recovery testing may be performed with the UAF hoods on or off

11.3.2 Dilution System Design

Original Content (ISPE)

11.3.2 Dilution System Design

The four fundamental requirements of a turbulent flow dilution cleanroom are as follows:

  1. Air supplied to the space should be significantly cleaner than the space condition to be maintained.
  2. Extract systems should be designed and located at low level to facilitate effective removal of particulate contamination, otherwise the air change calculation may be based upon the removal of clean air. This can be visualized during smoke testing.
  3. Nearly complete mixing of the clean supply and room air is required to achieve the dilution effect (i.e., adequate dilution efficiency).
  4. Volume of clean air supplied should be sufficient to offset particulate gains in the space and, hence, maintain the "in operation" condition (i.e., adequate dilution volume).

Once airflow volume (such as m³/hour) is determined to achieve adequate dilution, air change rates may be calculated.

FDA guidance [3] suggests that 20 ACH is typically acceptable for ISO 8 cleanrooms. This value, of course, is not absolute from a design point of view. To calculate the actual airflow requirement, the following should be considered:

  • Heat gains within the space
  • Exfiltration and exhaust requirements
  • Particulate gains within the space under worst case conditions to maintain classification
  • Required recovery time (from "in use" to "at rest" conditions)

Calculating air volumes to offset heat gains is a standard HVAC system design issue.

As seen in Section 11.2.1, the number of particles generated within the manufacturing area can be quite considerable, particularly if there are a number of operators or moving equipment and conveyors in the space. Therefore, at a minimum, the supply of clean air from the HVAC system should offset the instantaneous particulate gain.

The requirement of recovery time can either come from a regulatory basis (EU) or may be an operational necessity. If a facility is to operate on a shift basis, a fast recovery time may help optimize the available manufacturing time.

Teaching Notes

Four Basic Requirements of a Dilution System

Importance of Low-Level Returns

If the return is located high up, it may draw away the clean air that has just been supplied while dirty air remains in the work area. A smoke test can make this problem clearly visible.

Four Factors That Determine Airflow

Actual airflow = max(Q_thermal, Q_exhaust, Q_particle, Q_recovery)

Where:
  Q_thermal  = airflow required to offset the heat load
  Q_exhaust  = makeup for leakage and exhaust air
  Q_particle = airflow required to offset particle generation
  Q_recovery = airflow required to meet the recovery time

Take the largest of the four as the design airflow.

FDA Recommendation on ACR for ISO 8

FDA recommends 20 ACH for ISO 8 cleanrooms, but this is not an absolute figure. The actual design must be calculated from the four factors above, and the final ACR may be higher or lower than 20.

Commercial Value of Recovery Time

Recovery time is not only a regulatory requirement (EU GMP calls for 15-20 minutes) but also a key to optimizing capacity. In a plant running shifts, every 5 minutes saved on each recovery gives 30-60 extra minutes of production time per day.

11.4 Calculation of Air Change Rate

11.4.1 Particle Gain versus Air Change Rate

Original Content (ISPE)

11.4.1 Particle Gain versus Air Change Rate

The calculation (first approximation) of supply air volume required to offset particulate gain is very simplistic but provides a good indication of minimum air change rates. It also relies on two major basic assumptions:

  • Perfect mixing of supply and room air
  • Supply air contains, essentially, zero particles of the size used as the basis of calculation (i.e., 0.5 μm)

The simplistic equation for required airflow is related to the rate of particle generation (in particles per time) divided by the desired particle concentration (in particles per unit volume), yielding volume per time.

This form of calculation is useful particularly for rooms within aseptic suites that are small, have a relative high number of people, and only small thermal heat gains to be affected, e.g., corridors, changing rooms.

If the airflow volume to the room and the room's volume are known, air change can be expressed as:

Air Changes/Hour (or ACH) = Airflow Volume/Hour ÷ Room Volume

For example, a 1000 ft³ room served by 400 ft³/minute (or cubic feet per minute (CFM)) of air supply has 24 ACH (400 × 60/1000 = 24). This airflow volume (400 CFM) may be less than is needed to satisfy room cooling requirements.

Teaching Notes

Calculating Airflow to Offset Particle Gain

Basic Formula: Airflow to Offset Particle Gain

       G (particles/time)
Q = ---------------------------
     C_max (particles/volume)

Where:
  Q     = required supply airflow (m³/hr or ft³/min)
  G     = particle generation rate (particles/hr)
  C_max = maximum allowable particle concentration (particles/m³)

Two Basic Assumptions

  1. Perfect mixing: supply air mixes completely and uniformly with room air
  2. Zero particles in supply air: HEPA-filtered supply air contains approximately zero 0.5 µm particles

Perfect mixing cannot be achieved in practice, so this is a "first approximation" that gives a reference value for the minimum ACR.

Basic ACR Formula

ACH = Q / V

Where:
  ACH = air change rate (changes/hour)
  Q   = supply airflow (m³/hr)
  V   = room volume (m³)

Worked Example

Given:
  Room volume = 1,000 ft³
  Supply airflow = 400 CFM

Calculation:
  Q (ft³/hr) = 400 × 60 = 24,000 ft³/hr
  ACH = 24,000 / 1,000 = 24 ACH

Note: this airflow may not be enough to meet
the room cooling requirement; take the larger
of this and the heat load calculation result.

Applicable Scenarios

This particle-offset calculation is particularly suitable for:

  • Small rooms within the aseptic area (corridors, gowning rooms)
  • Areas with relatively high personnel density
  • Locations with a small heat load but significant particle generation

11.4.2 Recovery Period versus Air Change Rates

Original Content (ISPE)

11.4.2 Recovery Period versus Air Change Rates

If a minimum recovery period is required, this factor may be the deciding criterion for the air change rate. Figure 11.6 is a simplified model for calculating the relationship between air change rate and recovery period. Again, this model is based on the two major assumptions given above (good mixing efficiency with clean supply air).

Figure 11.6: Recovery Period versus Air Change Rates

Figure 11.6 shows, by assuming a simple exponential decay, how the recovery period changes greatly with air change rate. For example, a 100-fold recovery, from ISO 7/Grade B to ISO 5/Grade A, with 20 ACH, takes approximately 14 minutes. With 30 ACH, it takes approximately 9 minutes.

In general, it is more important to achieve target recovery than to achieve target air change rate.

Teaching Notes

Calculating Recovery Time

Exponential Decay Model

C(t) = C₀ × e^(-n × t)

Where:
  C(t) = particle concentration at time t
  C₀   = initial particle concentration
  n    = air change rate (ACH)
  t    = time (hours)
  e    = base of natural logarithm ≈ 2.718

Recovery Time Formula

To recover from C₀ to C_target:

         ln(C₀ / C_target)
t_rec = -------------------
              n

Where ln is the natural logarithm

Worked Example: 100-Fold Recovery

Scenario: recovery from ISO 7/Grade B to ISO 5/Grade A
       requires a 100-fold recovery (particle concentration reduced to 1/100)

Calculation:
  ln(100) = 4.605

  At 20 ACH:
  t = 4.605 / 20 = 0.230 hr = 13.8 min ≈ 14 min

  At 30 ACH:
  t = 4.605 / 30 = 0.154 hr = 9.2 min ≈ 9 min

  At 40 ACH:
  t = 4.605 / 40 = 0.115 hr = 6.9 min ≈ 7 min

  At 60 ACH:
  t = 4.605 / 60 = 0.077 hr = 4.6 min ≈ 5 min

Key Principle: Recovery Takes Priority over ACR

Achieving the target recovery time is more important than achieving the target air change rate.

This means:

  • ACR is the means; recovery time is the goal
  • If mixing efficiency is high, a lower ACR can still achieve the target recovery
  • If mixing efficiency is poor, even a high ACR may fail to meet the target

Exercise: Calculating Recovery Time

Scenario: in an ISO 8 cleanroom, particle concentration rises to 10 times the standard during operation. The HVAC system provides 25 ACH.

  1. How long does it take to recover to the standard?
  2. If recovery is required within 5 minutes, what should the minimum ACR be?

11.5 Process Knowledge

Original Content (ISPE)

11.5 Process Knowledge

This should be read in conjunction with Section 5.7.

Typical process and production information, required to assess the risk and impact of the operations on environmental classifications and protection systems (i.e., HVAC and UAF units) follows:

a. Product Flows:

  • At what point the product or product contact surface becomes sterile
  • How the product enters the aseptic manufacturing area
  • At what point the product is exposed to the environment
  • How the product is placed into its final container
  • Whether the product has to be transferred into its final container before it is finally sealed
  • How the product is protected until it is sealed
  • At what point the product is considered sealed in its final container
  • How the product leaves the aseptic manufacturing area

b. Container/Closure Flow:

  • What kind of washing the container/closures need
  • What type of sterilization cycle the container/closures need
  • How pre-sterilized components enter the aseptic manufacturing area
  • How the container/closures requiring sterilization enter the aseptic manufacturing area
  • Whether the container/closures need cooling in the aseptic area
  • How the container/closures are fed into the filling machine
  • How the sterile stopper bowl is protected and where it is located
  • How the container/closures are handled after filling and sealing

c. Operator Intrusion:

  • At what points in the process operators intervene with the product
  • At what points in the process operators intervene with container/closures that contact the product, and the extent, frequency, and type of intervention
  • How the container/closures and product are transferred and handled within the aseptic manufacturing area
  • How many operators are required in the preparation area
  • How many operators are required in the aseptic manufacturing area
  • Where operators stand in the aseptic area under normal operation

d. Equipment:

  • What type of washing equipment is used before the sterilization of container/closures
  • What type of sterilization equipment is used to transfer container/closures into the aseptic area
  • How pre-sterilized equipment enters the aseptic manufacturing area
  • If any accumulation of sterilized product final containers is required
  • Whether any parts of the equipment produce large particulate loads
  • Whether the equipment items that contain exposed sterilized components, or product, need regular operator intervention
  • How equipment is maintained, whether from within the aseptic area or from outside the area

e. General:

  • What other items need to enter the aseptic manufacturing area
  • How other items enter the aseptic area
  • Whether there are any storage requirements for product contact parts (machine parts, filters, etc.) within the aseptic area
  • What the cleaning/disinfection regime is for the area
  • Required hours of operation for the facility
  • Whether doors are interlocked or alarmed to maintain air pressure differential
Teaching Notes

Process Information Required for HVAC Design

Why Is Process Knowledge Essential to HVAC Design?

An HVAC system is not designed in isolation; it must be designed around process requirements. Process knowledge determines:

  • What level of environmental protection is needed
  • Which steps carry the highest contamination risk
  • How many personnel and how many interventions are involved
  • The dynamic air effects of the equipment

Analogy: HVAC Design Is Like Tailoring

HVAC design is like tailoring a suit: you must first know the wearer's build (process requirements), the occasion (type of aseptic operation) and the weather (external environment) before you can design a suitable system. Applying a standard template often leads to over-design or under-design.

Direct Impact of Personnel Interventions on HVAC

The personnel intervention information in 11.5(c) directly affects:

  • Particle generation rate estimation (number of people × activity level)
  • Air change rate calculation (must offset particle generation)
  • UAF protected zone configuration (intervention points need additional protection)
  • Recovery time requirements (speed of recovery after personnel leave)

11.5.1 Sterilizer Types

Original Content (ISPE)

11.5.1 Sterilizer Types

This should be read in conjunction with Section 5.7.1.

The following information assists in the critical integration of tunnel sterilizer equipment with the HVAC systems.

Dynamic equipment, such as integrated depyrogenation tunnels, are complicated items that rely on finely balanced internal airflows to achieve consistent sterilizing conditions. Such equipment may draw air from or discharge air to the room in which it is located, as well as air to the area it serves. These volumes can vary considerably depending upon whether the machine is on or off, and when on, at what temperature it is operating.

These variables make the machine dynamic with respect to the rooms at the in-feed and outflow points. Changes in air volume drawn into the machine under differing operating conditions must be considered fully, and stabilizing measures taken. If not, DPs relative to the aseptic area may be lost or change dramatically, ultimately with a potential for reverse airflow.

Figure 11.7: Typical Radiant Heat Sterilizing Tunnel Airflows

Notes for Figure 11.7:

  • All air volume flow rates are shown in m³/hr.
  • Due to differing air temperatures, the air density varies, and hence volumetric quantities change throughout the machine. (Using the Ideal Gas Law, air in the cooling zone is approximately twice as dense as air in the heating zone.) An important consideration at the qualification stage is where volumetric measurements are taken for the tunnel and under what conditions the measurements are taken.

Traditional high temperature HEPA filters are limited in operation to 250°C (482°F), but many depyrogenation tunnels and ovens operate at much higher temperatures. Once a high temperature HEPA filter has been "burned in" (operated above its temperature rating), the binders in the filter media have started to break down and the filter is often incapable of passing a leak test scan. Alternative means to verify low particle levels in the hot zone are needed. Newer high temperature HEPA filters claim to be capable of higher temperatures and ongoing leak test scans.

Teaching Notes

Depyrogenation Tunnels and HVAC Integration

The Challenge of Dynamic Equipment

The depyrogenation tunnel is one of the most complex integration points in HVAC design, because:

  • The tunnel draws air from the room and also discharges air to the room
  • Airflow varies with operating state and temperature
  • Airflow differs enormously between start-up/shut-down and different temperature conditions

Ideal Gas Law and Density Change

PV = nRT

At constant pressure:
  V ∝ T  (volume is proportional to temperature)

Heating zone (~350°C = 623 K)
Cooling zone (~25°C = 298 K)

Density ratio = 623/298 ≈ 2.09

This means: air density in the cooling zone is
about twice that of the heating zone, so at the same
mass flow rate the volumetric flow rates differ greatly.

Risk of Pressure Differential Reversal

If the dynamic airflow of the tunnel is not adequately considered, the following may result:

  • Pressure differential between the aseptic area and adjacent areas is lost or reversed
  • Reverse airflow is created, carrying contaminated air into the aseptic area
  • A serious GMP compliance issue

Stabilization measures must be designed for every operating state of the tunnel.

Limitations of High-Temperature HEPA Filters

Conventional high-temperature HEPA filters have an upper temperature limit of 250°C, but many depyrogenation tunnels operate well above this. Once a filter has been "burned":

  • The filter media binder begins to decompose
  • The filter cannot pass leak test scanning
  • Alternative methods are needed to verify particle levels in the hot zone

Newer high-temperature HEPA filters are claimed to withstand higher temperatures and support continuous leak testing, but they should be validated carefully.

Key Considerations During Qualification

When measuring volumetric flow on the tunnel, the following must be recorded:

  • Measurement location (heating zone/cooling zone/infeed end/outfeed end)
  • Measurement conditions (on/off, operating temperature)
  • Actual air temperature (affects density and volumetric flow rate)

Section Summary

Summary (English)

Key Takeaways: Appendix 1a (11.1–11.5)

Core Principles

  1. Personnel are the #1 contamination source — particle generation rates vary 50–100x depending on activity level. Robust contamination assumptions are essential for cleanroom design.
  2. External particles are manageable — with proper multi-stage filtration, outdoor air percentage has minimal impact on cleanroom performance.
  3. Two ventilation strategies — dilution (turbulent) for ISO 7 and below; displacement (UAF) for ISO 5/Grade A. Most facilities use a "mixed flow" approach combining both.
  4. Four factors determine airflow — thermal load, exhaust requirements, particle offset, and recovery time. The largest value governs the design.
  5. Recovery time trumps ACR — achieving target recovery is more important than hitting a specific air change number.
  6. Process knowledge drives HVAC design — product flows, container/closure flows, operator intrusions, equipment dynamics, and general operations must all inform the HVAC design.
  7. Dynamic equipment is critical — depyrogenation tunnels create variable air demands that can compromise pressure differentials if not properly stabilized.

  1. What are the two basic assumptions underlying the simplified ACR calculation?
  2. Why is low-level return air preferred over high-level return in dilution cleanrooms?
  3. How does temperature affect volumetric flow rates in a depyrogenation tunnel?
  4. Name the four factors that determine minimum supply airflow volume.
  5. Why does ISPE say "recovery is more important than ACR"?
Summary

Key Points: Appendix 1a (11.1-11.5)

Core Principles

  1. Personnel are the number one source of contamination: the particle generation rate varies 50-100 times with activity level. Establishing robust contamination assumptions is the critical first step in cleanroom design.
  2. External particles can be managed: with appropriate multi-stage filtration, the outside air fraction has very little effect on cleanroom performance.
  3. Two ventilation strategies: dilution ventilation is suitable for ISO 7 and below; displacement ventilation is used for ISO 5/Grade A. Most facilities adopt a mixed flow design.
  4. Four factors determine airflow: heat load, exhaust requirements, particle offset and recovery time; the maximum is the design basis.
  5. Recovery time takes priority over ACR: achieving the target recovery time is more important than achieving a specific air change rate.
  6. Process knowledge drives HVAC design: all five categories of process information (product flow, container flow, personnel interventions, equipment, general items) are indispensable.
  7. Dynamic equipment is critical: the variable air demand of depyrogenation tunnels can upset pressure differentials, so stabilization must be designed in.

Self-Assessment Questions

  1. What are the two basic assumptions behind the simplified ACR calculation?
  2. Why do dilution cleanrooms prefer low-level returns to high-level returns?
  3. How does temperature affect the volumetric flow rate of a depyrogenation tunnel?
  4. What are the four factors that determine the minimum supply airflow?
  5. Why does ISPE say that "recovery is more important than ACR"?
