13.1 Acronyms and Abbreviations

Overview of Abbreviations and Categories

HVAC and Air Handling Terms

  • ACH / ACR — Air changes per hour / air change rate: a core indicator of cleanroom air quality
  • AHU — Air handling unit: the core equipment for cleanroom air treatment
  • ASHRAE — American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers: a primary source of HVAC design standards
  • HEPA — High-efficiency particulate air filter: the key filtration element of a cleanroom
  • HVAC — Heating, ventilation and air conditioning system: a core system in facility design
  • MERV — Minimum efficiency reporting value: a filter efficiency rating
  • UAF / UFH — Unidirectional airflow / unidirectional flow hood (laminar flow hood)
  • ULPA — Ultra-low penetration air filter
  • VAV — Variable air volume system

Barrier Systems and Isolation Technology

  • RABS — Restricted access barrier system: an open design that relies on air overspill for protection
  • RTP — Rapid transfer port: the key interface for transferring materials into and out of an isolator
  • VHP — Vaporized hydrogen peroxide: the preferred method for isolator decontamination
  • BFS — Blow-fill-seal: an advanced aseptic processing technology

Quality and Regulatory Terms

  • cGMP — Current good manufacturing practice
  • CPP / CQA — Critical process parameter / critical quality attribute
  • QbD — Quality by design: the core concept of modern drug development
  • ICH — International Council for Harmonisation: the global body for harmonizing pharmaceutical regulation
  • PIC/S — Pharmaceutical Inspection Co-operation Scheme
  • EM / EMS — Environmental monitoring / environmental monitoring system
  • CFU — Colony-forming unit: the standard unit for microbial counts

Process and Utilities

  • CIP / SIP — Clean-in-place / sterilize-in-place
  • WFI — Water for injection: the highest grade of water in sterile manufacturing
  • TOC — Total organic carbon: a key parameter for water quality monitoring
  • PAT — Process analytical technology
  • FIT — Filter integrity test
  • CCIT — Container closure integrity test

Commonly Confused Abbreviations

  • DOP vs. DEHS vs. PAO — All three are aerosol challenge media used for HEPA filter integrity testing. DOP (dioctyl phthalate) has been replaced by DEHS or PAO because of health concerns, but the industry still commonly calls it the "DOP test"
  • DP — Differential pressure, not Drug Product. In facility design documents, DP almost always means differential pressure
  • RSR — Room-side replaceable (a HEPA filter installation method), not RSF (residual sealing force)
  • CNC vs. UC — CNC (controlled not classified) areas have filtered ventilation, while UC (unclassified) areas are general support areas

13.2 Definitions: A – B

Acceptance Criteria

Measurable terms under which a test result will be considered acceptable.

Action Level

A requirement or condition set by the user, which, when exceeded, requires immediate intervention, including the investigation of cause and corrective action.

Air Change Rate (ACR)

The number of times the total air volume of a defined space is replaced in a given unit of time. This is computed by dividing the total volume of the subject space (in cubic feet) into the total volume of air exhausted from (or supplied to) the space per unit of time.

Airlock

Intermediate room or area that is normally ventilated and used to minimize the transfer of airborne contamination from one area to another. A room or space designed to act as a means of transfer between areas of different air classification or quality.

Alert Point

Used in determining when a parameter is drifting toward the extremes of the operating range.

Ampoule

A heat sealed all glass or all plastic container for sterile, injectable pharmaceutical products.

As-Built (ISO 14644-1)

Condition where the cleanroom or clean zone is complete with all services connected and functioning, but with no production equipment, materials or personnel present.

Aseptic

Free from disease-producing microorganisms. (PDA TR 22)

Aseptic Core

(See: Aseptic Processing Area)

Aseptic Process Simulation

(See: Media Fill)

Aseptic Processing (PDA TR 22)

Handling sterile materials in a controlled environment, in which the air supply, materials, equipment, and personnel are regulated to control microbial and particulate contamination to acceptable levels.

Aseptic Processing Area

Area in which the product is formulated, filled into containers, and sealed. Also known as the aseptic core.

At Rest (ISO 14644-1)

Condition where the cleanroom or clean zone is complete with equipment installed and operating in a manner agreed upon, but with no personnel present.

Autoclave

An apparatus into which moist heat (steam) under pressure is introduced to sterilize or decontaminate materials placed within (e.g., filter assemblies, glassware, etc.).

Automated System

Any facility system or piece of equipment that is PLC or computer controlled.

Background Environment

The environment that surrounds a critical area.

Barrier System

A system of physical partitions that affords ISO 5/Grade A protection by partially separating its interior from the surrounding environment utilizing airflow.

Bidirectional (Traffic)

Traffic pattern such that materials and personnel may enter and leave through an area.

Bioburden

The concentration of microbial matter per unit volume. Microbial matter includes viruses, bacteria, yeast, mold, and parts thereof.

Definitions A – B: Commentary

The Three Cleanroom States (ISO 14644-1)

Understanding the three cleanroom test states is fundamental to facility qualification:

  • As-Built — The facility is complete, services are connected and operating, but there is no production equipment, material or personnel. This is the test state used when accepting the construction work
  • At Rest — Equipment is installed and running, but no operating personnel are present. Used to confirm the capability of the HVAC system
  • In Operation — Normal production state with personnel present and working. This is the test condition for routine environmental monitoring

CDMO perspective: client audits often ask for particle data in all three states, so they must be clearly distinguished and complete records kept.

Terms Related to the Aseptic Core

  • Aseptic — Free from pathogenic microorganisms
  • Aseptic Processing — Handling sterile materials in a controlled environment, controlling air, materials, equipment and personnel to maintain acceptable levels of microbial and particulate contamination
  • Aseptic Processing Area / Aseptic Core — The area where product is compounded, filled and sealed
  • Aseptic Process Simulation — Also known as media fill: replacing the product with culture medium to evaluate the aseptic assurance capability of the process

Alert Point vs. Action Level: A Common Confusion

  • Alert Point — A parameter is drifting toward the extreme of its operating range. When triggered, it calls for attention and trend analysis, but does not necessarily require stopping the line immediately
  • Action Level — When exceeded, immediate intervention is required, including investigating the cause and taking corrective action

Practical reminder: in an environmental monitoring program, the basis for setting Alert and Action limits must be supported by data (usually historical trend data) and cannot be set arbitrarily.

Barrier System

A barrier system uses physical partitions to provide ISO 5/Grade A protection and partially separates its interior from the surrounding environment through airflow.

Key phrase: "partially separating". This is the fundamental difference between RABS and an isolator. RABS relies on air overspill rather than a complete seal.

Other Important A-B Terms

  • Acceptance Criteria — Measurable conditions used to determine whether a test result is acceptable
  • Ampoule — An all-glass or all-plastic heat-sealed container used for sterile injectable drugs
  • Autoclave — Equipment that sterilizes using pressurized moist heat (steam)
  • Background Environment — The environment surrounding a critical zone (for example, an ISO 7/Grade B area surrounding an ISO 5/Grade A area)
  • Bioburden — The concentration of microorganisms per unit volume, including viruses, bacteria, yeasts, molds and their fragments
  • Bidirectional Traffic — A flow pattern in which personnel and materials enter and exit through the same area

Definitions: C

Calibration

A comparison of a measurement standard or instrument of known accuracy to detect, correlate, report, or eliminate by adjustment, any variation in the accuracy of the unknown standard or instrument.

Campaigning

(See: Temporal Separation)

Classified Space

An area with airborne viable and non-viable particle contamination controlled within preset limits. A cleanroom designated by ISO Standard 14644-1 volume units ("in operation") or European Community (EC) Grades A, B, C, D ("at rest" and "in operation"). For pharmaceutical manufacture, a classified space implies ongoing environmental monitoring.

Clean Area

An area where particulate and microbial levels are specified (e.g., a filling room – ISO 7/Grade B).

Cleaning

Action of removing and dissolving or dispersing soiling from a surface. Cleaning may be effected by one or more of the following means: physico-chemical (detergent action); chemical (e.g., sodium hydroxide); biochemical (e.g., enzymes); physical (e.g., shear forces caused by brushing or hosing). Cleaning efficiency is also dependent on the length of time and temperature of application.

Cleanroom (ISO 14644-1)

Room in which the concentration of airborne particles is controlled and which is constructed and used in a manner to minimize the introduction, generation, and retention of particles inside the room, and in which other relevant parameters, e.g., temperature, humidity, and pressure, are controlled as necessary.

Closed Process

A process condition when the product, materials, critical components or container/closure surfaces are contained and separated from the immediate process environment within a closed/sealed process equipment or enclosure.

Colony Forming Unit (CFU)

A measure of the number of bacteria present in the environment or on the surfaces of an aseptic processing room; measured as part of qualification and ongoing monitoring.

Commissioning

The documented process, verifying that equipment and systems are installed according to specifications, placing the equipment and systems into active service, and verifying its proper operation.

Compendial

Official; purported to comply with USP, EP, or JP.

Compounding

The bringing together into a homogenous mix of active ingredients, excipient, and solvent components.

Concurrent Processing

Two or more products being processed at the same time.

Contamination

The undesired introduction of impurities of a chemical or microbiological nature, or of foreign matter, into or onto a raw material, intermediate, or API during production, sampling, packaging or repackaging, storage or transport.

Controlled Not Classified (CNC)

An area without airborne particle limits, but with filtered ventilation.

Critical Area (FDA 2004)

An area designed to maintain sterility of sterile materials. Sterilized product, containers, closures, and equipment may be exposed in critical areas. Also known as critical zone.

Critical Process Parameter (CPP)

A process parameter whose variability has an impact on a critical quality attribute and therefore should be monitored or controlled to ensure the process produces desired quality.

Critical Process Step

For sterile products, this normally is an activity where product or product contact parts are exposed to the surrounding environment.

Critical Quality Attribute (CQA)

A physical, chemical, biological, or microbiological property or characteristic that should be within an appropriate limit, range, or distribution to ensure product quality.

Cross-Contamination

Contamination of a starting material, an intermediate product, or a finished product with another starting material or product during production.

Definitions C: Commentary

Space Classification System: The Most Important Foundation of Facility Design

  • Classified Space — An area in which airborne viable and non-viable particle contamination is controlled within predefined limits, per ISO 14644-1 or EU GMP Annex 1 Grade A/B/C/D. Key point: a classified space means environmental monitoring must be performed continuously
  • Clean Area — An area with specified particulate and microbiological levels (for example, a filling room at ISO 7/Grade B)
  • Cleanroom — ISO 14644-1 definition: a room in which the concentration of airborne particles is controlled, and which is constructed and used in a manner that minimizes the introduction, generation and retention of particles
  • CNC — Controlled Not Classified — No airborne particle limits but with filtered ventilation. Commonly found in transition areas such as the outer side of gowning rooms and corridors

Open Process vs. Closed Process: A Key Distinction

Closed Process: The product, materials or critical components are sealed in closed equipment and isolated from the environment. A closed process can be carried out in a lower-grade environment.

By contrast, an Open Process is defined in a later paragraph: the product is exposed to the environment and must be handled in a correspondingly higher-grade environment.

CDMO operational impact: being able to justify a process as "closed" is an important strategy for lowering facility classification requirements (and therefore operating costs).

The Quality-by-Design Triangle: CPP, CQA, Critical Process Step

  • CQA (Critical Quality Attribute) — A physical, chemical, biological or microbiological property required to ensure product quality
  • CPP (Critical Process Parameter) — A process parameter whose variability affects a CQA and therefore needs to be monitored or controlled
  • Critical Process Step — For a sterile product, usually a step in which the product or product-contact surfaces are exposed to the surrounding environment

The logical chain of the three: identify the CQAs, determine the CPPs that affect the CQAs, find the Critical Process Steps that involve exposure, then design the corresponding facility protection measures.

Other Important C Terms

  • Calibration — Comparing a standard of known accuracy with the instrument under test to eliminate accuracy deviations. Calibration is a foundation of qualification and validation work
  • Commissioning — The documented verification process after equipment and systems are installed. Note: Commissioning is not the same as Qualification, but the two are closely related (see ISPE Vol.5)
  • Compounding — Mixing the active ingredient, excipients and solvent into a homogeneous drug solution
  • Compendial — Conforming to the official standards of the USP (United States Pharmacopeia), EP (European Pharmacopoeia) or JP (Japanese Pharmacopoeia)
  • Cross-Contamination — Contamination between different raw materials or products. CDMO multi-product facilities must pay particular attention to it
  • Concurrent Processing — Processing two or more products at the same time. Requires strict segregation and cross-contamination prevention measures

Definitions: D – F

Decontamination (FDA 2004)

A process that eliminates viable bioburden via use of sporicidal chemical agents.

Depyrogenation

Removal or destruction of endotoxins. (See: Dry Heat Sterilization)

Design Limit

The specified range, or accuracy of a controlled variable, used by the designer to determine the performance requirements of an engineered system.

Differential Pressure (DP)

Between adjoining rooms or zones, measured in Pascals (Pa) (1" wg = 254 Pa).

Disinfection

Removal, destruction, or deactivation of microorganisms on objects or surfaces. (See: Sanitization)

Disposables

Pre-sterilized products, equipment, and packaging designed to be used once (single-use) or a few times, depending on specific circumstances, and discarded.

Documented

The parameter value (or evidence that the value is within control limits) is recorded at some predefined frequency for future reference.

Dry Heat Sterilization

Sterilization utilizing a heating oven or continuous tunnel (gas or electric heated) as opposed to steam sterilization in an autoclave usually used for glassware and metal parts. In depyrogenation, temperatures of 250°C (482°F) result in sterilization and the inactivation of endotoxin present on the surface of the equipment.

Endotoxin

Cell wall debris (lipopolysaccharide) from Gram-negative bacteria. (See: Pyrogen)

Environmental Process Limits

Environmental limits that, if exceeded, may affect product quality adversely.

Excipient

An inactive ingredient used in the formulation of a drug product.

Extractables

Chemical substances that can be removed from polymeric materials using appropriate solvents (e.g., polar and non-polar).

Flow

Architectural terms for material or personnel traffic pattern in the facility.

Formulation

1. (noun) The chemical and physical composition of a drug product. 2. (verb) The act of compounding a drug product.

Functionality

Suitability for the intended purpose.

Definitions D – F: Commentary

Disinfection vs. Sanitization vs. Decontamination: How Do They Differ?

  • Disinfection — Removing, destroying or inactivating microorganisms on objects or surfaces. The broader concept
  • Sanitization — A part of decontamination that reduces viable microorganisms to a defined acceptable level. Usually uses chemical agents or heat
  • Decontamination — Using a sporicidal agent to eliminate viable bioburden. The most thorough, and suited to demanding applications such as isolators

Hierarchy: Decontamination (most stringent) > Disinfection > Sanitization. Which method to choose depends on the target microorganisms and the environmental classification.

Sterilization and Depyrogenation Terms

  • Depyrogenation — Removing or destroying endotoxin. Usually requires dry heat treatment at 250°C
  • Dry Heat Sterilization — Sterilization using a heated oven or continuous tunnel, suitable for glassware and metal parts. 250°C achieves both sterilization and depyrogenation
  • Endotoxin — Cell wall fragments (lipopolysaccharides) of Gram-negative bacteria that can cause a fever response
  • Pyrogen — A substance that can cause a rise in body temperature, usually meaning bacterial endotoxin

Differential Pressure (DP) and Design Limits

  • Differential Pressure — The pressure difference between adjacent rooms or areas, measured in pascals (Pa). 1 inch of water column = 254 Pa. Pressure differential cascades are a key means of maintaining cleanroom classification
  • Design Limit — The range or accuracy of a controlled variable used by designers to determine the performance requirements of engineered systems
  • Environmental Process Limits — Environmental limits which, if exceeded, may adversely affect product quality

Other D-F Terms

  • Disposables — Pre-sterilized single-use products, equipment and packaging materials. Also known as Single-Use Systems (SUS), an important tool for modern CDMOs to reduce the risk of cross-contamination
  • Extractables — Chemicals that can be extracted from polymeric materials using solvents. Together with Leachables, they form the two aspects of E&L studies
  • Excipient — An inactive ingredient in a drug formulation
  • Flow — The traffic pattern of materials or personnel in a facility; an architectural design term
  • Formulation — The chemical and physical composition of a drug (noun); or the act of preparing the drug (verb)

Definitions: G – L

Gowning

Protective garments and the act of donning protective garments.

High Efficiency Particulate Air (HEPA) Filter

A filter with an efficiency in excess of 99.97% for 0.3 µm particles.

Humidifier

A device for adding moisture to room air.

Hydrophilic

Having a strong affinity for water; attracting, dissolving in, or absorbing water; readily absorbing moisture; having strong polar groups that readily interact with water. Its opposite is hydrophobic.

Hysteresis

The difference between the readings obtained when a given value of the measured variable is approached from opposite directions.

In Operation (or In-Use)

Room condition in which processing is being performed with operators present.

In-Process Control (IPC)

Checks performed during production to monitor and, if appropriate, to adjust the process to ensure that the intermediate or API (drug substance) conforms to its specifications and/or other defined quality criteria.

Isolator

A decontaminated unit meeting ISO 5/Grade A conditions that provides uncompromised, continuous, isolation of its interior from the surrounding environment. Isolators can be "open" or "closed".

Leachables

Typically, a subset of extractables; chemical substances that migrate into the drug product from process equipment or its container under normal conditions of use and/or storage.

Local Protection

Measures, such as hoods providing HEPA filtered air or other appropriate devices, procedures, or equipment design features, to protect the product from potential environmental contaminants.

Lyophilizer

A freeze dryer.

Lyophilization

The creation of a solid from a liquid by means of freezing, sublimation, and desorption.

Definitions G – L: Commentary

Isolator vs. RABS vs. Local Protection

These three terms represent three different levels of aseptic protection:

  • Isolator — A decontaminated ISO 5/Grade A unit that provides "uncompromising, continuous" isolation. It can be open or closed. The isolator is the highest level of barrier technology
  • RABS (Restricted Access Barrier System) — Provides an enclosed but not closed environment, using rigid walls and air overspill to separate the interior from the exterior. Offers less protection than an isolator
  • Local Protection — A HEPA-filtered air hood or other suitable device that protects the product from environmental contaminants. The most basic means of protection

Protection level: Isolator > RABS > Local Protection (LP/GAAS).

CDMO decision: an isolator requires higher upfront investment but lowers the background environment requirement (ISO 7 or ISO 8 is sufficient), whereas RABS still needs an ISO 7/Grade B background. The choice should consider product type, batch size and client requirements.

HEPA Filters: The Gatekeepers of the Cleanroom

A high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter has a filtration efficiency of more than 99.97% for 0.3 µm particles.

Key knowledge points:

  • 0.3 µm is the particle size at which a HEPA filter is least efficient (Most Penetrating Particle Size, MPPS)
  • In comparison, an ultra-low penetration air (ULPA) filter is more efficient (99.999% at 0.12 µm) and is used in special, more demanding applications
  • The RSR (Room Side Replaceable) installation method allows filters to be replaced from the cleanroom side, avoiding the contamination risk of the technical interstitial space

Extractables vs. Leachables: The Core Distinction in E&L Studies

  • Extractables — Chemicals extracted from polymeric materials using strong solvents. They represent the "worst-case" potential migrants
  • Leachables — A subset of Extractables. Substances that migrate from equipment or containers into the drug product under normal use/storage conditions

Relationship: Extractables studies come first (screening), followed by Leachables studies (confirmation under actual conditions). A CDMO must perform an E&L assessment for each client product.

Other G-L Terms

  • Gowning — Protective garments and the act of putting them on. The gowning procedure is a core element of personnel contamination control
  • Hydrophilic — Having a strong affinity for water. The opposite is hydrophobic. Affects filter selection and material compatibility
  • Hysteresis — The difference in reading when a measured value is approached from opposite directions. An instrument characteristic that must be considered during calibration
  • Lyophilizer — A freeze dryer. Lyophilization is the process of converting a liquid into a solid through freezing, sublimation and desorption
  • In-Process Control (IPC) — Checks performed during production to monitor and, if necessary, adjust the process so that the product meets its specification

Definitions: M – O

Maintainability

The ease with which maintenance can be performed.

Media Fill

Method used to evaluate the efficacy of an aseptic process by substituting microbiological media for the normally processed product. Also known as Process Simulation Test or Aseptic Process Simulation.

Medical Device

A diagnostic or therapeutic article that does not achieve any of its principal intended purpose through chemical action within or on the body. Such devices include diagnostic test kits, crutches, electrodes, pacemakers, arterial grafts, intraocular lenses, and orthopedic pins or other orthopedic equipment.

Monitoring (ISO 14644-2)

Observations made by measurement in accordance with a defined method and plan to provide evidence of the performance of an installation. This information may be used to detect trends in operational state and to provide process support.

Non-Viable

Opposite of viable, not alive.

Normal Operating Condition

Values of a parameter that are normally observed while a process is operating. The normal operating condition should be within the alert and action limits.

Open Process

A process condition when the product, materials, or container/closure surfaces are exposed to the immediate process environment at a stage/time when such exposure could influence the quality or purity of the product.

Operational ("In Operation") (ISO 14644-1)

Agreed condition where the cleanroom or clean zone is functioning in the specified manner, with equipment operating and with the specified number of personnel present.

Ozone Depleting Substance (ODS)

Chemical substance, usually consisting of some combination of chlorine, fluorine, or bromine plus carbon, such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFC) and hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFC).

Overseal

Capping and crimping.

Definitions M – O: Commentary

Media Fill: A Core Capability Indicator for a CDMO

Media Fill is a method that uses microbiological growth medium in place of product to evaluate the performance of an aseptic process. It is also called a Process Simulation Test or Aseptic Process Simulation.

Why a CDMO must master this term:

  • Media Fill is a regulatory requirement to demonstrate sterility assurance capability
  • Client audits almost always ask about Media Fill frequency, batch size and acceptance criteria
  • EU GMP Annex 1 (2022) sets stricter requirements for Media Fill
  • For details, see PDA TR22 (included in this knowledge base)

Open Process vs. Closed Process: A Side-by-Side View

  • Open Process — The product, materials or container/closure surfaces are exposed to the surrounding environment, and this exposure may affect product quality or purity
  • Closed Process — Defined earlier: the product is isolated from the environment in closed equipment

Facility design impact: the environmental grade requirement for an open process step is usually 1-2 grades higher than for a closed process. For example, open filling requires ISO 5/Grade A, whereas compounding in a closed system can be done at a lower grade.

Monitoring: The Precise Definition in ISO 14644-2

Monitoring is the observation of measurements made according to an established method and plan, to provide evidence of the performance of the facility.

Key elements:

  • There must be a "defined method and plan"
  • The purpose is to provide "evidence of installation performance"
  • It can be used to detect trends in the operating state
  • It carries different regulatory implications from Verification and Validation

Other M-O Terms

  • Maintainability — The ease with which maintenance can be performed. Facility design should consider: is the equipment easy to dismantle for cleaning? Is the HEPA filter easy to replace?
  • Normal Operating Condition — The parameter values typically observed while the process is running, which should lie within the Alert and Action limits
  • Non-Viable — Not living; the opposite of Viable. Environmental monitoring is divided into two types: viable (living particles) and non-viable (non-living particles)
  • Overseal — Capping and crimping, the final step in sealing a vial
  • Ozone-Depleting Substances (ODS) — Chemicals containing chlorofluorocarbons or bromocarbons, whose use is restricted by environmental regulations

Definitions: P – Q

Particle Count

Airborne particle count of both viable (living) organisms and non-viable (inert) particles. Measured in particles per cubic foot (multiply by ~35.3 to obtain particles per cubic meter).

Particulate

Usually a solid particle large enough to be removed by filtration.

Parison

The hollow melted plastic tube extruded from the die head of a blow molding machine. The parison is expanded within the mold by air pressure to form a container.

Permeability

The ability of a body to pass a fluid under pressure.

Physical Separation

The separation of materials, spaces, or operations by means of physical barriers to prevent their mixing or overlap. Also known as Spatial Separation.

Potent

A substance that is active in relatively low doses or concentrations.

Pre-filter (HVAC)

Air filter placed ahead of a more efficient air filter to reduce the loading and extend the life of the higher efficiency filter.

Procedural Separation

The separation of materials, spaces, or operations by means of operational controls to prevent their mixing or overlap.

Process Contact Surface (ASME BPE)

A surface under design operation conditions that is in contact with, or has the potential to be in contact with, raw materials, in-process materials, APIs, clean utilities (e.g., WFI, CIP, pure steam, process gases), or components (e.g., stoppers) and where there is a potential for the surface to affect product safety, quality, identity, strength, or purity.

Process Gases

Gases which can affect product quality.

Process Support Systems

Systems that do not contact product; they are generally engineering systems.

Process Systems

Systems that may contact the drug substance or could otherwise directly impact product quality.

Process Validation

A documented program that provides a high degree of assurance that a specific process will consistently produce a result meeting pre-determined acceptance criteria.

Product Contact Surface

A process contact surface that is in contact with, or has the potential to be in contact with, a product where the product is defined by owner/user.

Pure Steam (USP)

Water that has been heated above 100°C (212°F) and vaporized in a manner that prevents source water entrainment. It contains no added substance. The level of steam saturation or dryness, and the amount of non-condensable gases are to be determined by the pure steam application.

Purified Water

Water for the preparation of medicinal products, other than those that require the use of water which is sterile and/or apyrogenic. Prepared by distillation, by ion exchange, or by any other suitable method.

Pyrogen

An agent capable of inducing an increase in body temperature; usually refers to fever caused by bacterial endotoxins.

Q8, Q9, Q10

ICH guidance documents dealing with pharmaceutical development, quality risk management, and pharmaceutical quality systems, respectively.

Qualification

Action of proving and documenting that equipment or ancillary systems are properly installed, work correctly, and actually lead to the expected results. Qualification is part of validation, but the individual qualification steps alone do not constitute process validation.

Quality Assurance (QA)

The activity of, or group responsible for, ensuring that the facility and systems meet GMP requirements.

Quality by Design (QbD)

A systematic approach to development that begins with predefined objectives and emphasizes product and process understanding based on sound science and Quality Risk Management.

Quality Risk Management

A systematic process for the assessment, control, communication, and review of risks to the quality of the drug (medicinal) product across the product lifecycle.

Definitions P – Q: Commentary

Segregation Strategies: Physical vs. Procedural vs. Temporal Separation

ISPE Vol.3 defines three segregation strategies for preventing cross-contamination:

  • Physical/Spatial Separation — Separating materials, spaces or operations by physical barriers to prevent mixing or overlap. The most reliable method
  • Procedural Separation — Separating materials, spaces or operations by operational controls. Relies on SOP execution
  • Temporal Separation (Campaigning) — Ensuring that two materials are not present in the same space at the same time

Reliability ranking: Physical > Temporal > Procedural. CDMO multi-product facilities usually combine all three strategies.

Surface Classification: Process Contact vs. Product Contact

  • Process Contact Surface — ASME BPE definition: a surface that is in contact, or may come into contact, under design operating conditions, with raw materials, intermediates, API, clean utilities (such as WFI, CIP, pure steam, process gases) or components (such as rubber stoppers)
  • Product Contact Surface — A subset of Process Contact Surface: a surface that is in contact, or may come into contact, with the "product" (as defined by the owner/user)

Why the distinction matters: product contact surfaces have stricter requirements for material, surface roughness and cleaning validation.

Water System Hierarchy: Pure Steam, WFI, Purified Water

  • Pure Steam — Water heated above 100°C and vaporized in a way that prevents entrainment of the source water. Used where the steam comes into contact with product or preparations
  • Water for Injection (WFI) — Purified by distillation or reverse osmosis and meeting the bacterial endotoxin limit (<0.25 EU/ml). The highest water quality requirement in sterile manufacturing
  • Purified Water — Used in the preparation of medicinal products other than those requiring sterile and/or pyrogen-free water

Quality ranking: Pure Steam > WFI > Purified Water. See ISPE Baseline Vol.4 Water & Steam Systems for details.

Quality System: ICH Q8/Q9/Q10 and QbD

  • Q8 — Pharmaceutical Development
  • Q9 — Quality Risk Management
  • Q10 — Pharmaceutical Quality System
  • QbD (Quality by Design) — Starts with predefined objectives and emphasizes product and process understanding based on science and risk management
  • Qualification — The documented act of demonstrating that equipment is correctly installed, operates properly and produces the expected results. Note: Qualification is part of Validation, but individual qualification steps on their own do not constitute process validation

Qualification vs. Validation: A Precise Distinction

Many people use these two terms interchangeably, but the ISPE definitions are very clear:

  • Qualification — Applies to "equipment and ancillary systems": demonstrating that they are installed correctly, operate properly and give the expected results. Includes IQ/OQ/PQ
  • Validation (process validation) — Applies to "processes": providing a high degree of assurance that a specific process will consistently produce results that meet predetermined acceptance criteria

Simple rule of thumb: Qualification confirms "equipment capability", Validation confirms "process capability".

Definitions: R – S

Recovery Time

The time after an upset in a room's HVAC environmental parameters for the room to return to "normal" conditions, such as a return to acceptable humidity levels after a room wash down. This occurs within a certain number of air changes after the upset source is removed, minimally six to ten, depending on the severity of the upset, the quality of the air supply, and the degree of mixing of room air.

Restricted Access Barrier System (RABS)

An aseptic processing system that provides an enclosed, but not closed, environment meeting ISO 5/Grade A conditions utilizing a rigid wall enclosure and air overspill to separate its interior from the surrounding environment.

Relative Humidity (RH)

A measure of the water vapor content of room air, expressed as a percentage.

Risk Assessment

A systematic process of organizing information to support a risk decision to be made within a risk management process. It consists of the identification of hazards and the analysis and evaluation of risks associated with exposure to those hazards.

Sanitization

That part of decontamination that reduces viable microorganisms to a defined acceptance level; normally achieved by using a chemical agent or heat to reduce microbial levels.

Sporicidal Agent

An agent that destroys bacterial and fungal spores.

Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)

Instructions that specify how an activity is to be accomplished.

Sterile

Absence of life; usually refers to absence of viable microorganisms.

Sterilization

The act or process (physical or chemical) that destroys or eliminates all forms of life (e.g., microorganisms); despite being stated as an absolute, the action of sterilization usually is stated in terms of probability.

Sterilizing Filter

A filter that, when challenged with the microorganism Brevundimonas diminuta, at a minimum concentration of 107 organisms per cm2 of filter surface, produces a sterile effluent.

Definitions R – S: Commentary

RABS: The Precise Definition of a Restricted Access Barrier System

RABS: An aseptic processing system that provides an "enclosed, but not closed" environment meeting ISO 5/Grade A conditions, using rigid walls and air overspill to separate the interior from the surrounding environment.

Analysis of the key wording:

  • "enclosed, but not closed" — This is the core difference between RABS and an Isolator. RABS has a physical enclosure but is not airtight
  • "air overspill" — The protection mechanism of RABS: positive-pressure airflow spills out from the interior, preventing outside air from entering
  • "rigid wall enclosure" — Uses rigid walls (not flexible curtains), which is what distinguishes RABS from an ordinary cleanroom

For a detailed comparison, see PDA PtC-12 (RABS topic) and PDA PtC-Isolators (isolator topic) in this knowledge base.

Recovery Time: A Key HVAC Design Metric

Recovery Time: The time required for a room's HVAC environmental parameters to return to normal conditions after a disturbance.

  • At least 6-10 air changes are needed for recovery (depending on the severity of the disturbance, the quality of the supply air and the degree of air mixing)
  • EU GMP Annex 1 requires Grade B areas to recover to the at-rest standard within 15-20 minutes
  • Recovery time testing is a required part of cleanroom qualification

Terms Related to Sterility and Sterilization

  • Sterile — Free of living organisms; usually meaning free of viable microorganisms. Note: although expressed as an absolute concept, in practice it is expressed as a probability
  • Sterilization — A process (physical or chemical) that destroys or eliminates all forms of life. Usually expressed as PNSU (probability of a non-sterile unit), such as 10-6
  • Sterilizing Filter — A filter that produces a sterile effluent when challenged with Brevundimonas diminuta (the minimum challenge organism) at a concentration of at least 107/cm2. See PDA TR26
  • Sporicidal Agent — A chemical agent that can destroy bacterial and fungal spores. Spores are the most resistant form of microorganism
  • Sanitization — A part of decontamination that reduces viable microorganisms to a defined acceptable level

Other R-S Terms

  • Relative Humidity (RH) — The amount of water vapor in room air, expressed as a percentage. One of the HVAC control parameters
  • Risk Assessment — A systematic process of organizing information to support a risk management decision. Includes hazard identification, risk analysis and risk evaluation
  • Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) — A document of instructions specifying how an activity is to be carried out

Definitions: T – W

Temporal Separation

The separation of products or process ingredients such that two materials do not exist in the same space at the same time. Also known as Campaigning.

Terminal Filter

HVAC air filtration located at the entry point of air supply to the room (usually at the ceiling).

Terminal Sterilization

The process applied to product sealed in its final container that transforms a non-sterile product into a sterile one.

Toxic

A substance which is harmful.

Unclassified Area

Support area peripheral to manufacturing (e.g., warehouse, office).

Unidirectional Airflow (UAF) (ISO 14644-4)

Controlled airflow through the entire cross-section of a clean zone, with a steady velocity and approximately parallel streamlines. This type of airflow results in a directed transport of particles from the clean zone.

User Requirements Specification (URS)

Generally, the first in a series of specification documents. It provides a high-level description of the user's expectation of the project scope, with emphasis on product parameters and process performance parameters.

Validation

(See: Process Validation)

Verification

The act of reviewing, inspecting, testing, checking, auditing, or otherwise establishing and documenting whether items, processes, services, or documents conform to specified requirements.

Vial

A final container for a parenteral or diagnostic product. Sealed with a rubber closure and overseal. Generally required to be class I borosilicate glass.

Viable

Living.

Volatility

A measure of how quickly a substance forms vapors at ordinary temperatures. The more volatile the substance is, the faster it evaporates, and the higher the concentrations of vapor (gas) in the air.

Water for Injection (WFI) (USP)

Water purified by distillation or by reverse osmosis, it contains no added substance, and it meets the purity requirements of purified water. Although not intended to be sterile, it meets a test for a limit of bacterial endotoxin (less than 0.25 USP Endotoxin Units/ml).

Definitions T – W: Commentary

Terminal Sterilization vs. Aseptic Processing: The Two Sterility Strategies

  • Terminal Sterilization — The process of converting a non-sterile product, already sealed in its final container, into a sterile product. Usually uses autoclaving or irradiation
  • Aseptic Processing — Handling sterilized materials in a controlled environment, maintaining sterility throughout

Basis for selection: if the product can tolerate terminal sterilization conditions (heat, radiation), terminal sterilization should be preferred because it provides a higher sterility assurance level (SAL 10-6). Many biologics cannot tolerate it and can only use aseptic processing.

CDMO perspective: most CDMO client products are biologics, which require aseptic filling rather than terminal sterilization.

Unidirectional Airflow (UAF): The Core of Cleanroom Aerodynamics

Unidirectional Airflow: Controlled airflow through the entire cross-section of a clean zone with steady velocity and approximately parallel streamlines. This type of airflow directionally carries particles out of the clean zone.

  • ISO 5/Grade A areas must use unidirectional airflow
  • Typical velocity: 0.36-0.54 m/s (per EU GMP Annex 1)
  • The term "laminar flow" is technically imprecise; the formal term should be UAF
  • The terminal filter is installed at the supply air inlet (usually in the ceiling) and is the hardware basis for achieving UAF

Container and Packaging Terms

  • Vial — The final container for injectable or diagnostic products, sealed with a rubber stopper and an aluminum overseal. Type I borosilicate glass is usually required. See PDA TR87 (glass vial handling) and PDA TR43 (classification of container defects)
  • Parison — In the BFS (blow-fill-seal) process, the hollow tube of molten plastic extruded from the die head, which is inflated by air pressure in the mold to form the container

Other T-W Terms

  • Temporal Separation / Campaigning — Ensuring that two materials are not present in the same space at the same time. A common strategy in CDMO multi-product facilities
  • Unclassified Area — A support area outside the manufacturing area (such as a warehouse or office)
  • URS (User Requirements Specification) — The first of the series of specification documents, describing the user's expectations for the project scope, with emphasis on product parameters and process performance parameters
  • Verification — Reviewing, inspecting, testing, checking, auditing or otherwise confirming whether an item conforms to specified requirements
  • WFI (Water for Injection) — Purified by distillation or reverse osmosis; bacterial endotoxin <0.25 EU/ml
  • Volatility — A measure of how quickly a substance forms vapor at ambient temperature; affects the choice of cleaning agents and disinfectants

Appendix 3 of ISPE Baseline Guide Volume 3 provides a comprehensive glossary comprising:

  • 90+ acronyms and abbreviations covering HVAC systems, quality systems, regulatory bodies, barrier technologies, water systems, and process equipment
  • 80+ detailed definitions of technical terms essential for sterile manufacturing facility design, operation, and qualification

  • Quality systems: CPP, CQA, QbD, Qualification, Validation, Risk Assessment
